true_positives.golden_comment: The downsize method is defined twice. The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dead duplicate `downsize` method shadows real definition

Lines 145-147 define `self.downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})`, and lines 149-151 then redefine `self.downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={})`. In Ruby the second definition wins and the first is unreachable. The live signature is `(from, to, dimensions_string, opts)`, but the leftover four-arg definition is misleading to readers and any caller that still passes `width, height` positionally (matching the dead signature) will silently misbehave because Ruby will treat the fourth positional argument as the `opts` hash. The first definition must be deleted.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Client-side upload validation hardcoded to 10MB, ignores site setting

The previous code read the per-type cap from `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']`; it has been replaced with a hardcoded `10 * 1024` (10MB). This is a regression: site administrators who configure `max_image_size_kb` (or `max_attachment_size_kb`) to any value other than 10240 will see inconsistent behavior. Files between the configured limit and 10MB pass the client-side check but are rejected by the server (HTTP 413); files over 10MB are rejected by the client even though the server would accept them when the configured limit is higher. The validation must continue to honor `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Animated GIFs cannot be downsized: gifsicle rejects percentage strings

The controller calls `OptimizedImage.downsize(tempfile.path, tempfile.path, "80%", allow_animation: SiteSetting.allow_animated_thumbnails)`. For `.gif` inputs with `allow_animation: true`, `optimize` dispatches to `downsize_instructions_animated` (lines 137-139), which forwards to `resize_instructions_animated` (lines 115-124). That helper shells out to `gifsicle --resize-fit #{dimensions}`. gifsicle's `--resize-fit` requires pixel dimensions (`WxH`) and does not accept percentage strings like `"80%"`, so the command fails. `convert_with` swallows the failure (it only logs), the return value is ignored by the controller, the file size never decreases, and after 5 iterations the oversized file is uploaded anyway. The downsize path must either pass pixel dimensions, compute an actual size target from `max_image_size_kb`, or use an ImageMagick-only path for the size-reduction loop (the thumbnail for the post can still be done with gifsicle separately).

false_negatives.golden_comment: The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.

false_positives.candidate:
413 error message hardcodes 10MB instead of site limit

The 413 handler previously displayed `Discourse.SiteSettings.max_image_size_kb` in the `file_too_large` i18n message; it now displays a hardcoded `10 * 1024`. When an upload is rejected by the server because it exceeds the configured `max_image_size_kb`, the user sees the wrong limit (e.g. "10240 KB") rather than the actual configured limit, which is confusing and undermines the purpose of the setting.

Loop continues without checking whether downsize succeeded or met the target

After the downsize attempt, the controller neither checks the boolean returned by `OptimizedImage.downsize` nor verifies that `tempfile.size` actually shrank. A failure (e.g. animated GIF, broken image, ImageMagick error) leaves the file at its original size, so the `attempt > 0 && tempfile.size > SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes` guard is satisfied until `attempt` runs out, at which point `Upload.create_for` is called with an oversized file. The user receives no indication that automatic downsizing failed and the resulting upload will be rejected (or worse, stored over the limit) downstream. After the loop, the code must verify `tempfile.size <= SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes` and return an error payload (with an i18n message) when it is not.

New automatic-downsize feature has no tests

The PR adds non-trivial logic (size reduction loop, animated handling, integration with `OptimizedImage.downsize`, the new dimension-string API, and the change to URL download limits) but the changed-files list contains only production source. There are no controller specs verifying that oversized images are actually reduced, that GIFs in `allow_animation` mode are handled, that failures surface as errors, that the loop terminates, or that URL-downloaded files are bounded correctly. At minimum: a spec that an oversized PNG is downsized and accepted; a spec for an oversized animated GIF; a spec for the case where the image cannot be reduced below the limit within 5 attempts; and a spec for the JS-side validation against the site setting.

Synchronous ImageMagick downsize runs on the upload request thread

The downsize loop runs up to five ImageMagick invocations inline in `create_upload`, which is called from `UploadsController#create` either directly (API synchronous path) or via `Scheduler::Defer` (asynchronous path). For images up to 10MB and concurrent uploads, blocking the worker on CPU-bound image processing for many seconds per upload will back up the queue and lengthen upload latency. The resize work should be moved into a dedicated background job (`Jobs.enqueue(:downsize_upload, ...)` or similar) and the controller should merely mark the upload as `pending_optimization`.

URL-downloaded tempfiles are now trusted up to 10MB before validation

`FileHelper.download` is called with `10.megabytes` instead of the previous `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes`. Combined with the new in-process downsize, any user (when `is_api?`) can submit a URL pointing to a 10MB payload, force a full download, and only then attempt downsizing. There is no rate limit, content-type check before download, or guard against repeated large fetches, so this widens the resource-exhaustion surface for the API. The download cap should remain bounded by `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb` (with a configurable, smaller multiple) rather than a hardcoded 10MB, and/or the URL path should require admin privileges.

true_positives.golden_comment: The EmbeddableHost model's before_validation callback calls self.host.sub! to strip http://, https://, and path segments, but if self.host is nil, this raises NoMethodError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
before_validation crashes when host is nil

The `before_validation` callback calls `self.host.sub!(/^https?:\/\//, '')`. If the model is built/saved with `host: nil` (which happens when an admin submits the form with no host, or with a malformed JSON body, or when a malicious POST sends `embeddable_host[host]=`), `nil.sub!` raises `NoMethodError`, bypassing the format validator and surfacing as a 500 error instead of a clean validation failure (422). It should guard with `self.host &&` or use non-mutating assignment.

true_positives.golden_comment: The update and destroy methods in Admin::EmbeddableHostsController do not validate the existence of the EmbeddableHost record retrieved by ID. If EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first returns nil (i.e., the host does not exist), attempting to call methods on the nil object (e.g., save_host or destroy) will result in a NoMethodError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
update/destroy crash when record not found

`update` and `destroy` do `host = EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first` and then call methods on `host` (e.g. `save_host(host)`, `host.destroy`) without checking whether it was found. Any PUT/DELETE with a non-existent or non-numeric id (including requests where the record was concurrently removed) will raise `NoMethodError` on nil and return a 500. Should `return not_found` (or render 404) when the lookup yields nil.

true_positives.golden_comment: The SQL query in the `app/controllers/admin/embeddable_hosts_controller.rb` file uses string interpolation (`'#{h}'`) to insert values, which is vulnerable to SQL injection. It should use parameter binding or proper quoting to prevent this security vulnerability.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
SQL injection in data migration

The migration interpolates the host string read from `site_settings.embeddable_hosts` directly into a raw `execute` SQL statement: `execute "INSERT INTO embeddable_hosts (host, category_id, created_at, updated_at) VALUES ('#{h}', #{category_id}, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP)"`. Hosts come from admin-entered free text. A host value containing an apostrophe (e.g. `foo's.example.com`) or a multi-statement payload (e.g. `evil'); DROP TABLE users; --`) will break the migration or execute arbitrary SQL, since `execute` runs as a single connection.exec (multiple statements allowed). Use a parameterized query or, better, instantiate the model: `EmbeddableHost.create!(host: h, category_id: category_id)`.

false_negatives.golden_comment: record_for_host compares lower(host) = ? but does not normalize the parameter’s case, so mixed‑case referer hosts may fail to match even though comparison intends to be case‑insensitive.

Because this migration inserts embeddable_hosts rows with raw SQL, any existing embeddable_hosts values that include http:// or /https:// or path segments won’t go through the EmbeddableHost model’s normalization, so the new host lookup (which compares only the bare host) may fail for migrated data. Consider ensuring that migrated hosts are normalized to the same format as newly created EmbeddableHost records so existing embedding configurations keep working.

The contents of `category_fabricator.rb` and `embeddable_host_fabricator.rb` have been swapped, resulting in the loss of original category fabricators and potentially causing errors in fabricator usage.

The migration accesses execute(...)[0]['id'] without checking if the query returned any rows, which causes a crash when no embed_category setting exists. This can lead to a broken feature when attempting to edit category/host relationships.

false_positives.candidate:
Controller spec is a stub; create/update/destroy untested

The new `Admin::EmbeddableHostsController` spec only asserts inheritance from `Admin::AdminController`. The real surface area — `create`, `update`, `destroy`, the `save_host` flow, and the nil-record handling — has zero coverage, which is why the bugs above (nil host in `save_host`, nil record in update/destroy) are invisible to CI. At minimum, add specs that exercise create with a valid host, update with an unknown id (expect 404), and destroy with an unknown id.

Dead translation key admin.embedding.edit

The new locale block adds `edit: "edit"` under `admin.embedding`, but no template, component, or JS file references `admin.embedding.edit` (the only edit-related string is `admin.embedding.confirm_delete`). Remove the unused key to keep the locale file aligned with the UI.

EmbeddingController spec is a stub

Same problem: the only assertion is that the class is a subclass of `Admin::AdminController`. There is no coverage for `show`, `update`, the `fetch_embedding` before-filter, or the OpenStruct payload it builds. Add at least one request spec for `GET /admin/customize/embedding` that asserts the returned JSON includes `embeddable_hosts` with the correct shape.

Host regex rejects valid long-TLD domains

`\A[a-z0-9]+([\-\.]{1}[a-z0-9]+)*\.[a-z]{2,5}(:[0-9]{1,5})?(\/.*)?\Z/i` caps the TLD at 5 letters. Legitimate gTLDs longer than 5 chars exist (e.g. `.museum`, `.travel`, `.coop` happens to fit, but `.technology`, `.international`, `.directory` etc. all fail). The format validator should accept TLDs of at least 2 characters, e.g. `\.[a-z]{2,}` (and case-insensitively since `/i` is used).

Imported topic ends up with nil category if record_for_host misses

Previously the imported topic was forced into `SiteSetting.embed_category`; now it is forced into `eh.try(:category_id)`. `record_for_host` returns false when no row matches, so on a race (host deleted between `TopicRetriever.invalid_host?` and `TopicEmbed.import`) the post is created with `category: nil` and falls through `Topic#ensure_topic_has_a_category` to the uncategorized category — bypassing any admin-configured per-host category and silently breaking the embed flow. Either fail loudly (return nil and let the job retry) or fall back to a clearly documented default category rather than silently degrading to uncategorized.

Missing model tests for nil/blank/invalid hosts

The new model spec only exercises three happy paths (`http://`, `https://`, path trimming) and `host_allowed?` lookups. There is no test for `EmbeddableHost.new(host: nil).valid?`, no test for invalid hosts (e.g. `not a host`, `localhost`, long-TLD hosts like `.museum`), no test that an existing record returns its hosts from `record_for_host` case-insensitively, and no test that creating two hosts with the same name is (or isn't) permitted. These would catch the nil-host crash, the TLD regex bug, and duplicate-host data integrity issues.

Serializer duplicates attributes via both macro and methods

`attributes :id, :host, :category_id` is declared at the top of the class, and then each of those three attributes is also defined as an explicit method returning `object.<attr>`. With `ApplicationSerializer` (ActiveModel::Serializer), `attributes` already wires the methods, so the explicit `def id/def host/def catbody_id` definitions are dead code that obscure the contract. Either drop the explicit methods or drop the `attributes` macro; doing both is confusing and risks subtle regressions if the serializer base class changes its convention.

save_host does not guard against missing embeddable_host param

`host.host = params[:embeddable_host][:host]` assumes `params[:embeddable_host]` is always present. A request without the `embeddable_host` key (malformed body, blank form submission, or an attacker-controlled POST) raises `NoMethodError` on nil. Guard with `return render_json_error(...)` or `params.require(:embeddable_host).permit(...)` so the controller responds with a clear 400/422 instead of a 500.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: Potential nil pointer exception - if no TopicUser record exists, tu will be nil and calling methods on it will crash
true_positives.matched_candidate:
NoMethodError crash when the caller has no TopicUser record

Line 105 reads `tu = TopicUser.find_by(user_id: current_user.id, topic_id: params[:topic_id])`. This can legitimately return nil — a user may have been emailed about a topic they never visited, so no `topic_users` row exists. Line 107 then calls `tu.notification_level`, which raises NoMethodError on nil and produces a 500 response for the person clicking the unsubscribe link. Either create the TopicUser row first (via `TopicUser.change`/`TopicUser.track_visit!`) or treat nil as the current regular level before comparing.

true_positives.golden_comment: Typo in property name: 'stopNotificiationsText' should be 'stopNotificationsText' (missing 'n' in 'Notifications')
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Typo `stopNotificiationsText` (double 'i')

The property on line 5 is named `stopNotificiationsText` (`Notificiations` has two i's). The template `app/assets/javascripts/discourse/templates/topic/unsubscribe.hbs` (line 3) references the same misspelled identifier via `{{{stopNotificiationsText}}}`, so the wire-up works, but the misspelling should be corrected to `stopNotificationsText` in both files for clarity.

false_positives.candidate:
No assertion verifies the per-topic unsubscribe URL appears in the email body

The new `unsubscribe_url:` argument is plumbed through to the message builder but the test on lines 178-180 only asserts `match(builder.template_args[:user_preferences_url])`. There is no `expect(message_with_unsubscribe.body).to match('/t/1234/unsubscribe')` (or equivalent) to cover the new `%{unsubscribe_url}` interpolation in `server.en.yml`'s `unsubscribe_link` text. The PR's headline feature (the per-topic link in the email) has no automated coverage as a result.

No controller spec added for the new unsubscribe action

The PR adds a brand-new action (`def unsubscribe`, line 98) but ships no test for it in `spec/controllers/topics_controller_spec.rb` or anywhere else. Coverage is needed for: requires login, only mutates the caller's own TopicUser row, handles a missing TopicUser gracefully, redirects when the slug mismatches, toggles between regular and muted, and rejects the GET state-change concern (or asserts it is replaced by a POST).

No guardian authorization check before mutating state

The action does not call `guardian.ensure_can_see!(@topic_view.topic)` (or any equivalent authorization). Although the TopicUser write is scoped to `current_user.id` so the user can only mutate their own row, the redirect uses `@topic_view.topic.unsubscribe_url` and the action is reachable for any topic the user can fetch. An explicit authorization check consistent with the rest of the controller is missing, and combined with the GET-mutation issue above it widens the surface for both information disclosure and unintended writes.

Unsubscribe action performs writes via GET (CSRF-vulnerable and prefetchable) The new `def unsubscribe` action (lines 98-116) is wired to GET routes (`get "t/:slug/:topic_id/unsubscribe"` and `get "t/:topic_id/unsubscribe"` in config/routes.rb), but it writes to the database by setting `tu.notification_level` and calling `tu.save!` (lines 107-113). Rails' CSRF protection only applies to non-GET requests, so any logged-in Discourse user who loads a third-party page embedding `` (or an iframe) will be silently unsubscribed from that topic. Modern email clients and link-previewers also auto-fetch links, so the unsubscribe can fire the moment the recipient opens the email, before they ever click. The action should either render a confirmation page with a POST form, or use a signed/tokenized link (mirroring the existing `email#unsubscribe` action), so the actual state change happens on a non-GET request.

true_positives.golden_comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Database write hidden inside validator via BlockedEmail.should_block?

EmailValidator.validate_each calls BlockedEmail.should_block?(value), which performs a write (increments match_count, sets last_match_at, calls record.save) as a side effect. Validators must be pure: this implementation causes an extra UPDATE on the blocked_emails table on every User validation. match_count is therefore inflated by every call to user.valid?, every save attempt (and the create flow calls valid? then save, so it is double-counted), admin edits in the console, test suites, and any code that calls .valid? on a User collection. Move the match-counting side effect out of the validator — e.g., call an explicit record_blocked_attempt! from UsersController#create after the block decision — and leave should_block? read-only.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.

false_positives.candidate:
EmailValidator spec only covers the BlockedEmail branch

The spec stubs BlockedEmail.should_block? and never exercises the whitelist/blacklist code paths. It does not verify: (a) an email matching SiteSetting.email_domains_whitelist is accepted, (b) an email not matching the whitelist is rejected with user.email.not_allowed, (c) an email matching SiteSetting.email_domains_blacklist is rejected, (d) the precedence rule (whitelist takes priority over blacklist), or (e) the early-exit when record.errors[attribute] is already populated by an earlier validator. These are real production code paths and need direct coverage.

Lost-update race on match_count / last_match_at

Lines 14–16 do a non-atomic read-modify-write: `record.match_count += 1` mutates the in-memory AR object, then `record.save` writes the row. Two concurrent signups for the same blocked email can both SELECT match_count=N, both compute N+1, and the second save overwrites the first, losing one increment (and possibly a concurrent last_match_at update). Replace this with a single atomic SQL statement, e.g.: `BlockedEmail.where(id: record.id).update_all(['match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ?', Time.zone.now])` so the increment and timestamp happen in one statement that the database serializes.

true_positives.golden_comment: The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Origin check is a fragile substring comparison that mishandles ports

Line 17 validates incoming postMessage events with `if (discourseUrl.indexOf(e.origin) === -1) { return; }`. This requires `e.origin` to be a substring of `discourseUrl`, which is the wrong shape for an origin check. It silently rejects legitimate origins whenever the configured `discourseUrl` and the browser's `e.origin` differ by a port (e.g. `http://example.com` vs `http://example.com:8080`), and conversely accepts attackers whose origin happens to be a prefix of the configured URL. The check should compare parsed origins (e.g. `new URL(discourseUrl).origin === e.origin`) so it handles scheme/host/port correctly.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
X-Frame-Options ALLOWALL is not a recognized value

Line 28 sets `response.headers['X-Frame-Options'] = "ALLOWALL"`. ALLOWALL is not one of the standardized values (DENY, SAMEORIGIN, or the deprecated ALLOW-FROM). Browsers that don't recognize it fall back to treating the header as absent, which means the embed page can be framed by any origin on the web, not just `SiteSetting.embeddable_host`. The intent of the referer check is undermined because the response is now freely embeddable anywhere. The recommended replacement is a `Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors <embeddable_host>` header.

true_positives.golden_comment: The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Stored XSS via URL interpolation in imported_from footer Line 13 interpolates the `url` parameter into HTML without escaping: `contents << "
#{I18n.t('embed.imported_from', link: "#{url}")} "`. The `url` originates from RSS item `link`/`id` (poll_feed.rb) or the Disqus XML import (disqus.thor), and is then persisted as `post.raw` with `cook_method = :raw_html`. Because the cooking pipeline is bypassed for `:raw_html`, the raw HTML is stored verbatim and rendered with `<%= raw post.cooked %>` in app/views/embed/best.html. A URL containing a single quote (e.g. `http://x.com/'>` attribute and injects arbitrary HTML/JS that executes inside the Discourse iframe origin. The XSS is persistent in a post authored by the configured `embed_by_username` (typically a privileged system user), giving the attacker the ability to act as that user against the Discourse API.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
NoMethodError if RSS items lack a content element

Line 35 calls `CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)` without a nil check. RSS and Atom feeds vary: some items expose the body as `description`, `summary`, or `content:encoded`, and `i.content` is nil for items that only have one of the others. When that happens `.scrub` raises NoMethodError, which aborts the entire scheduled poll and prevents any items in the feed (including valid ones already in the loop) from being imported. Guard with `content = i.content && CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)` (and similarly for `i.title`).

false_negatives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.
The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.

An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.

false_positives.candidate:
Race condition between TopicEmbed existence check and create

Lines 15-30 do `TopicEmbed.where(embed_url: url).first` and then, if blank, `TopicEmbed.create!` inside `Topic.transaction`. The check and the create are not atomic: two concurrent `import` calls for the same URL both observe `embed.blank?` and both proceed to `create!`, at which point the second one raises `ActiveRecord::RecordNotUnique` (the migration adds a unique index on `embed_url`). The exception is not rescued, so the post is rolled back but the caller (a job or a controller) sees an error and the user-visible 'Loading...' view loops forever. Use `find_or_create_by` with a rescue, or `TopicEmbed.lock` / an upsert to serialize the create.

Scheduled PollFeed job is executed synchronously inside a per-request job

`perform_retrieve` calls `Jobs::PollFeed.new.execute({})` inline (line 41) before falling through to the HTTP fetch. PollFeed downloads the entire RSS feed and processes every item, so every embed retrieval blocks on a full feed poll. This is also a concurrency hazard: concurrent retrieves can each trigger an independent synchronous poll, the job runs without Sidekiq retry/visibility, and any failure in the feed poll propagates into the per-URL retrieve. The synchronous call should be removed (let the scheduled job do its work independently) or replaced with `Jobs.enqueue(:poll_feed)`.

Stray require_dependency for unused email/sender

Line 1 has `require_dependency 'email/sender'`, but `email/sender` is not referenced anywhere in `Jobs::RetrieveTopic#execute`. It looks like a copy/paste leftover from another job. It forces Rails to load the mailer framework on every RetrieveTopic invocation for no reason; remove it.

TopicEmbed.import mutates the caller's contents argument in place

`import` appends the `imported_from` footer to `contents` via `contents << ...` (line 13). This mutates the caller's string in place. In `poll_feed.rb` the argument is `i.content` from SimpleRSS, and in `import_remote` it is `doc.content` from Readability; both are inputs the caller may still be holding. Beyond being surprising, the mutation also changes the SHA-1 of `contents` (computed on line 16 from the now-augmented string), so the content_sha1 stored in the embed reflects the appended footer rather than the imported article body. Use `contents +` or assign to a local variable.

embed_url column length is too small for many real URLs

Line 6 declares `t.string :embed_url, null: false`, which Rails maps to `varchar(255)` in PostgreSQL. embed_url is the lookup key used both to find the existing embed (TopicEmbed.topic_id_for_embed) and as the unique index target. Real-world embed URLs with tracking query parameters or deep paths routinely exceed 255 characters, so inserts will raise `value too long for type character varying(255)` and the import will be lost. Use `t.text` (and a btree index on a hash, or a length-bounded variant) so longer URLs are not truncated or rejected.

postMessage targetOrigin is set to request.referer, which can be empty

Line 11 passes `<%= request.referer %>` as the `targetOrigin` to `parent.postMessage(...)`. The HTTP Referer header is browser-controlled and frequently null (direct navigation, referrer policies, missing header). When it is nil the rendered output becomes `parent.postMessage(..., '')`, and an empty-string targetOrigin is treated as `*` (any origin) per the HTML5 spec, leaking the iframe height to any parent window. The targetOrigin must be a fixed, server-controlled value such as the configured `SiteSetting.embeddable_host` origin, not the per-request referer.

true_positives.golden_comment: -ms-align-items never existed in any version of IE/Edge; the correct legacy property is -ms-flex-align.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
align-items mixin emits non-existent -ms-align-items property

The `@mixin align-items` block contains `-ms-align-items: $alignment;`. No such CSS property has ever existed; the IE10 prefix for `align-items` is `-ms-flex-align`, which is already emitted on the line above. The `-ms-align-items` declaration is invalid CSS and dead output that should be removed.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Mixing float: left with flexbox causes layout issues. Further this PR removes the float-based right alignment for .d-header .panel, which may cause the login panel in the non-Ember/noscript header (where .panel is nested inside .row and not a flex item) to stack under the title instead of remaining right-aligned.
-webkit-box-ordinal-group and -moz-box-ordinal-group require values starting from 1, not 0. If $val is 0, this will cause incorrect rendering in older browsers, leading to layout issues.

false_positives.candidate:
Button float: right is ignored after flex refactor of .small-action

The `button` rule inside `.small-action` still sets `float: right`, but this PR turns `.small-action` into a flex container via `@include flexbox()` on line 264. Per the CSS spec, floats have no effect on flex items, so the `float: right` is ignored. The button will no longer be pushed to the right edge of `.small-action`; it will instead render in document order immediately after `.small-action-desc`. To preserve the original layout, the button needs a flex-based equivalent (e.g., `margin-left: auto` or a flex `order`/alignment rule), otherwise small-action posts will visibly regress.

order mixin emits non-existent -webkit-order property

The `@mixin order` block contains `-webkit-order: $val;`. There is no `-webkit-order` property in any spec or browser; the relevant WebKit declarations are `-webkit-box-ordinal-group` (already present) or the unprefixed `order` (already present). The `-webkit-order` line is invalid and outputs no-op declarations that should be removed (or replaced with `-webkit-flex-order` only if a real implementation is targeted).

true_positives.golden_comment: The include_website_name method is missing the required ? suffix. Rails serializers expect include_ methods to end with ? for conditional attribute inclusion, a convention followed by other methods in this serializer. Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. Additionally, the '.' << website_host string concatenation should be replaced with '.' + website_host or '.#{website_host}' to avoid mutating string literals, which can lead to issues.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
include_website_name missing trailing question mark

The new inclusion guard is defined as `def include_website_name` (without `?`), but ActiveModel::Serializer looks for a predicate method named `include_#{attr}?` (with the `?`) to decide whether to include an attribute. Every other inclusion guard in this file uses the `?` suffix (e.g. `include_email?`, `include_card_image_badge?`, `include_stats?`, `include_suspend_reason?`, `include_suspended_till?`, `include_user_fields?`, `include_topic_post_count?`). Without the `?` the framework will not recognize this as an inclusion check, so `website_name` will be serialized whenever it is non-nil even when `website` is blank, and the `website.present?` check becomes dead code. This also contradicts the intent expressed in the new spec which expects `website_name` to be absent when there is no website.

false_positives.candidate:
Path used in display drops query string and fragment

`URI(website.to_s).path` returns only the path component; the query string and fragment are discarded. For a URL like `http://example.com/users?section=profile#bio` the displayed name will be `example.com/users`, losing information the user entered. If only the host/path is desired, that is fine, but it should be a deliberate choice; if the full URL minus scheme/userinfo is the goal then `request_uri` minus the scheme/host (or the original string with scheme stripped) would preserve the query/fragment. There is also no handling for non-ASCII/percent-encoded paths or trailing slashes (e.g. `http://example.com/` displays as `example.com/`).

URI(website.to_s) parsed repeatedly in website_name

`website_name` calls `URI(website.to_s)` up to three times (once for `.host`, and up to twice more for `.path` in the branches that append the path). `website` is also re-invoked via the `def website` method each time, which makes another user_profile lookup. This should be parsed once into a local variable (e.g. `uri = URI(website.to_s) rescue nil`) and reused, and `website` should be memoized, to avoid redundant parsing/property lookups on every user serialization.

true_positives.matched_candidate:

true_positives.golden_comment: The route provides the group's ID in params[:id], but the code attempts to read it from params[:group_id], causing the action to fail. This results in a broken feature when trying to access group memberships.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
delete/put "members" are member routes, but controller reads params[:group_id]

`delete "members" => "groups#remove_member"` and `put "members" => "groups#add_members"` are written directly inside the `resources :groups` block (not inside a `collection do`), so Rails treats them as member routes at `/admin/groups/:id/members` and only populates `params[:id]`. However, `Admin::GroupsController#add_members` (line 66) and `#remove_member` (line 85) both call `params.require(:group_id).to_i`, so every real browser request will raise `ActionController::ParameterMissing: param is missing or the value is empty: group_id`. The RSpec tests pass only because the test invocation explicitly passes `group_id:` in the params hash, masking the bug. Fix either by moving the routes into a `collection do` block (so `group_id` is a query param) or by changing the controller to use `params[:id]`.

In the next action, capping the next offset at user_count can produce an empty page (e.g., total equal to limit results in offset == total, showing 2/2 with no members). This can cause confusing UX on the last page.

` anywhere in the file (the only tag inside the loop is the ``). This produces invalid HTML and will cause the browser to insert an implicit `

add_members does not strip whitespace from split usernames

false_negatives.golden_comment: The @loaded_locales instance variable in translate_accelerator.rb is lazily initialized and accessed by multiple concurrent threads without synchronization.

Consider normalizing the input locale (e.g., to a symbol) when checking/loading here to avoid double-loading if the same locale is passed as a String vs Symbol (also applies to other locations in the PR).

false_positives.candidate:
Fallback array is rebuilt on every request and every translation lookup

`FallbackLocaleList#[]` allocates a fresh `[locale, SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym, :en].uniq.compact` array on every call. After this PR, it is invoked once per request by `I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!` and again on every `I18n.t` lookup through the `Fallbacks` backend. The standard `I18n::Locale::Fallbacks` memoises the result per locale. Caching the array (e.g. with a `@cache = {}` keyed by `locale.to_sym`) avoids the per-call allocation and the repeated `SiteSetting.default_locale`/`to_sym` work in the hot path.

FallbackLocaleList inherits from Hash but does not implement the I18n::Locale::Fallbacks contract

The class replaces the standard `I18n::Locale::Fallbacks` (which itself extends Hash) but only overrides `[]` and adds `ensure_loaded!`. The real class also defines `[]=`, `defaults`, and `defaults=`. With this replacement, any caller that does `I18n.fallbacks[locale] = [...]` or reads/writes `I18n.fallbacks.defaults` will silently use Hash defaults — our `[]` always recomputes from `SiteSetting.default_locale`, so any explicitly configured fallbacks are ignored without warning. Iterating `I18n.fallbacks.each` will likewise yield nothing because the underlying hash is empty. Either implement the missing methods (store explicit overrides and consult them before computing) or stop inheriting from Hash so the misleading API surface is removed and behaviour is explicit.

No specs cover the new server-side localization fallback behaviour

The diff adds a non-trivial behaviour change (custom `FallbackLocaleList` with a `[locale, SiteSetting.default_locale, :en]` chain, eager loading via `I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!` from a `before_filter`, and a new `I18n.ensure_loaded!` patch in `translate_accelerator.rb`) but ships without any test files. At minimum there should be specs covering: the fallback order when user_locale, default_locale and `:en` are distinct; that a missing key in the user locale falls back to the default locale and then English; that `set_locale` preloads all three locales so the first `I18n.t` call after a switch does not return a missing translation; and the `uniq`/`compact` behaviour when `default_locale == :en` or `user_locale == default_locale`. Without these, regressions in fallback ordering or loading will not be caught.

SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym raises NoMethodError when default_locale is nil

`FallbackLocaleList#[]` evaluates `SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym` on every call, and `FallbackLocaleList#ensure_loaded!` (called from `ApplicationController#set_locale` on every request) also reaches this expression. If `SiteSetting.default_locale` is nil (e.g. before the site settings row exists, during a fresh install/seed, or in a misconfigured environment), `to_sym` raises NoMethodError and crashes the request. The trailing `.compact` does not guard this case, because the exception is raised before `compact` runs. Use a safe form such as `[locale, SiteSetting.default_locale&.to_sym, :en].compact.uniq` and ensure there is at least one non-nil element.

`compact` silently swallows a nil I18n.locale instead of surfacing the bug

`[locale, SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym, :en].uniq.compact` relies on `compact` to drop a nil `locale`. A nil `I18n.locale` is an upstream problem (e.g. `current_user.effective_locale` returning nil in `ApplicationController#set_locale`) and translations will still resolve via `[default_locale, :en]`, hiding the misconfiguration. Either remove `compact` so the nil propagates as a real error, or replace it with an explicit guard that logs/warns when `locale` is nil and falls back intentionally.

true_positives.golden_comment: The OptimizedCursorPaginator in organization_auditlogs.py attempts to use negative slice offsets on Django querysets, but Django querysets do not support negative slicing and will raise an AssertionError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Negative-offset path is misleadingly documented and unsafe

The `enable_advanced_features and cursor.offset < 0` branch claims in its comments that 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically', that it 'enables access to data beyond normal pagination bounds', and that 'This is safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level'. None of these are true: Django translates `queryset[-N:M]` into `LIMIT (M-N) OFFSET -N`, which PostgreSQL rejects as a non-positive OFFSET, so the request 500s. The framing of 'efficient bidirectional pagination' misrepresents what negative slicing does — it returns the last N rows of the queryset, not an arbitrary position. The 'safe because permissions' justification conflates row-level authorization (which the queryset already enforces) with pagination-boundary integrity; allowing a client to choose a negative offset bypasses the `offset >= 0` invariant that BasePaginator and the rest of the pagination pipeline assume. The whole branch should be removed; it adds no legitimate functionality and exists only behind a parameter that is already gated to superusers, which makes the misleading comments more concerning.

true_positives.golden_comment: get_item_key assumes a numeric key, but the paginator is used with order_by=-datetime in the audit logs endpoint; calling math.floor/ceil on a datetime will raise a TypeError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator crashes with datetime ordering

OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key does `value = getattr(item, self.key)` and then `int(math.floor(value) ... )`. When used with `order_by="-datetime"` (as the new audit-logs endpoint does), `value` is a `datetime` object, and `math.floor(datetime)` raises `TypeError: float argument required, not datetime.datetime`. The existing DateTimePaginator has special handling (`float(value.strftime("%s.%f")) * self.multiplier`) for exactly this reason; OptimizedCursorPaginator is essentially a copy of `Paginator` (numeric-only) and is not a drop-in replacement for DateTimePaginator. The new `?optimized_pagination=true` path on the audit logs endpoint will 500 for any superuser/global-admin caller.

false_negatives.golden_comment: When requests are authenticated with API keys or org auth tokens (which have user_id=None), organization_context.member is None. Line 71 attempts to access organization_context.member.has_global_access without checking if member is None, causing an AttributeError crash when optimized_pagination=true is used, even though the request passed all permission checks with valid org:write scope.
Importing non-existent OptimizedCursorPaginator

false_positives.candidate:
BasePaginator.get_result changes behavior for all subclasses, not just audit logs

The diff replaces `results = list(queryset[offset:stop])` with `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` and `results = list(queryset[start_offset:stop])`. This is a behavior change on a shared base class that affects every paginator inheriting from BasePaginator (DateTimePaginator, Paginator, MergingOffsetPaginator callers, etc.), not just the new OptimizedCursorPaginator. The PR title and description only mention audit logs and contain no mention of this base-class change, so reviewers of the other endpoints will not see it. The accompanying comment ('allow negative offsets to enable efficient bidirectional pagination') is the opposite of what the code does for non-prev cursors — it clamps negative offsets to 0, restricting rather than allowing them. This should either be reverted or split into its own PR with a real justification.

No tests for OptimizedCursorPaginator or BasePaginator change

The PR introduces a new paginator class with non-trivial behavior (enable_advanced_features flag, negative-offset branch, datetime-incompatible get_item_key/value_from_cursor) and modifies BasePaginator.get_result, but adds no tests. There are no tests covering: (1) the optimized audit-logs endpoint path, (2) pagination of datetime-ordered querysets through OptimizedCursorPaginator, (3) the negative-offset branch under enable_advanced_features, (4) the new max(0, offset) clamping in BasePaginator for non-prev cursors. Given that the new code is broken for datetime ordering, the lack of tests is what allowed the regressions to ship.

OptimizedCursorPaginator.value_from_cursor returns raw timestamp instead of datetime

value_from_cursor returns `cursor.value` directly. For datetime-keyed cursors that value is a Unix-timestamp integer produced by DateTimePaginator.get_item_key. The caller (BasePaginator.build_queryset) substitutes it into `WHERE <col> <= %s`, producing a comparison between a `datetime` column and an integer like `... WHERE datetime <= 1699999999000`, which PostgreSQL rejects with `operator does not exist: timestamp without time zone >= integer`. DateTimePaginator converts the integer back to a datetime; OptimizedCursorPaginator does not. Together with the get_item_key issue, the optimized audit-logs path is broken end-to-end.

Query-string flag exposes broken/unsafe paginator path to admins with no test coverage

The new `?optimized_pagination=true` parameter routes the request through OptimizedCursorPaginator for any superuser or any member with global access. As noted above that paginator crashes on datetimes, mishandles cursor values, and contains the unsafe negative-offset branch. Gating behind `is_superuser or has_global_access` does not mitigate these issues; it just limits who sees the 500s. A security-relevant control surface (pagination of the audit log) is being routed through a new, untested code path with multiple bugs and a misleadingly-commented 'advanced' feature.

cursors.py change is comment-only and the comment is misleading

The diff adds two comment lines above `self.offset = int(offset)`. There is no code change — `int(offset)` was already there. The comment ('Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios / This enables efficient reverse pagination from arbitrary positions in large datasets') implies new functionality that was not actually added, and propagates the same misleading framing as the paginator changes. Either remove the comment or implement the documented behavior in a single place with a real test.

true_positives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator's negative-offset branch in get_result() passes cursor.offset directly as start_offset to queryset slicing when enable_advanced_features is True and cursor.offset < 0.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Django ORM does not support negative slicing, so negative offset path always crashes

The new `OptimizedCursorPaginator` branch uses `results = list(queryset[start_offset:stop])` with `start_offset = cursor.offset` when `cursor.offset < 0`. Django's `QuerySet.__getitem__` asserts `k.start >= 0` and raises `AssertionError('Negative indexing is not supported.')` on any slice whose `start` is negative. Therefore the only thing the 'advanced feature' does is make the request raise 500. The accompanying comment 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is false. The audit logs endpoint unconditionally passes `enable_advanced_features=True`, so any client that supplies a cursor with a negative offset (or any code path that constructs one) will crash.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In BasePaginator.get_result(), when cursor.is_prev is True, it sets start_offset = offset without clamping, allowing negative offset values to be passed to queryset slicing.
OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key uses floor/ceil on a datetime key (order_by='-datetime'), causing TypeError.
Accessing .has_global_access on organization_context.member can raise an AttributeError when organization_context is None, particularly for non-superuser non-member users.

false_positives.candidate:
Comments and docstrings lie about safety, optimization, and Django support

Several new comments are misleading: (1) `paginator.py` line 179: 'Performance optimization: ... allow negative offsets to enable efficient bidirectional pagination' — the change actually clamps non-prev offsets to 0, it does not allow them. (2) `paginator.py` line 877: 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' — Django explicitly asserts `k.start >= 0` and raises on negative slicing. (3) `paginator.py` line 879: 'This is safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level' — permissions don't gate which rows an offset selects, only which rows the queryset can see; an admin user can still trigger a crash or expensive scan. (4) `organization_auditlogs.py` lines 68-76 repeat the same false framing about 'optimized paginator for high-performance' navigation. (5) `cursors.py` lines 26-27 add a 'Performance optimization' comment over a line that is byte-identical to the original. These comments will mislead future maintainers about the actual semantics and risks.

Default SUM aggregate in ZUNIONSTORE corrupts `end_timestamp_precise` scores for duplicate payloads

`zunionstore set_key 2 set_key span_key` is invoked with the implicit default `AGGREGATE SUM`. If a member (span payload) ever exists in both `set_key` and `span_key` (which can occur on Kafka retries or any path where the same payload was inserted twice with different timestamps), its score after the union becomes the arithmetic sum of the two timestamps rather than either one. Those scores drive eviction (`zpopmin`) and any downstream ordering; a corrupted score means the wrong spans get evicted and the 'oldest-first' eviction contract is broken. The script should pass an explicit `AGGREGATE MIN` (or `MAX`) to preserve a single timestamp per payload.

No tests for new eviction logic, score semantics, or OptimizedCursorPaginator

The Lua eviction block lines 58-64 (`if span_count > 1000 then zpopmin ...`) and the SUM-aggregate implication of `zunionstore` are entirely untested: no test inserts >1000 spans into a single segment to verify the eviction, no test verifies that `end_timestamp_precise` is preserved through unions, and no test exercises the off-by-one between the Lua cap (1000) and `max_segment_spans` (1001). Likewise `OptimizedCursorPaginator` (paginator.py lines 821-911) has no tests at all - not for the normal path, not for the negative-offset branch, and not for the `enable_advanced_features` flag. Without tests, the silent regressions above (redirect loop reduction, score corruption, Django crash) cannot be caught.

OptimizedCursorPaginator duplicates BasePaginator without any actual optimization

`OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result` is a near-verbatim copy of `BasePaginator.get_result`. The only behavioral difference is the `enable_advanced_features and cursor.offset < 0` branch (which, per the other finding, crashes Django). There is no optimized query path, no streamlined boundary handling, and no measurable performance benefit. The docstring's claims of 'performance optimizations for high-traffic endpoints' and 'Optimized query path for large datasets' are unsubstantiated. A subclass that only adds one (broken) branch is significant duplication that will drift from the base implementation.

Redirect-follow loop limit lowered from 10000 to 1000 silently breaks deep segment trees

The previous code used `for i = 0, 10000 do` and carried a comment explaining that exceeding this limit means segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly. The new code lowers the bound to `for i = 0, 1000 do` without any rationale, so any trace whose redirect chain exceeds 1000 hops will resolve to a `set_span_id` that is not the true root. The subsequent `zunionstore`/`zpopmin` will then operate on the wrong set, leaving the actual root segment orphaned and producing an incomplete or empty flushed segment. This is a silent data-integrity regression for deep traces.

Removed `max_segment_spans` Python guard while Lua hardcodes a different (1000) limit

The old `_load_segment_data` had `if len(payloads[key]) > self.max_segment_spans: ... skip segment`. This guard is deleted, so the only cap on segment size is the new Lua eviction at line 62 (`if span_count > 1000 then redis.call('zpopmin', set_key, span_count - 1000) end`). Two issues: (1) `SpansBuffer.__init__` still accepts and stores `max_segment_bytes`/`max_segment_spans`, so the configurable Python limit is now dead and will diverge from the Lua hardcode if anyone changes the constant. (2) The Lua limit is 1000 but `max_segment_spans` defaults to 1001, so the effective cap silently drops by 1. If the Lua eviction is bypassed (e.g., a Redis upgrade changes `ZUNIONSTORE` cardinality semantics, or a future code path skips the script), there is no Python backstop and segments can grow unbounded.

Rolling deploy will see WRONGTYPE errors until old SET data expires

The new code treats every `span-buf:s:*` and `span-buf:sr:*` key as a sorted set (`zcard`, `zunionstore`, `zpopmin`). The previous version stored these as plain Redis sets (`sunionstore`, `scard`). Any keys written by the old version that are still within their TTL will cause `WRONGTYPE Operation against a key holding the wrong kind of value` errors on the next `EVALSHA` of this script, crashing the consumer's `process_spans` pipeline. There is no migration step in the diff, no versioned key prefix, and no defensive `TYPE` check in the Lua script. This will produce a noisy, multi-TTL-window outage during cutover in any environment with non-empty Redis state.

Span NamedTuple adds a required field in the middle, breaking positional construction

`Span` is a public NamedTuple exported from `sentry.spans.buffer`. The new `end_timestamp_precise: float` is inserted between `payload` and `is_segment_span`, has no default, and shifts `is_segment_span` to the last position. Any caller that constructs `Span(...)` positionally (the 7th argument previously implied `is_segment_span`) will silently mis-bind: a positional `True` becomes the `end_timestamp_precise` value and `is_segment_span` defaults to `False`, causing incorrect is-segment logic downstream. It also breaks unpickling of old `Span` pickles and any external code that mirrors this shape. The field should be added at the end (with a default) or supplied only via keyword to preserve positional compatibility.

`max(0, offset)` silently changes BasePaginator behavior for callers passing negative non-prev offsets

The diff replaces `results = list(queryset[offset:stop])` with `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset`. For non-prev cursors, any negative `cursor.offset` previously propagated to Django (which would raise on negative slicing); now the offset is silently clamped to 0 and the first page is returned as if no cursor were supplied. Any caller that intentionally relied on the old raise-on-bad-cursor semantics (e.g., for validation) will instead get a wrong page returned with no error. The change is presented as a 'performance optimization' rather than a behavior change; if the intent really is to silently coerce, that contract should be explicit and documented.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache key uses non-deterministic hash()

The cache key is built with `hash(tuple(sorted(snuba_params.project_ids)))`. CPython randomizes the hash seed for tuples/strings per-process (PYTHONHASHSEED), so the same project set produces a different key in every web/worker process. The 60s cache therefore never shares data across processes, defeating the stated 'performance optimization during traffic spikes'. The PR description claims this cache avoids 'expensive repeated option lookups during high-traffic periods', but with N workers you still get N independent option lookups. Replace `hash(...)` with a deterministic digest (e.g. `hashlib.md5(str(tuple(sorted(project_ids))).encode()).hexdigest()`) or just stringify the tuple.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling(), the check `if client_sample_rate:` treats 0.0 as falsy, so a sample_rate of 0.0 is silently skipped and never set on normalized_data.

The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.

false_positives.candidate:
Comments around upsampling block are misleading

The newly added comments in `_get_event_stats` make claims that don't match the code: 'Early upsampling eligibility check for performance optimization ... This cached result ensures consistent behavior across query execution' (it isn't actually cached at the call site, and the helper's cache is broken by the hash() issue), and 'Apply upsampling transformation just before query execution ... This late transformation ensures we use the most current schema assumptions' (schema does not change at runtime, and the transformation isn't late in any meaningful sense — it runs before every branch). These comments will mislead future readers about what the code does and why; either justify the comments accurately or remove them.

Error-sampling context silently overwrites an existing sample_rate

`_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling` runs unconditionally during `store_event` and writes `normalized_data['sample_rate'] = float(client_sample_rate)` whenever `contexts.error_sampling.client_sample_rate` is truthy, without checking whether `sample_rate` was already set. Any pre-existing `sample_rate` (e.g. set by ingest earlier in the pipeline, by a different sampling decision, or by a test fixture) is silently overwritten. The bare `except Exception` blocks also swallow any unexpected type of `contexts` value, hiding malformed payloads. The function should at most set `sample_rate` if it is currently missing, and should not catch arbitrary `Exception`.

Repeated lazy imports inside hot helper

`_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` performs `from sentry.snuba import discover, errors` and later `from sentry.snuba import transactions` inside the function body on every call. Even with module caching this is avoidable per-call dict lookups, and it is invoked from the timeseries hot path of every organization events stats request. If the lazy style is only to dodge a circular import, move both imports to module scope in one statement and resolve the cycle properly.

Upsampling check runs unconditionally on every stats request

`is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(...)` is invoked unconditionally on every `_get_event_stats` call, including for non-error datasets and for projects that are not allowlisted (the common case). Even with a hot cache this still does a cache key construction (with the broken `hash()`), a cache get, and a dataset/parse check per call. Move the check inside the branches where `final_columns` is actually used, or short-circuit cheaply on dataset (transactions/spans/metrics) before touching the cache.

invalidate_upsampling_cache is dead code

`invalidate_upsampling_cache` is defined and documented as 'This should be called when the allowlist configuration changes to ensure cache consistency', but nothing in the PR (or elsewhere in the diff) ever calls it. With the 60s TTL, removing a project from `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist` will continue to return stale `is_eligible=True` results for up to a minute, meaning queries against that org/project will keep being rewritten to `upsampled_count()` even after the operator un-allowlisted it. Either wire up invalidation on option writes, or remove the unused helper to avoid implying a guarantee that isn't there.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoded empty data passed to TableWidgetVisualization causes it to always render an empty table instead of displaying actual results when the feature flag is enabled.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TableWidgetVisualization receives hardcoded empty data

true_positives.golden_comment: Analytics events are recorded before the feature flag check, resulting in analytics being logged for all requests, including those that return 404 due to the feature being disabled. This can lead to misleading analytics data.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Analytics recorded before feature flag check

The endpoint records the `preprod_artifact.api.assemble` analytics event before checking whether the `organizations:preprod-artifact-assemble` feature flag is enabled for the organization. Denied requests (where the feature flag is off) still record analytics, which will inflate the event count and any dashboards/metrics derived from it. The analytics event key tracked in the replay breadcrumb is renamed from `replay.view_html` to `replay.view-html`. true_positives.golden_comment: The exported function TwoFactor handles backup codes and is in BackupCode.tsx. Inconsistent naming.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
BackupCode component is exported as default function TwoFactor

The file apps/web/components/auth/BackupCode.tsx declares `export default function TwoFactor(...)`. Two other components in this PR are also named TwoFactor (apps/web/components/auth/TwoFactor.tsx and EnableTwoFactorModal imports it). The mismatch causes confusion in stack traces / DevTools and creates a real collision risk if anyone re-exports these modules together. Rename the function to BackupCode (or BackupCodeInput) to match the file name and the other new component.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because backupCodes are decrypted and mutated in memory before being written back, two concurrent login requests using the same backupCode could both pass this check and update, so a single backup code may effectively be accepted more than once if used concurrently, weakening the intended one-time-use semantics.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Backup code is not atomically consumed; concurrent logins can reuse a code

The backup code is looked up with backupCodes.indexOf(...) and then nulled out in a separate prisma.user.update. Between the read and the write, two concurrent signIn attempts (e.g. two browser tabs) can both observe the same code at the same index, both null it, and both be authenticated, allowing a single-use backup code to be used more than once. The same race exists in disable.ts (the indexOf succeeds but the consumed code is only later wiped by the unconditional backupCodes: null in the final update). Use a conditional update (e.g. updateMany where the code is still present, or store used codes with a unique marker) so consumption is atomic.

true_positives.golden_comment: Object URL for backup codes is not revoked on component unmount, leading to a potential memory leak. This can cause increased memory usage over time, especially if the component is mounted and unmounted frequently.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Object URL for backup codes download is never revoked on close

backupCodesUrl is created with URL.createObjectURL and only revoked when handleSetup is invoked again. There is no cleanup on modal close (onOpenChange / Cancel button), no useEffect cleanup, and resetState() does not reset backupCodesUrl. Each successful setup leaks a Blob and its object URL (containing the plaintext backup codes) for the lifetime of the page. Add a useEffect cleanup that calls URL.revokeObjectURL(backupCodesUrl) on unmount/close, and revoke inside resetState.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Error message mentions 'backup code login' but this is a disable endpoint, not login

Backup code validation is case-sensitive due to the use of indexOf(). This causes validation to fail if a user enters uppercase hex characters, as backup codes should be case-insensitive for a better user experience.

false_positives.candidate:
Continue button at QR step has misleading type=submit and onClick

The QR step Continue button is declared `type="submit"` and `onClick={() => setStep(SetupStep.EnterTotpCode)}`. It lives inside <Form handleSubmit={handleEnable} ...>, so clicking it both fires handleEnable (which sends a request to /api/auth/two-factor/totp/enable with whatever stale totpCode is still in the form, or undefined) and changes the step. The visible behavior appears to work only because the enable endpoint errors out when 2FA is already enabled, but this is an unintended API call. Use type="button" here so clicking it does not submit the form.

Exhausted backup codes surface as IncorrectBackupCode, not MissingBackupCodes

After a user has consumed all backup codes, the stored JSON array consists entirely of nulls. backupCodes.indexOf(...) still returns -1, so the user is told IncorrectBackupCode rather than MissingBackupCodes (and they cannot tell that they have no codes left). Detect the all-null case (e.g. !backupCodes.some(Boolean)) and throw ErrorCode.MissingBackupCodes before the indexOf check.

JSON.parse of decrypted backup codes has no error handling

JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(user.backupCodes, process.env.CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY)) will throw if the stored ciphertext is corrupted, the encryption key is rotated, or the data shape is unexpected. An uncaught throw here aborts the entire authorize() callback and surfaces as an InternalServerError, locking the user out. Wrap the decrypt + JSON.parse in try/catch and convert failures into a clean ErrorCode (e.g. MissingBackupCodes or InternalServerError) so authentication degrades gracefully.

JSON.parse of decrypted backup codes has no error handling

Same issue as in next-auth-options.ts: JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...)) is unguarded. A corrupt/rotated backupCodes blob will crash the disable endpoint with an uncaught exception (500), preventing the user from disabling 2FA. Catch the error and return a typed error (e.g. MissingBackupCodes) instead.

No end-to-end coverage for backup code login or backup code disable

The PR introduces an entire authentication path (login with backup code, disable 2FA with backup code, marking codes as used) that has no e2e coverage. The TODO at line 12 acknowledges this, but the new code paths are exactly where regressions are most dangerous (auth bypass, accidental single-use violation). Add at minimum: (1) login with a backup code (and confirm the code is consumed), (2) login with a previously-used backup code fails with IncorrectBackupCode, (3) disabling 2FA via the 'Lost access' button with a backup code.

Stale internal state shown after closing the modal with the X button

Dialog's onOpenChange (the X / overlay close path) does not call resetState(). The component remains mounted with the previous step, dataUri, secret and backupCodes. Reopening the modal after closing it via X can show an old QR code, old TOTP secret and the previously generated backup codes. resetState should be invoked from onOpenChange (or equivalent), and the displayed data should be cleared when the modal is dismissed without completion.

backupCodes state is implicitly typed as never[]

`const [backupCodes, setBackupCodes] = useState([]);` infers never[], so .map(formatBackupCode) on body.backupCodes only compiles because body.backupCodes is any. There is no compile-time guarantee that the state actually contains strings, and the explicit type <string[]>([]) (or the inferred type from body.backupCodes) would catch a future API shape change.

formatBackupCode referenced before it is defined

handleSetup uses formatBackupCode at line 95, but formatBackupCode is declared as a const at line 163, below the handler. This works only because handleSetup is invoked asynchronously after render. It is fragile (moving handleSetup to a hook or memoizing it would TDZ-crash) and makes the file hard to read. Move the formatBackupCode declaration above its first use.

twoFactorLostAccess not reset when disable modal is closed via X

The twoFactorLostAccess state is only reset after a successful disable. Closing the dialog with the X button (onOpenChange) does not reset it, so the next time the modal is opened the BackupCode input is shown instead of the TOTP input. Reset twoFactorLostAccess (and clear the form/values) when the dialog is closed without a successful submit.
