The function must return a normalized token object (parsed from the sync JSON plus token shape) and propagate provider-specific data on the non-sync branch, or each integration needs its own dispatcher.

false_negatives.golden_comment: parseRefreshTokenResponse returns a Zod safeParse result ({ success, data, error }), not the credential key object. Persisting that as key stores the wrapper instead of the token payload; we should store the parsed data or use schema parse.

The `refreshOAuthTokens` function is passed `credentialId` instead of `userId`, which breaks the credential sync functionality by causing incorrect user lookups. This issue can lead to failures in syncing user credentials, impacting user experience.

The Salesforce integration checks `response.statusText` instead of `response.ok` when handling OAuth token refresh responses. This can lead to unreliable behavior, as a successful response may not be correctly identified, resulting in the use of stale credentials and potential authentication failures.

The `jsforce.Connection` is created using stale `credentialKey.access_token` and `credentialKey.instance_url` after a token refresh, which can lead to authentication failures and incorrect data access. Ensure that the connection is established using the refreshed token values instead.

The `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse` function can throw on invalid payloads, resulting in 500 Internal Server Errors instead of the expected 400 Bad Request responses. This can lead to confusion for clients and hinder proper error handling.

false_positives.candidate:
Decryption failure and bad payload not handled

`symmetricDecrypt` will throw if the encrypted blob is malformed or the key is wrong, and `JSON.parse` will throw if the decrypted plaintext is not valid JSON. Neither is caught, so the handler returns a 500 with the stack trace leaking to the caller instead of a 4xx with a clear message. Also, after a successful decrypt+parse, `keys` is `unknown` (since it is `JSON.parse(...)`); it is written to `credential.key` without any schema check (no zod, no type guard), so any JSON object - including something that isn't a valid OAuth token shape - will be persisted. At minimum the handler should validate `keys` is an object with the fields the downstream app actually expects, and wrap the decrypt+parse in try/catch returning 400.

SalesforceCalendarService.refreshes access token on every getClient() call

Lines 75-100 unconditionally POST to Salesforce's token endpoint inside `getClient`, then overwrite `credential.key` in the database, even when the existing access token is still valid. `getClient` is called once per service instance (line 57), so a service that is held across many operations will refresh exactly once per construction - but more importantly, every API operation that constructs a new `SalesforceCalendarService` (which is the typical usage pattern in this repo, see e.g. how other CalendarService implementations are instantiated per-call) hits Salesforce for a token refresh whether or not refresh is required. This both wastes a refresh_token use (Salesforce will eventually return `invalid_grant` once the refresh token rotates out) and can trip rate limits. Refresh should be gated on token expiry, mirroring the other integrations (`isExpired` checks before calling refresh).

Sync endpoint HTTP errors are not detected; raw Response is returned

The function returns the `Response` object unconditionally (line 15) without checking `response.ok`. If the self-hoster's sync endpoint returns 401/403/429/500, the raw error response body is handed to downstream code as if it were a successful token response, then parsed with the (already broken) `minimumTokenResponseSchema` and discarded, leaving the credential unchanged on disk with no error logged. The caller has no way to know refresh failed. A `if (!response.ok) throw new Error(...)` is required, and the function should surface token refresh failures.

Webhook endpoint allows writing credentials for arbitrary user IDs with a single shared secret

The endpoint authenticates the caller only with a single shared header secret (lines 24-29). Once that secret is known (it is shared by every Cal.com deployment enabling this feature and there is no per-tenant signing), any caller can POST `{userId: <int>, appSlug, keys}` and overwrite that user's credentials. `userId` is a sequential integer from the users table, so attackers can iterate. There is no per-user HMAC, no per-deployment signing key bound to the user, and no proof that the caller is authorized to manage that specific user's third-party account. Concretely this lets one compromised self-host instance push attacker-controlled OAuth tokens (which can include an `access_token` issued to the attacker's account on Google/Microsoft/Zoom/etc.) into any user's Cal.com account, which the app will then use to read/insert calendar events and create meetings on behalf of the victim. Also note the header comparison `req.headers[name] !== secret` is non-constant-time and will throw/always-fail if the header is sent twice (Next.js parses duplicate headers as an array).

fetch() to sync endpoint has no Content-Type header and no auth

The body is `new URLSearchParams({...})` but no `Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded` header is set, so the receiving server is not guaranteed to parse the body as a form (it will see an empty body in many frameworks, and `calcomUserId`/`appSlug` will be undefined server-side, making every refresh call effectively a no-op). Additionally, there is no authentication on this outbound call: the sync endpoint cannot distinguish a request coming from this Cal.com instance from any other HTTP client that knows the URL. The endpoint should at minimum require a shared secret / signature header that the self-hoster validates.

findFirst + create/update on credentials is not atomic (race condition / duplicate rows)

Lines 62-90 do a `findFirst` followed by either `update` or `create` on `prisma.credential` based on whether a row was found. There is no transaction or unique constraint check; if two webhook calls for the same (userId, appId) race (e.g. the self-hoster retries, or a user reinstalls while a webhook is in flight), both can observe no existing row and both `create`, producing two credential rows for the same user/app. Subsequent refresh/lookup code in this repo commonly uses `findFirst` for these (e.g. office365video callback line 79 does `findMany` and deletes duplicates by hand, but the webhook path does not), which means the duplicate row will be silently picked up by whichever path queries first and the other becomes dead weight (or causes the wrong row to be updated). The (userId, appId) pair needs a unique constraint or the write needs to use an upsert/transaction.

true_positives.golden_comment: The logic for checking team admin/owner permissions is incorrect. This condition uses AND (&&) which requires both isTeamAdmin AND isTeamOwner to be true, but it should use OR (||) since a user needs to be either an admin OR an owner to have permission.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
isTeamAdminOrOwner uses AND instead of OR, blocking team admins

Lines 46-48 compute the team permission with `await isTeamAdmin(...) && await isTeamOwner(...)`. The variable name and intent ('admin OR owner') clearly require `||`. As written, a user must be both an admin AND an owner of the team to pass the check; ordinary team admins (and owners who are not also admins) are rejected with FORBIDDEN even though the route is meant to be available to them. This silently breaks the feature for almost all legitimate team users.

true_positives.golden_comment: The sendAddGuestsEmails function in email-manager.ts passes the full calendarEvent.attendees array when determining which attendees receive AttendeeScheduledEmail vs AttendeeAddGuestsEmail, but checks if newGuests.includes(attendee.email) where newGuests is the input guests array.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Emails are sent for the full original `guests` input, including duplicates and rejected entries

`sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)` passes the raw request `guests` (not `uniqueGuests`) to determine who is a 'new' guest. If the input contains an existing attendee's email (e.g., user re-submits), that attendee will be classified as 'new' and receive the 'Scheduled' email instead of the 'Guests Added' email. If duplicates appear in the input, the membership check still works on `attendees.map(...)`, so the wrong existing attendee could get the wrong template. Pass the deduped `uniqueGuests` (or a normalized Set of new emails) into the email function.

true_positives.golden_comment: uniqueGuests filters out existing attendees and blacklisted emails but does not deduplicate duplicates within the input; createMany can insert duplicate attendee rows if the client submits repeated emails.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`uniqueGuests` is not actually deduplicated and ignores case

The filter on lines 74-78 only removes entries that match an existing attendee's email (case-sensitive `===`) and any entry in the blacklist (lowercased). It does NOT deduplicate the input, so submitting `['a@x.com','a@x.com']` produces two `createMany` rows with identical emails (unless a unique constraint saves it, which is not visible here). It also treats email comparison as case-sensitive even though emails are case-insensitive, so `Guest@x.com` would not be detected as already present if the existing attendee is `guest@x.com`. The misleading name plus the lack of de-duplication can produce duplicate attendee rows and double calendar invites.

true_positives.golden_comment: Starting with an array containing an empty string may cause validation issues. Consider starting with an empty array [] and handling the empty state in the MultiEmail component instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Validation only shows generic 'must be unique and valid' for any failure

The local schema is `z.array(z.string().email()).refine(unique)`. Initial state is `[""]`, so the very first click of 'Add' with no input typed fails on the `email()` check (empty string), but the user is shown 'Emails must be unique and valid' — which is not what is wrong. There is also no per-field error and no live validation; the error only appears after clicking submit. Either fix the message to reflect the actual problem, or run validation per row on change.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The addGuests.handler.ts blacklist check uses blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest) after lowercasing the blacklist but not the input guest emails, allowing attackers to bypass BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS restrictions by submitting emails with uppercase characters.

The `sendAddGuestsEmails` function does not check the `disableStandardEmails` flags in the `EventType` metadata, which may result in sending emails to hosts/attendees even when standard emails are disabled for the event type.

false_positives.candidate:
'Additional guests' action is shown for every booking regardless of status

The new `add_members` action is appended to `editBookingActions` with no gating on `isUpcoming`, `isConfirmed`, `isPending`, or non-cancelled status. Users can open the dialog for past, cancelled, or rejected bookings; the server-side handler does not block them either. The dialog should at minimum be hidden (or disabled with explanation) for non-actionable booking states, and the server should reject them.

Any existing attendee can add arbitrary guests

Permission is granted to the organizer, team admins/owners, OR any existing attendee (`isAttendee = !!booking.attendees.find(a => a.email === user.email)`). Any booked attendee can therefore inject new emails into the booking, mutate the underlying calendar event, and trigger calendar-invite emails to recipients of their choosing. This is a privilege escalation relative to typical calendar products where only the organizer can grow the attendee list, and it exposes a vector for spam / calendar-invite abuse. The check should be limited to the organizer (and team admins/owners), not all attendees.

EventManager is built with the requesting user's credentials, not the organizer's

`const credentials = await getUsersCredentials(ctx.user)` and `new EventManager({ ...user, credentials })` use the caller (which may be a team admin or any attendee) instead of the booking organizer. The calendar event being updated belongs to the organizer, and `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking)` runs with the wrong credentials. When the caller is not the organizer (e.g., a team admin or attendee) the calendar update will silently fail or update the wrong account. Credentials and identity should come from the organizer (e.g., `getUsersCredentials(organizer)` or `new EventManager({ ...organizer, credentials })`).

Guests schema has no min/max length and accepts unbounded input

`guests: z.array(z.string().email())` allows any length. With the `addGuests` mutation callable by any attendee of a booking, this is a cheap DoS / abuse vector: a single request can submit thousands of emails, triggering thousands of `createMany` rows, calendar API calls in `EventManager.updateCalendarAttendees`, and an unbounded number of emails in `Promise.all(emailsToSend)`. There is no rate limiting in the handler either. A reasonable cap (e.g., 1-50) should be added at the schema layer.

Handler never checks booking status, event-type policy, or recurrence

The handler mutates booking attendees and external calendar events without verifying booking.status (ACCEPTED/PENDING/CANCELLED/REJECTED), without checking booking.endTime (past bookings), without checking eventType.disableGuests, and without handling recurringEventId (a guest added to one instance will not appear in other instances, producing a confusing state). All of these should be rejected up front.

Mutates the `value` prop instead of using a local default

`value = value || [];` reassigns the destructured prop in place. With React, props are immutable from the callee's perspective; this either no-ops or, if the consumer passes a non-frozen array, mutates the caller's array on every render. It should be `const values = value ?? [];` (or default via destructuring) so that subsequent `value.map(...)`/`value.push(...)` use a local copy.

No error handling for calendar update or emails; partial state on failure

`eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking)` and `sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)` are the only steps that sync with external systems. `updateCalendarAttendees` is not wrapped in try/catch; a calendar provider failure throws out of the handler after the DB has already been updated with the new attendees. `sendAddGuestsEmails` is wrapped in try/catch but only `console.log`s the error. Result: attendees can exist in the DB without being on the calendar video call and without receiving any notification. Either both side-effects must be transactional/compensating, or the DB write must happen last and roll back on failure.

No transaction/locking around attendee creation; double-clicks create duplicates

The handler reads the booking, filters out existing emails, then `prisma.booking.update({ data: { attendees: { createMany: { data: guestsFullDetails } } } })`. Two concurrent submissions (e.g., user double-clicks, or two tabs) can both read the booking before either writes, both compute `uniqueGuests` with the same emails, and both succeed in `createMany`, producing duplicate Attendee rows. The whole flow (read -> filter -> createMany -> calendar update -> emails) is not wrapped in a transaction or guarded by any unique constraint on (bookingId, email), so this leaves the booking in an inconsistent state with duplicate attendees and duplicate external calendar invites.

Organizer email subject assumes attendees[0] exists

`organizer-add-guests-email.ts` builds the subject with `name: this.calEvent.attendees[0].name`. If a handler ever calls `sendAddGuestsEmails` for a booking whose `attendees` array is empty (or where the recipient's distinct attendee list excludes any), this throws `Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'name')` and the whole `Promise.all` rejects. Use optional chaining / fallback (e.g., `this.calEvent.attendees[0]?.name ?? this.calEvent.organizer.name`).

`teamId ?? 0` makes isTeamAdmin/isTeamOwner query with team id 0

When `booking.eventType?.teamId` is null (a personal/one-on-one booking), the code calls `isTeamAdmin(user.id, 0)` and `isTeamOwner(user.id, 0)`. If any user happens to be an admin/owner of team id 0, they would satisfy this branch on a personal booking they do not own. The team-membership check should be conditional on `booking.eventType?.teamId` actually being set (e.g., `if (booking.eventType?.teamId)` then check, else skip), not fallback to 0.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Lost-update race condition on retryCount increment

Both the else branch (line 184) and the catch block (line 195) update retryCount via a read-modify-write: `retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1`. The `reminder.retryCount` value was read by the initial `findMany` at the start of the handler. If a second instance of this cron handler (or an overlapping invocation) has already updated the same row between the read and this update, the second writer will overwrite the first writer's increment using the stale value. The net retryCount will be off by at least one, causing premature (or never-triggered) deletion. The fix is to use Prisma's atomic increment: `data: { retryCount: { increment: 1 } }`, which does not require reading the current value. This is especially relevant because the cleanup at the top of the handler (line 29) will delete the row once `retryCount > 1`, so a lost update can directly cause data loss.

true_positives.golden_comment: The deletion logic in scheduleSMSReminders.ts incorrectly deletes non-SMS workflow reminders (e.g., Email, WhatsApp) that have retryCount > 1. This occurs because the retryCount condition within the OR clause for deletion lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing it to apply to all reminder types instead of only SMS reminders, which is the intended scope of this function.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
deleteMany cleanup deletes non-SMS reminders with retryCount > 1

The new OR branch in the cleanup deleteMany (lines 38-42) deletes any WorkflowReminder with `retryCount > 1` regardless of `method`. This handler is only responsible for SMS scheduling, so it should not be deleting EMAIL or WHATSAPP reminders. While the current codebase only increments retryCount for SMS, the column is on the shared `WorkflowReminder` model and any future code path that bumps retryCount for other methods (or pre-existing data from another env) would be silently deleted by this SMS-only cron. Add `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` to the retryCount branch to scope the cleanup correctly.

false_positives.candidate:
Catch block increments retryCount for transient errors, not just scheduling failures

The catch block (lines 189-199) wraps the entire try body, which includes non-Twilio work: `prisma.profile.findFirst`, `getBookerBaseUrl`, `customTemplate`, `smsReminderTemplate`, and `bookingMetadataSchema.parse`. A transient failure in any of these (DB blip, malformed booking metadata, template variable missing) will increment retryCount exactly the same as a permanent Twilio failure like an invalid phone number. After 2 such transient errors the reminder is permanently deleted even though `twilio.scheduleSMS` was never reached or would have succeeded. The retry-counting should be scoped to the `twilio.scheduleSMS` call (and its returned falsy case), not the whole try block, or transient errors should not count toward the retry budget.

Else branch unreachable when message or sendTo is empty, so retryCount never advances

The else branch that increments retryCount (lines 178-187) is nested inside `if (message?.length && message?.length > 0 && sendTo)`. If `message` is empty/null or `sendTo` is missing, neither the success path nor the retryCount increment runs, but `scheduled` remains false. Such reminders will never have retryCount incremented, so they will never be cleaned up by the new `retryCount > 1` branch and will sit indefinitely (only deleted when `scheduledDate <= now`). This was a pre-existing latent issue but is now more relevant because the new cleanup logic was specifically introduced to prevent indefinite retention of unprocessable reminders. The empty-message/missing-sendTo case should also bump retryCount (or be cleaned up) so the same retry budget applies.

No tests added for the new retry-count cleanup and increment behavior

The PR introduces a non-trivial state machine: a new column, a new cleanup branch (`retryCount > 1`), and two new retryCount increments (else + catch). None of these behaviors are covered by tests. At minimum, tests should cover: (1) reminders are deleted after the retryCount threshold; (2) reminders below the threshold are kept; (3) successful scheduleSMS updates `scheduled=true` and does not bump retryCount; (4) falsy return from scheduleSMS bumps retryCount; (5) thrown errors bump retryCount. Without these, future refactors can silently regress the retry budget.

Off-by-one between description and implementation: 2 attempts before deletion, not "twice failed"

The PR description says "after scheduling failed twice we delete the workflow reminder", but the implementation starts retryCount at 0 and deletes when `retryCount > 1`, meaning the row is deleted after the second failure only on the *third* cron invocation (the third invocation's cleanup deletes it because retryCount is now 2). The initial state counts as the first attempt, so the reminder is actually scheduled twice before being given up on. If the intent is "after 2 failed attempts", the description is accurate but ambiguous; if the intent is "try once, then retry once, then give up", that's what the code does. Either way, a comment near the cleanup query documenting the semantics (`retryCount > 1` means "has already been retried once") would prevent future confusion. This is also a documentation defect because the comment on line 28 ("delete all scheduled sms reminders where scheduled date is past current date") was not updated to reflect the new OR branch.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getBaseConditions(), the else if (filterConditions) and final else branches are unreachable. This is because getAuthorizationConditions() always returns a non-null Prisma.Sql object, making authConditions always truthy, which means only the first two if/else if conditions are ever evaluated.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dead branch in getBaseConditions: authConditions is always truthy

`buildAuthorizationConditions` always returns a `Prisma.Sql` value (either a real condition or `NOTHING_CONDITION`), never null/undefined. Therefore `authConditions` in `getBaseConditions` is always truthy, and the `else if (filterConditions)` branch on line 76 is unreachable - it can only execute if `authConditions` is falsy, which never happens. This is not a functional bug (the conditions still resolve correctly) but it indicates a misread of the type contract and leaves misleading code. Either remove the dead branch and the unreachable `else { return NOTHING_CONDITION; }`, or change `getAuthorizationConditions` to return `Prisma.Sql | null` and return `NOTHING_CONDITION` explicitly only at call sites, so the truthiness checks become meaningful.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Fetching userIdsFromOrg only when teamsFromOrg.length > 0 can exclude org-level members for orgs without child teams; consider deriving from teamIds (which includes orgId) or removing the guard so org-only orgs still include member user bookings.

false_positives.candidate:
Caching behavior is now untested

The class still caches `cachedAuthConditions` (line 49) and `cachedFilterConditions` (line 50), and the getAuthorizationConditions/getFilterConditions methods still gate their build behind `=== undefined` (lines 84-87 and 91-94). However, the entire `describe("Caching", ...)` block that previously verified (a) the first call builds conditions and (b) the second call returns the cached value with reference equality was removed by this PR. There is no remaining coverage proving the cache works, that two concurrent calls don't both populate it (a small race exists because the read-then-await-then-assign sequence is not atomic), or that the cached Prisma.Sql values are still usable as raw query fragments after the assignment. At minimum the deleted cache tests should be ported to the new `Prisma.sql` comparison style.

Integration test queries denormalized table that may not contain created records

The test creates a booking via `prisma.booking.create({...})` (lines 456-466) but the final query targets `BookingTimeStatusDenormalized` (line 482). `BookingTimeStatusDenormalized` is a separate denormalized table/view typically populated via triggers, materialized view refresh, or background jobs - it is not automatically populated by inserting a `Booking` row. If the sync is not configured or has not run in the test environment, the query will return `[]` and `expect(results).toEqual([{ id: userBooking.id }])` will fail for reasons unrelated to the SQL conditions under test. This makes the test unreliable as a real validation of the constructed SQL. Either insert directly into `BookingTimeStatusDenormalized`, trigger whatever sync the production code relies on, or assert against a table that reflects the data immediately. The previous `findMany`-based test had the same dependency, but converting it to `$queryRaw` made the dependency more explicit and did nothing to address it.

Public `findMany` method removed without updating callers in this PR

The service previously exposed `async findMany(findManyArgs: Prisma.BookingTimeStatusDenormalizedFindManyArgs)` and is now replaced with `getBaseConditions()` returning `Prisma.Sql`. This is a breaking change to the class's public surface. The diff does not show updates to other callers in the repo (e.g. any API route, tRPC procedure, or service consumer that imported `InsightsBookingService` and called `.findMany(...)`); those imports will fail to compile after this lands. A maintainer should grep the codebase for `InsightsBookingService` consumers and migrate them, or keep a delegating `findMany` wrapper to preserve backward compatibility.

true_positives.golden_comment: The updateManyByCredentialId call uses an empty data object, which prevents Prisma's @updatedAt decorator from updating the updatedAt timestamp. This results in inaccurate cache status tracking, as the timestamp isn't updated when the cache is refreshed. To fix this, explicitly set the updatedAt field.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
updateManyByCredentialId called with empty data is a no-op

`await SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {});` passes an empty `data` object. Prisma's `@updatedAt` directive only fires when actual fields change, so calling `updateMany` with `{}` does nothing — no row is touched and `SelectedCalendar.updatedAt` is NOT bumped, contrary to the comment immediately above it. The call either needs an explicit field set (e.g. `{ updatedAt: new Date() }`) or should be removed if there is no `@updatedAt` column on `SelectedCalendar`. As written it silently does nothing on every cache refresh.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: macOS-specific sed syntax with empty string after -i flag will fail on Linux systems
true_positives.matched_candidate:
sed syntax is macOS/BSD-only

`sed -i '' -E "s|^GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL=.*|GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL=$TUNNEL_URL|" "$ENV_FILE"` uses BSD sed's `sed -i ''` (empty-string backup suffix) convention, which is a no-op (or 'unknown command') on GNU sed. On Linux the script will silently fail to update `.env`, then `GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL` will still point at the old tunnel/port and Google webhooks will misroute. Either use `sed -i.bak ...; rm -f "$ENV_FILE.bak"` or write the file with a portable tool (printf/awk) or branch on `uname -s`.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Throwing a generic Error for authentication failures results in a 500 response in tRPC. Instead, it should return a structured TRPCError with an appropriate code, such as FORBIDDEN, to accurately reflect the error type.
Date is formatted with hardcoded 'en-US' locale instead of using the user's locale from useLocale, which can lead to incorrect date representation for users in different locales.

false_positives.candidate:
Existing rows get DEFAULT NOW() which misrepresents staleness

The migration sets `updatedAt TIMESTAMP(3) NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW()`. For every existing CalendarCache row that has not been rewritten by Prisma since the migration, the column is set to the moment the migration ran, not to the actual last cache write time. Combined with `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds`, this surfaces a misleading 'Last updated: <few minutes ago>' for legacy cache that could be weeks old. Consider backfilling `updatedAt` from a closer proxy (`expiresAt - INTERVAL '30 days'` or the existing last write timestamp if available) so the UI's 'Last updated' is meaningful for legacy data.

Non-interactive cache status is wrapped in DropdownMenuItem

Lines 84-97 wrap a purely informational 'Cache Status / Last updated …' block in a `<DropdownMenuItem>`. `DropdownMenuItem` is the clickable element of a radix dropdown menu — clicking it (which users naturally do to try to focus/read it) triggers the dropdown's selection handler and closes the menu, hiding the very information they were looking at. Wrap the static text in a plain `<div>` (or a `<DropdownMenuLabel>`) so the dropdown stays open. The second `<DropdownMenuItem>` further down is the real action and is fine.

deleteCache mutation does not invalidate connectedCalendars query

After a successful deleteCache mutation, the component never invalidates the trpc query that populated `cacheUpdatedAt`. Compare with the disconnectMutation further down which calls `utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars.invalidate()` in `onSettled`. Without an invalidation, after the user confirms cache deletion the UI continues to show the same 'Last updated' timestamp (the deleted row's data is still in the React Query cache) until some other action triggers a refetch. The proper fix is to also invalidate `viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars` from deleteCache's `onSettled` (or `onSuccess`) so the timestamp updates immediately.

getCacheStatusByCredentialIds ignores expiresAt

`getCachedAvailability` (line ~95) filters cache rows by `expiresAt: { gte: new Date(Date.now()) }` so only fresh entries are treated as cache hits. The new `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` does not — it just groups all rows. The UI surfaces the result as 'Cache Status / Last updated', which now reports a timestamp even for cache entries that have already expired and would never be served. This is inconsistent with the read path and will mislead users into thinking they have a fresh cache when there is none. Add an `expiresAt: { gte: new Date(Date.now()) }` filter (or document explicitly that the status is intentionally historical).

true_positives.golden_comment: Asynchronous functions deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are called without await inside forEach loops. This occurs during booking rescheduling/cancellation, and workflow/workflow step deletion/updates. Consequently, scheduled workflow reminders may not be reliably cancelled, potentially leaving them active.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Fire-and-forget reminder cancellation in requestReschedule

`bookingToReschedule.workflowReminders.forEach((reminder) => { deleteScheduledEmailReminder(...); deleteScheduledSMSReminder(...); })` (lines 489–495) does not await the async helpers, which themselves swallow errors via console.log. When the organizer requests a reschedule, the user will see the mutation succeed even if the SendGrid/Twilio cancellation actually failed, and the original booking's reminder will still fire.

true_positives.golden_comment: When immediateDelete is true, the deleteScheduledEmailReminder function cancels the SendGrid email but fails to delete the corresponding WorkflowReminder record from the database. This creates orphaned database entries and is inconsistent with the immediateDelete: false path, which marks the record as cancelled. The SendGrid DELETE API call is also omitted in this path.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
immediateDelete path leaves reminder row without cancelled flag

When called with `immediateDelete=true` (handleNewBooking.ts reschedule path), the function only POSTs the cancellation to SendGrid and `return`s — it never sets `cancelled: true` and never deletes the DB row. The row is later cleaned up by the CRON's `deleteMany` once `scheduledDate` passes. That is fine for cleanup, but a developer reading the code (or grepping for `cancelled: true`) will not realize that immediate cancels do not flow through the same state as deferred cancels. Add a code comment, or also write `cancelled: true` for parity so the audit trail is consistent.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The 'cancelled' field is nullable, which can lead to existing records having null values instead of a default of false. This can cause incorrect behavior in the application when checking the cancellation status of reminders.

false_positives.candidate:
CRON early-exits on first SendGrid error, stranding remaining cancellations

The `for (const reminder of remindersToCancel)` loop (lines 56–73) calls `await client.request(...)` and pushes the DB delete into `workflowRemindersToDelete`. The whole block is inside a single `try { ... } catch (error) { console.log(...) }`. When any SendGrid call rejects (very likely once you approach the 100‑pending‑cancel cap, which is the very issue this PR exists to mitigate), the for-of terminates, none of the remaining reminders in `remindersToCancel` are processed in this run, and the partial `workflowRemindersToDelete` is never `Promise.all`'d. The next run will only re-pick those whose `scheduledDate` is still within the next hour; everything else is silently lost and the email goes out. Consider processing each reminder in its own try/catch (or `Promise.allSettled`) so a single failure does not abort the rest.

Cancelled-reminder loop is fully sequential with no batching

`remindersToCancel` is processed one SendGrid call at a time inside a `for ... of` with no `Promise.all`/`allSettled` and no explicit batch size. If a spike of cancellations lands within the one-hour window (the case the PR is built for), the CRON's 15-minute budget can easily be exceeded; at scale it will also amplify the chance of hitting SendGrid's 100‑pending‑cancellation limit per request. Batching the SendGrid calls (or at least running them in parallel with a concurrency limit) would reduce wall time and make the CRON more predictable.

DB record leaks when Twilio cancel throws

`if (referenceId) { await twilio.cancelSMS(referenceId); }` followed by `prisma.workflowReminder.delete(...)` inside a single try means that if `twilio.cancelSMS` rejects, the catch block runs and the DB row is never deleted. There is no retry path, so a stale `WorkflowReminder` with a now-orphaned Twilio SID will remain in the database. Combined with the cascade delete on the booking, this is bounded, but the row will live forever in the (rarer) case of an SMS scheduling retry or a bug elsewhere that cancels a non-existent SID.

Email reminders are unconditionally flagged cancelled, even ones that were never scheduled

Previously the loop guarded with `if (reminder.scheduled && reminder.referenceId)` and otherwise just deleted the DB row. The new code calls `deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId)` for every reminder. When `referenceId` is null (i.e., a not-yet-scheduled future reminder sitting in the CRON queue), `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` deletes it from the DB, which is correct, but this is now happening via a different code path with no test coverage and is invisible to anyone reading the diff. Worth a code comment, or a regression test that exercises `cancelled=true` set with `referenceId=null` (which currently falls into the `!referenceId` branch and silently deletes instead of marking cancelled).

Initial deleteMany strips cancelled reminders without notifying SendGrid

The first action of the CRON is `prisma.workflowReminder.deleteMany({ where: { method: WorkflowMethods.EMAIL, scheduledDate: { lte: dayjs().toISOString() } } })`. It does not filter on `cancelled`. Any reminder whose `scheduledDate` has passed (including a cancelled one that the cancel branch did not get to process in time) is removed from the DB, but if the SendGrid `scheduled_sends` cancel never actually landed, the email is still in SendGrid's queue and will be delivered. Today the cancel branch runs before the deleteMany in the previous code path — verify this ordering and that the deleteMany is intentionally after the cancel pass; otherwise very-late cancellations may still leak.

No automated test added for the new cancellation pipeline

The PR introduces a non-trivial state change (new `cancelled` column, new deferred-cancel path in the CRON, new function signatures) and rewrites cancellation in four call sites, but ships no unit or integration test for it. Specifically there is no test for: (1) the CRON processing reminders whose `scheduledDate` is within the next hour, (2) cancellation requests close to the 100 SendGrid cap, (3) handleCancelBooking/handleNewBooking/bookings.tsx correctly setting `cancelled=true` instead of deleting, or (4) the dead try/catch in handleNewBooking.ts. Given the bug the PR is fixing and that prior fixes have regressed, this is a meaningful gap.

Unrelated UI change bundled into the bug-fix PR

The condition for rendering the phone-number block was changed from `(isPhoneNumberNeeded || isSenderIdNeeded)` to `isPhoneNumberNeeded`. That is a behaviour change for the SMS_ATTENDEE workflow step UI (it stops rendering the phone/verify-code panel for SMS_ATTENDEE) and is unrelated to the workflow-reminder cancellation fix. It should either be split into its own PR with a clear description or reverted, otherwise the changelog/comment history for the cancellation fix becomes misleading.

deleteScheduledEmailReminder silently swallows all errors

The function wraps every code path (DB delete, SendGrid cancel, and `cancelled=true` update) in a single try/catch that only `console.log`s the error. Callers in handleCancelBooking, handleNewBooking and the requestReschedule mutation have no way to know whether cancellation succeeded, and there is no retry, monitoring hook, or persisted failure state. When SendGrid returns an error (e.g., 100 pending cancellations reached, or batch already dispatched) the only record is a console line and the email still goes out.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
forEach(async) pushes to apiDeletes asynchronously, racing with the later Promise.all

In the recurring-event cancellation branch, `bookingToDelete.user.credentials.filter(...).forEach(async (credential) => { ... apiDeletes.push(deletedEvent); })` is used. `Array.prototype.forEach` does not await async callbacks, so the synchronous execution falls through immediately after the loop is set up. The pushes of `deletedEvent` (which itself is the result of `await calendar?.deleteEvent(...)`) into `apiDeletes` happen asynchronously. Later, the code does `await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes));` (line 652). Because the forEach is not awaited, some async callbacks may not have pushed their promises yet when `Promise.all` is called, so those calendar events will never be deleted. This was a pre-existing bug in the original sync version (the callback was already async), but the PR makes it strictly worse by inserting an additional `await getCalendar(credential)` before the push, widening the race window. The fix is to replace forEach with `for (const credential of ...)` and await it, matching the pattern used a few lines below at line 480.

true_positives.golden_comment: Consider adding try-catch around the await to handle import failures gracefully
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Async forEach swallows errors and leaves deletions fire-and-forget in vital reschedule

The code uses `try { bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... await getCalendar(...); await calendar?.deleteEvent(...) ... }); } catch (error) { ... }`. Two problems: (1) `Array.prototype.forEach` does not await async callbacks, so the outer `try/catch` only catches errors thrown synchronously during the forEach setup — any rejection from the awaited `getCalendar` or `deleteEvent` becomes an unhandled promise rejection. (2) Because the callbacks are not awaited, the `Reschedule` function returns `true` immediately after launching the forEach, so callers cannot rely on calendar/video cleanup having completed. The PR converts `getCalendar` to async, widening the window during which these promises are unresolved. The same pattern exists in `packages/app-store/wipemycalother/lib/reschedule.ts` (line 125) and `packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings.tsx` (line 553), and the same caveat applies in `packages/features/bookings/lib/handleCancelBooking.ts` (line 460, already noted separately).

false_positives.candidate:
await apiDeletes is a no-op and paid-booking cancellations return before integrations finish

At line 617 in the `if (bookingToDelete && bookingToDelete.paid)` branch, the code does `await apiDeletes;`. `apiDeletes` is an array of Promises, not a Promise itself, so `await` on a non-thenable just resolves to the array value immediately — this line does not wait for any calendar/video deletion to complete. The function then sets `req.statusCode = 200` and returns `"Booking successfully cancelled."` without having actually deleted the calendar/video events. The non-paid branch correctly uses `await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes));` at line 652. This should be `await Promise.all(apiDeletes);`. This is a pre-existing bug but directly related to the async-flow changes in this PR.

getCalendarCredentials now returns Promise in the calendar field, breaking its synchronous contract

getCalendarCredentials is an exported synchronous function. Before this PR it returned objects whose `calendar` field was a fully constructed Calendar instance. After this PR, the function still declares a synchronous signature but internally calls `getCalendar(credential)` which is now async, so the `calendar` field stored in each returned item is a `Promise<Calendar | null>`. Any external consumer that calls `getCalendarCredentials` and uses `item.calendar` directly (calling methods on it, checking truthiness, etc.) will receive a Promise object and break — for example `item.calendar.listCalendars()` would return a Promise of a Promise, or the truthiness check would always be true (a Promise is truthy). Only the in-file consumer `getConnectedCalendars` was updated (`const calendar = await item.calendar;`); any other call sites across the codebase are silently broken. Either the function must be made async (with all callers updated) or the calendar construction must happen inside the function before returning.

getVideoAdapters loads apps sequentially instead of in parallel

After this PR, `getVideoAdapters` uses a `for (const cred of withCredentials)` loop that awaits each `appStore[appName]` dynamic import one after another. When called with multiple credentials (e.g. from `getBusyVideoTimes`), the dynamic imports run sequentially rather than concurrently. Since dynamic imports are independent I/O operations (Webpack fetches chunks in parallel), this serializes what could be parallel work. The previous synchronous reduce was effectively zero-cost per iteration, but the new version pays the full latency of each import sequentially. Using `Promise.all(withCredentials.map(...))` would allow the chunks to load concurrently, reducing total latency.

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Working hours check uses identical start/end, ignoring eventLength

In checkIfIsAvailable the local variables `start` and `end` are both set to `slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute()`. The intent is clearly to compare the slot's start and end (start + eventLength) against workingHour.startTime/endTime, but because `end` is identical to `start`, the slot's duration is never checked. A slot that begins inside the working window but extends past workingHour.endTime (e.g. a 60-min event at 16:30 with working hours 9:00-17:00, ending at 17:30) will be accepted as within working hours. This directly breaks the fixed-host round-robin fix: fixed hosts can be booked for slots that run past the end of their working hours.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))

false_positives.candidate:
Date comparison uses system local timezone, giving inconsistent results across servers

Both sides of the comparison `dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes").format("YYYY MM DD") === slotStartTime.format("YYYY MM DD")` rely on the dayjs default (system local) timezone. When the server's timezone differs from organizerTimeZone, a slot that falls on the next day in the organizer's tz can still format to the same date string as the override on a UTC server, causing an incorrect match. The check should explicitly format in the organizer's timezone (e.g. `.tz(organizerTimeZone).format(...)` on both sides).

No test for the fixed-host round-robin date override scenario the PR claims to fix

The PR description and the linked issues (#8207, #8329) state that the bug being fixed is that date overrides on fixed hosts were not honoured for round-robin events. The only test added in this PR extends the existing single-user test with a second timezone check; it does not create a round-robin event type with a fixed host and a non-fixed host, set a date override on the fixed host, and assert that slots are restricted to times when the fixed host is available. Without such a test the primary fix is unverified and regressions in checkIfIsAvailable (such as the UTC/organizer-tz mismatch above) will not be caught.

checkIfIsAvailable compares UTC slot times against organizer's timezone values

slotStartTime is computed as `time.utc()`, putting it in UTC mode, while workingHour.days/startTime/endTime and the override's start/end are in the organizer's timezone. The day-of-week test `workingHour.days.includes(slotStartTime.day())` therefore compares a UTC day against the organizer's days array, and `slotStartTime.hour()/minute()` return UTC values that are compared against minutes-since-midnight in the organizer's tz. For a host in IST (+5:30), a slot at 14:00 IST (08:30 UTC) is in workingHour.days for Monday in IST but slotStartTime.day() reports the UTC day, and slotStartTime.hour() returns 8 which is less than workingHour.startTime=540 (9:00 IST) - the slot is wrongly marked outside working hours. Same mismatch affects the override range check, so the date-override fix is broken for any non-UTC host.

checkIfIsAvailable ignores dateOverride.timeZone added by the new TimeRange type

The PR adds `timeZone?: string` to the TimeRange type, and the router populates it from availability.timeZone (and now respects each override's own timeZone if set). But checkIfIsAvailable only takes `organizerTimeZone` into account and the `dateOverrides` parameter type is declared as `{ start: Date; end: Date; }[]` with no timeZone field, so the override's own timeZone is inaccessible. For overrides whose stored timeZone differs from the host's current timeZone (e.g. user created an override while travelling), `dayjs.tz(date.start, organizerTimeZone)` will compute the wrong utcOffset and the override will be matched against the wrong time range. The type should be widened to include `timeZone?: string` and the body should prefer `date.timeZone ?? organizerTimeZone`.

override.timeZone is dereferenced without a fallback, despite being optional in TimeRange

The new code calls `dayjs(override.start.toString()).tz(override.timeZone).utcOffset()`. The TimeRange type declares `timeZone?: string`, and the only place in the codebase that supplies it is the trpc router (`timeZone: availability.timeZone`). If any other caller of `getSlots` (or legacy date-override rows that don't carry timeZone through whatever fetcher is used) supplies an override without timeZone, `.tz(undefined)` will fall back to the system timezone (or throw depending on dayjs-tz behaviour) and the conversion `offset = inviteeUtcOffset - organizerUtcOffset` will be wrong for every override on that event type, silently producing bogus slots. A safe fallback like `override.timeZone ?? timeZone` or requiring callers to always provide it would prevent this. The same applies to the new `WorkingHours` import and the call signature in the router, which should document or enforce the timezone expectation.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code attempts to access integration.metadata[sender][login] without checking for the existence of the sender key. This causes a KeyError for integrations where the sender metadata was not set during creation
true_positives.matched_candidate:
KeyError if integration.metadata lacks 'sender'

The check `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` assumes that `sender` is always present in the integration metadata. However, `build_integration` only adds `sender` to metadata when `state.get("sender")` is truthy (line ~377). If the GitHub webhook did not include a sender (or did not run before this view), `integration.metadata["sender"]` raises KeyError, surfacing as a 500 instead of the intended graceful `error(...)` response. The code should use `integration.metadata.get("sender", {}).get("login")` (or guard the lookup explicitly) so that a missing sender is treated like any other invalid installation request.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Null reference if github_authenticated_user state is missing
OAuth state uses pipeline.signature (static) instead of a per-request random value

false_positives.candidate:
Generic error masks real cause from logs

Several distinct failure modes (state mismatch, missing access_token, missing user login, sender mismatch, missing integration) all funnel into the same `error(...)` response with the user-facing message 'Invalid installation request.' and no logging of the specific reason. Because `error()` is reached from multiple call sites without any distinguishing log line, an operator triaging production failures has no way to tell from logs or user reports which branch was hit. At minimum, each `return error(...)` site should emit a `logger.info`/`warning` with the specific cause (e.g., 'oauth state mismatch', 'oauth token exchange failed', 'github user mismatch').

No test for OAuth state mismatch

The PR description explicitly promises that the pipeline fails 'If there is a mismatch between state parameter supplied by user and pipeline signature', and the code at line 412 implements that check (`if request.GET.get("state") != pipeline.signature: return error(...)`). However, no test in `tests/sentry/integrations/github/test_integration.py` exercises this path by supplying a callback with a wrong `state`. Without such a test, regressions to the state check (or to how the signature is generated/compared) would go unnoticed.

No test for failed OAuth code exchange (wrong/reused code)

The PR description promises failure 'If GitHub could not generate correct access_token from the code (wrong or attempt of re-use of code)'. The branch at line 431 handles this, but no test in `test_integration.py` stubs `https://github.com/login/oauth/access_token` to return a body without `access_token` (or to return an error response) and asserts that the integration-failed template is shown. Coverage of the happy OAuth path exists, but the negative path the PR advertises is untested.

No test for get_user_info missing 'login'

The branch `if "login" not in authenticated_user_info: return error(...)` (line 435) is not covered by any test. There is no scenario in `test_integration.py` where the stub for `https://api.github.com/user` returns a payload without `login`, so a regression that, for example, accidentally trusts a different field or fails to validate the response would not be caught.

No test for missing 'sender' in integration metadata

The user-mismatch check at line 503 reads `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]`. There is no test that creates an Integration record whose metadata lacks `sender` (e.g., by emulating an installation webhook that omits the sender, or by manually constructing metadata). Combined with the fact that `build_integration` only sets `sender` when `state.get("sender")` is truthy, this means the new KeyError-on-missing-sender path is completely untested.

safe_urlopen not wrapped in try/except

The line `req = safe_urlopen(url=ghip.get_oauth_access_token_url(), data=data)` performs the OAuth code-for-token exchange, but unlike the subsequent `safe_urlread`/`parse_qsl` block, it is not wrapped in a try/except. Any network failure, DNS error, TLS error, or non-2xx HTTP response will raise an uncaught exception and turn into a 500, instead of returning the generic `error(...)` page that the surrounding code clearly intends to surface for failed exchanges. This contradicts the PR's stated guarantee that 'If GitHub could not generate correct access_token from the code' the user is shown the error dialog.

test_github_user_mismatch ignores init_path_1 response

In `test_github_user_mismatch`, `self.client.get(init_path_1)` is called but its response is neither asserted nor stored. If that request fails (e.g., 500, redirect to error template), the test silently continues and the subsequent webhook/install assertions lose their meaning because the pipeline state from the first request was never established. The response should be asserted (status 302 to the OAuth authorize URL) so a regression in the initial pipeline bootstrap is caught.

test_installation_not_found may not exercise the intended code path

The test stubs `/app/installations/{installation_id}` with a 404 and uses a hardcoded state `ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05` for the OAuth callback. After the first GET (which binds `installation_id` to pipeline state), the actual pipeline signature is whatever Sentry's Pipeline produces for that state; it almost certainly does not equal `ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05`. The test then asserts only the generic `b"Invalid installation request."` string, which is also produced by the state-mismatch branch. As a result the test passes whether the state check rejects the request or the not-found branch fires, and the 404 stub for `/app/installations/...` is never actually consumed (that endpoint is only called in `build_integration`, which never runs because the pipeline errors out first). The test should drive the OAuth callback with the real pipeline signature (or use a different setup) so it deterministically exercises the not-found branch.

true_positives.golden_comment: The AssignmentSource dataclass uses queued: datetime = timezone.now() as a default field value, which evaluates timezone.now() once at class definition time and shares that single datetime instance across all objects.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
AssignmentSource.queued default is a shared class-level value

The field default `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is evaluated once when the class body is executed at module import time, not per instance. Every AssignmentSource constructed without an explicit `queued` (which is every call site in this PR, including `from_integration`) shares the exact same datetime object captured at import time. The fix is to use `queued: datetime = field(default_factory=timezone.now)` so each instance gets the timestamp of its own creation. The current `test_to_dict` only asserts the field is non-null, so this regression goes undetected.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The method name has a typo: test_from_dict_inalid_data should be test_from_dict_invalid_data.
Method name says 'empty_array' but tests empty dict - consider renaming to 'test_from_dict_empty_dict' for clarity.
to_dict() returns a datetime for queued; if this dict is passed in task kwargs (e.g., via apply_async), JSON serialization may fail depending on the serializer, which can cause enqueue errors.

false_positives.candidate:
No coverage for deassign path with matching AssignmentSource

A new test `test_assignee_sync_outbound_assign_with_matching_source_integration` was added to verify that `assign` skips outbound sync when the source integration matches the target. The equivalent unassign path (`GroupAssignee.objects.deassign(...)` followed by `sync_group_assignee_outbound`) is not covered — the only deassign test (`test_assignee_sync_outbound_unassign`) only asserts the no-source case. Add a parallel test that passes an `AssignmentSource.from_integration(integration)` to `deassign` and asserts `mock_sync_assignee_outbound.assert_not_called()`, since `GroupAssigneeManager.deassign` also forwards `assignment_source` to `sync_group_assignee_outbound`.

from_dict silently returns None on deserialization failure, bypassing cycle protection

`from_dict` swallows any `ValueError`/`TypeError` and returns `None`. The only consumer (`sync_assignee_outbound`) treats `None` as 'no source' and then runs `should_sync` without the cycle guard, so any malformed or schema-drifted `assignment_source_dict` silently disables the very protection this PR introduces and re-enables the original sync loop. The dict is produced by the same code path that consumes it, so silent fallback is risky. Consider raising (so Celery retries / surfaces a metric) or at least logging a warning when reconstruction fails, and updating callers/tests accordingly.

sync_assignee_outbound is invoked with assignment_source kwarg that concrete subclasses may reject

The task now calls `installation.sync_assignee_outbound(external_issue, user, assign=assign, assignment_source=parsed_assignment_source)`. The abstract definition in `IssueSyncIntegration` still relies on `**kwargs` to absorb extra arguments, but concrete subclasses (e.g. the Jira/GitHub/etc. integrations) typically override `sync_assignee_outbound(self, external_issue, user, assign=True)` without `**kwargs` and without an `assignment_source` parameter. Calling those overrides with the new kwarg will raise `TypeError: ... unexpected keyword argument 'assignment_source'`, breaking assignee sync for every integration. The mock-based test `test_assignee_sync_outbound_assign` does not exercise real subclass signatures and therefore does not catch this. Either add `assignment_source: AssignmentSource | None = None` to the abstract signature (as was done for `sync_status_outbound`) and update every concrete override, or remove the kwarg from the call site until those overrides are updated.

sync_status_outbound signature change is unused dead code

`IssueSyncIntegration.sync_status_outbound` is updated to accept `assignment_source: AssignmentSource | None = None`, but no call site in this PR (or anywhere visible in the diff) ever constructs or forwards an `AssignmentSource` for the status path, and no caller of `sync_status_outbound` is modified. The parameter is dead until the status sync cycle is actually fixed, and it is inconsistent with `sync_assignee_outbound` (which still relies on `**kwargs` for the same purpose). Either thread `AssignmentSource` through the inbound status flow and add the cycle guard there, or revert the abstract signature change to avoid misleading readers.

true_positives.golden_comment: MetricAlertDetectorHandler inherits from StatefulDetectorHandler but only contains pass, failing to implement its required abstract methods: counter_names (property), get_dedupe_value(), get_group_key_values(), and build_occurrence_and_event_data(). This will cause a TypeError at runtime when the class is instantiated.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
MetricAlertDetectorHandler is now an uninstantiable abstract class registered as detector_handler

This change replaces `DetectorHandler` with `StatefulDetectorHandler` and removes the previously-present `def evaluate(...)` placeholder that returned `[]`. `StatefulDetectorHandler` declares four new abstract methods (`counter_names`, `get_dedupe_value`, `get_group_key_values`, `build_occurrence_and_event_data`), and `MetricAlertDetectorHandler` implements none of them. The class is therefore abstract. However, it is still referenced from `MetricAlertFire.detector_handler = MetricAlertDetectorHandler`, so any time `Detector.detector_handler` is accessed for a Detector with type `"metric_alert_fire"` (which `process_detectors` does unconditionally), `MetricAlertDetectorHandler(detector)` raises `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class MetricAlertDetectorHandler with abstract methods ...`. This aborts the entire `process_detectors` loop, preventing any further detectors in the list from being processed. Previously the class was concrete (it had a `def evaluate` that returned `[]`), so this is a regression. To fix, either implement the four abstract methods (with sensible stubs/raises-NotImplementedError where appropriate, but the class must still be concrete), or revert to `DetectorHandler` until the abstraction is actually built.

true_positives.golden_comment: Wrong value `6` passed for `group_2` occurrence — the data packet specifies `"group_2": 10`. Should be `10` to accurately reflect the test scenario, which will ensure the test produces the correct occurrence data.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
test_state_results_multi_group passes wrong value for group_2 to build_mock_occurrence_and_event

The test packet is `{"dedupe": 2, "group_vals": {"group_1": 6, "group_2": 10}}`, but the assertion builds the expected occurrence with `build_mock_occurrence_and_event(detector.detector_handler, "group_2", 6, PriorityLevel.HIGH)` — i.e., value 6 instead of 10. The mock currently ignores `value`, so the test passes, but as soon as a future change to `build_mock_occurrence_and_event` actually uses `value` (e.g., to embed it in evidence_data or the subtitle), the test will start asserting against a value the production code path will never produce, masking real regressions. false_negatives.golden_comment: Docstring says this returns a list of DetectorEvaluationResult, but the method now returns a dict keyed by DetectorGroupKey. Consider updating the docstring to match the new return type.

false_positives.candidate:
DetectorHandler.evaluate return type contract break not documented for third-party subclasses

The abstract `DetectorHandler.evaluate` signature changed from `list[DetectorEvaluationResult]` to `dict[DetectorGroupKey, DetectorEvaluationResult]`, and all in-repo subclasses were updated. The PR description mentions this, but any out-of-tree subclass of `DetectorHandler` (e.g., downstream open-source detectors) will silently start returning the wrong shape and either crash at iteration (`.values()` on a list raises AttributeError) or behave incorrectly when keys collide. Consider a deprecation period that accepts both shapes (e.g., coerce to dict internally) or a clearer changelog note in the docstring so subclass authors are explicitly warned.

build_occurrence_and_event_data called with PriorityLevel(new_status) but type was DetectorPriorityLevel

The new call is `self.build_occurrence_and_event_data(group_key, value, PriorityLevel(new_status))`. `new_status` is a `DetectorPriorityLevel` (an IntEnum defined in `sentry.workflow_engine.types`), not a `PriorityLevel`. Passing one enum's integer value to the other enum's constructor relies on the underlying integer values matching, which is true today but is a fragile coupling between two enums in different modules. If `PriorityLevel` and `DetectorPriorityLevel` ever drift (e.g., one gains a new level the other doesn't), this will raise `ValueError: ... is not a valid PriorityLevel`. Either convert via the enum's `.value`/`.name` mapping explicitly, or document and assert the invariant.

build_occurrence_and_event_data exceptions leave state inconsistent (dedupe already bumped)

In `evaluate_group_key_value`, `self.enqueue_dedupe_update(group_key, dedupe_value)` is called (line 265) before any later logic. Once `state_data.status != new_status`, the code reaches the new `else: result, event_data = self.build_occurrence_and_event_data(...)` branch. If that subclass hook raises (network failure, invalid `value` for the detector type, missing config, etc.), the function propagates the exception out of `evaluate_group_key_value`, the dict result is never produced, but the previously-enqueued `dedupe_updates[group_key]` and `state_updates[group_key]` still get committed by `handler.commit_state_updates()` after `process_detectors` catches the failure. On retry of the same data packet, `dedupe_value <= state_data.dedupe_value` will be true, so the data packet is permanently skipped and the issue is never produced. There is no try/except around `build_occurrence_and_event_data`, and no rollback of the enqueued dedupe/state update on failure. Either swallow and log errors (mirroring the `skipping_invalid_condition_group` branch), or roll back the dedupe/state enqueue when building the occurrence fails.
