false_negatives.golden_comment: In the SpanFlusher flush loop, metric tags inconsistently use 'shard' (e.g., in spans.buffer.flusher.produce and spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes) and 'shards' (in spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce) for the same shard identifier value. This prevents correct metric aggregation across flush stages — dashboards and alerts filtering by tag 'shard' will miss data tagged as 'shards' and vice versa.

Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.

Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.

false_positives.candidate:
CLI help for `--flusher-processes` is misleading

`help="Maximum number of processes for the span flusher. Defaults to 1."` implies that passing e.g. `--flusher-processes 8` always gives 8 processes. In reality `SpanFlusher.__init__` clamps via `self.num_processes = min(self.max_processes, len(buffer.assigned_shards))`, and the help also describes the CLI default of 1 rather than the SpanFlusher default of `len(assigned_shards)`. If a user passes a value greater than the number of assigned partitions, they will silently get fewer processes than expected. The help should note the cap.

Dead helper `_create_process_for_shard` is never called

The method `SpanFlusher._create_process_for_shard(shard)` (lines 127-132) is defined but has no callers. The only restart path is in `_ensure_processes_alive`, which invokes `_create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards)` directly. The single-shard helper is dead code and should either be removed or wired into the restart path so callers can target a specific shard.

Docstring claims one process per shard, but processes shard subsets

The class docstring (line 32) says 'Creates one process per shard for parallel processing.' That is no longer true: `__init__` actually creates `min(max_processes, len(assigned_shards))` processes and groups shards via `i % num_processes`. With `flusher_processes=2` and 4 shards, the docstring is misleading and the round-robin assignment also has performance implications (e.g., adjacent shards can end up in different processes and cross shard/processes). The docstring should describe the actual grouping behavior.

Per-submit Redis memory probe now scales with process count

Original code did one `self.buffer.get_memory_info()` call per submit. New code iterates `for buffer in self.buffers.values(): memory_infos.extend(buffer.get_memory_info())`, so the consumer issues N Redis probes per submit where N equals the number of flusher processes (up to one per shard). Even though `submit` is described as not hot, on every call we now do N network round-trips to gather data that conceptually represents the same underlying Redis memory. Consider caching or aggregating memory info once per flush cycle instead of once per submit.

`flusher_processes=0` is silently coerced to `len(assigned_shards)`

In `SpanFlusher.__init__`, `self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` treats 0 as falsy and falls back to one process per shard. An operator passing `--flusher-processes 0` likely expects 'no flusher' or an error, not a default-override that spawns more processes than they asked for. Use an explicit `None` check instead of `or`, or document/validate that 0 is not accepted.

`if not process:` guard in `_ensure_processes_alive` is dead

`self.processes` is populated in `_create_process_for_shards` and never has `None` values, so `if not process: continue` (line 222) is unreachable. Either remove the check or, if the intent was to skip dead slots, document why None entries would ever appear (e.g., a future graceful-shutdown slot).

`process.kill()` followed by immediate respawn can produce duplicate flushes

In `_ensure_processes_alive`, the unhealthy process is `kill()`-ed (non-blocking) and `_create_process_for_shards` is invoked immediately. The old subprocess may still be alive for some time (kill delivery, Redis I/O in flight), during which both the old and new flusher processes can independently call `buffer.flush_segments` and `producer.produce` on the same shard. That can produce duplicate `BUFFERED_SEGMENTS` messages on Kafka. The original code had a similar race but only one flusher existed; now that shards are shared across processes, the blast radius is wider. Consider `process.join(timeout)` before respawn, or use `terminate()` plus a join so the previous process truly exits first.

`process_restarts` threshold allows one more restart than the constant suggests

The check is `if self.process_restarts[process_index] > MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS`, followed by increment + respawn. Tracing the counter: it starts at 0, is checked then incremented. With `MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS = 10` the counter reaches 11 before `11 > 10` triggers, so the consumer actually restarts the process 11 times before raising, not 10. This is an off-by-one that pre-dates this PR, but it is worth aligning either the constant (to `MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS - 1`) or the comparison (`>= MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS`) so the cap matches the name.

`test_flusher_processes_limit` never submits a message

The new test only asserts `len(flusher.processes) == 2`, `flusher.max_processes == 2`, `flusher.num_processes == 2` and that 4 shards are present in `process_to_shards_map`. It does not submit a payload, does not advance drift, and does not assert that any segment reaches the `produce_to_pipe`. The whole point of the multiprocess refactor is that shards split across processes are still flushed end-to-end; this test will silently pass even if the new `_create_process_for_shards` does not correctly wire shards to buffers or if the threading path is broken. Add at least one submit + flush assertion that exercises the cross-process flusher wiring.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling has a docstring that doesn't match the test implementation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Wrong assertion in test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling

The test 'test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling' sends two messages to the same subscription (so they end up in the same queue) and asserts `assert len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`. However, `OrderedQueueWorker.run()` wraps `self.result_processor(...)` in `try/except Exception/finally`, and the `finally` block always calls `self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(...)`. So even after the first call raises, the offset is still marked complete and the commit thread will commit it. The assertion expects no commit to happen, which is the opposite of what the code actually does. The test passes for the wrong reason and would still pass even if error handling was broken. Additionally, because both messages go to the same group/queue, the test does not exercise cross-group error isolation as its docstring claims - to actually verify that an error in one group does not block commits in another, the two results need different subscription_ids so they land in different queues.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The magic number 50 for max_wait is used repeatedly throughout the tests. Consider extracting this as a named constant to improve maintainability.

false_positives.candidate:
Group-to-queue assignment uses Python's randomized hash()

`get_queue_for_group` is `return hash(group_key) % self.num_queues`. Python's built-in `hash()` for strings is salted by `PYTHONHASHSEED` and is therefore not stable across processes. Within a single consumer lifetime the assignment is consistent (so per-group ordering is preserved), but after a restart the same subscription id may land on a different queue and worker. This is undocumented and brittle - if anything ever relies on a stable group->queue mapping across restarts (e.g. for deterministic drain order on partial shutdown, or for replay tooling), it will silently break. Use a stable hash like `hashlib.md5(group_key.encode()).digest()` or `zlib.crc32(group_key.encode())`.

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.join ignores its timeout parameter

`SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.join(self, timeout: float | None = None)` accepts a timeout but does not use it - it just calls `self.close()`. The arroyo framework passes a deadline via this argument so it knows how long to wait for graceful shutdown before forcefully terminating. By ignoring the timeout the strategy can exceed the caller's deadline, causing the consumer to be killed by the orchestrator and any in-flight offsets to be left as 'outstanding' (forcing re-delivery on the next start). `join` should propagate `timeout` to `self.commit_thread.join(timeout=...)` and to `FixedQueuePool.shutdown`/worker joins, and `close()` should also respect a deadline.

Unbounded queues with no backpressure despite docstring claim

In `FixedQueuePool.__init__`, each work queue is created with `queue.Queue()` (no maxsize). The class docstring promises 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up', but there is no fill - the queues are infinite. If a single group is slow or backed up (e.g. one subscription id hashes to the same queue and processing of one item blocks for a long time, or that group simply gets a burst of messages), items accumulate forever. Each `WorkItem` holds a reference to the original `Message` (and therefore the decoded `result` plus `KafkaPayload`), so the memory footprint is non-trivial. An unbounded queue in front of a single-worker-per-queue setup is a straightforward OOM risk and contradicts the docstring.

commit_function failure leaves offsets un-committed in the tracker and is silently retried forever

In `_commit_loop`, `self.commit_function(committable)` is called and only on success does the loop mark the offsets via `mark_committed`. If the commit raises (Kafka unavailable, broker timeout, etc.), the whole `except Exception` just logs and the same offsets are returned by the next `get_committable_offsets()` call and retried. Two problems: (1) if the commit partially succeeded before raising, the same offsets get re-committed to Kafka (duplicate commit), and (2) there is no backoff or alerting, so a persistent failure becomes an infinite tight retry loop that floods the logs and pegs CPU. The metric `remote_subscriptions.queue_pool.offsets_committed` is also incremented before the commit call, so it counts 'attempted' rather than 'succeeded' commits, which is misleading.

get_committable_offsets does an O(max_offset) scan per partition

`get_committable_offsets` iterates `for offset in range(start, max_offset + 1)` looking for the highest contiguous committed offset. If a partition has a small offset (e.g. 100) and a very large one (e.g. 1_000_000) - whether from a bug, rebalance after restart, or just a sparse stream - this allocates and walks ~1M ints per call, every second, from the commit thread. For a multi-partition topic with any sparse offsets this can dominate CPU. The check should walk the sorted `outstanding` set instead of scanning the integer range.

submit() silently drops messages whose value is not a BrokerValue when an error occurs

In `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit`, the `except Exception` handler only marks the offset complete when `isinstance(message.value, BrokerValue)`. If the message value is anything else (e.g. an `ImpulseValue` or any future arroyo value type) and either the decoder raises or the `assert isinstance(message.value, BrokerValue)` itself fails, the offset is never recorded. The message disappears from the strategy but arroyo will not have been told to commit it, so on restart the same message is re-delivered. If the failure is permanent (e.g. the codec can never decode that value type) this becomes an infinite redelivery of poison messages, with no observability beyond the one log entry.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial-cache precedence test does not actually set an allow

In 'Should deny on explicit cache deny entry' the comment at line 981 says 'Allow access to the dashboard to prove this is not checked', but the very next line sets the permission cache to map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}. With the value false, the cached-permission branch in Check would also have returned denied, so the test passes for the wrong reason and does not prove that the denial cache wins over an actual allow. To meaningfully exercise the precedence the cache should be set to {"dashboards:uid:dash1": true} (and ideally also assert that the permission store was never called).

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.

The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache can return stale results when permissions change

The permDenialCache is only ever written (at line 154) and never invalidated when a user's permissions change. Because the denial-cache lookup at line 117 runs before the permission cache (line 123) and the DB requery, a stale denial entry will short-circuit the request and return Allowed=false even after the user has been granted access. With shortCacheTTL = 30s, any grant that lands within 30s of an earlier deny will be ignored. Concrete scenario: user is denied → denial entry written; admin grants access via role/team within 30s; next Check returns false even though both the DB and the (refreshed) permission cache would now allow it. The denial cache needs explicit invalidation (or at minimum must be invalidated when permissions for the user change), otherwise the new "fallback to DB" path added by this PR is bypassed exactly when it is most needed.

Denial cache key does not account for folder-tree moves

userPermDenialCacheKey only includes the resource's direct parent folder, not the folder-tree state used by checkInheritedPermissions (service.go line 581, which walks tree.Ancestors(req.ParentFolder)). If the parent folder is later moved under an ancestor that the user does have access to, a previously-cached denial for (user, action, name, parent) will keep returning false for up to 30s even though the inherited permission check would now succeed. Example: dashboard X in folder A (user lacks access) → denial entry written; folder A is moved under folder B (user has access); user checks X → denial hit → denied. The denial cache entry should either be invalidated when folder moves happen or include a tree-version component in the key.

Denial cache key omits group/resource, allowing cross-API collisions

userPermDenialCacheKey is keyed by namespace + userUID + action + name + parent, where action is derived from (group, resource, verb). Two distinct APIs that happen to translate to the same action (e.g. dashboard.grafana.app/dashboards:get and dashboard.example.com/dashboards:get both yielding dashboards:read) will share denial entries, so a denial cached for one API would incorrectly deny checks on the other for the same name+parent. The key should include the group (and ideally the resource) so that denials are scoped to the API that produced them.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The applyTemplateVariables method is called with request.filters as the third parameter, but this parameter is not used in the corresponding test setup.

false_positives.candidate:
$__range queries no longer routed to non-splitting path because detection happens after interpolation

In `runSplitQuery`, `datasource.applyTemplateVariables` is now invoked on every kept target (line 299) BEFORE `partition(..., query => !querySupportsSplitting(query))` is evaluated (line 300). `querySupportsSplitting` relies on `isQueryWithRangeVariable(query.expr)` which uses `expr.includes('$__range')`. Because `templateSrv.replace` substitutes `$__range`/`$__range_s`/`$__range_ms` with numeric values, those strings are gone from `expr` by the time the check runs. As a result, queries such as `rate({app="frontend"}[$__range])` are now placed in `normalQueries` and get split across chunks instead of being routed to `nonSplittingQueries`. This is exactly the case the in-source comment on lines 285-287 warns against: when the chunk reaches the backend, `$__range` would be (re-)interpolated against the split timeRange and the result would be incorrect. Before this PR, `runSplitQuery` did not interpolate, so the `isQueryWithRangeVariable` check worked. The interpolation must be deferred until after the `$__range` / `querySupportsSplitting` classification, or the non-splitting partition must be computed from the original `request.targets`.

Mock `replace` does not handle built-in variables, masking the $__range regression

The new test `'Interpolates queries before execution'` (and the corresponding one in `shardQuerySplitting.test.ts`) override `replace` to substitute only `$__auto` and `$step`. They leave `$__range`/`$__range_s`/`$__range_ms` untouched. The real Grafana `templateSrv.replace` substitutes these built-ins. Because the mock preserves them, any future test using `$__range` will pass (the substring check finds the literal) while production silently drops them, so the regression described for `querySplitting.ts` cannot be caught by the current mock setup. The mocks should also replace built-in variables (e.g. `$__range` → `300s`) to reflect production, and a test asserting that a `$__range` query is not split should be added.

Queries are interpolated twice on the shard-splitting path

`runShardSplitQuery` (lines 49-52) maps every kept target through `datasource.applyTemplateVariables` and hands the resulting array to `splitQueriesByStreamShard`, which then constructs a `subRequest` whose `targets` are derived from those already-interpolated queries and passes that subRequest to `runSplitQuery` (line 163). `runSplitQuery` now also calls `applyTemplateVariables` on every kept target. Beyond wasted work, this is fragile: if `templateSrv.replace` (or a downstream format handler) is ever non-idempotent for any variable, the second pass would produce different output. The interpolation in `runShardSplitQuery` is redundant once `runSplitQuery` performs it itself; one of the two should be removed.

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TOCTOU race lets concurrent inserts bypass the device limit

`CreateOrUpdateDevice` does a `SELECT COUNT(*)` followed by an INSERT/UPSERT, with no transaction or row-level lock. Two simultaneous requests for distinct new device IDs can both observe `count < deviceLimit`, both fall through to the INSERT branch, and both succeed, pushing the active-device count above the configured `device_limit`. The same race exists between the count check and the subsequent UPDATE inside `updateDevice`. Wrap the count and the mutation in a single transaction (or otherwise serialize) so the limit is actually enforced under load.

true_positives.golden_comment: Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device tagging is now synchronous on every anonymous authentication

The previous implementation dispatched `TagDevice` in a goroutine with a `context.Background()` and a 2-minute timeout, so DB latency and DB errors did not block the auth path. The new code calls `a.anonDeviceService.TagDevice(ctx, httpReqCopy, ...)` inline using the request context. Every anonymous authentication now incurs an extra COUNT/INSERT/UPDATE round-trip plus, on Postgres/MySQL, the per-statement latency, and any transient DB error (or client disconnect that cancels `ctx`) will surface as a failed authentication even when no limit is configured. Consider keeping the fire-and-forget pattern (or a small bounded background context) for the no-limit case and only doing the synchronous, error-returning path when `AnonymousDeviceLimit > 0`.

true_positives.golden_comment: The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Stale devices cannot be re-activated when limit is reached

In `CreateOrUpdateDevice`, when `count >= s.deviceLimit` the code delegates to `updateDevice`, which only matches rows whose `updated_at` is within the last 30 days (`BETWEEN device.UpdatedAt - anonymousDeviceExpiration AND device.UpdatedAt + time.Minute`). Because the active-count query already excludes rows older than 30 days, a device that has not been seen for >30 days does not count toward the limit; but `updateDevice` still treats it as 'not found' and returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached`, so a legitimate returning device is rejected. The same code path returns the same error for a truly new device, conflating the two cases and breaking device re-activation for users who have been away longer than the expiration window. Either the limit-saturated path should DELETE/INSERT stale rows (since they don't count toward the active count) or it should fall back to the regular upsert when no existing row matches the device ID, regardless of age.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Local cache is populated before the DB write, hiding failures

In `tagDeviceUI` the local cache is `SetDefault`ed *before* `a.anonStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice` is called. If the DB write fails for any reason (DB blip, transient error, or the new ErrDeviceLimitReached that is returned for stale devices), the cache will continue to short-circuit writes for that device for the full 29-minute TTL, so the device will silently be absent from the DB even after the underlying problem clears. Set the cache entry only after a successful DB write, or pair it with a delete-on-error so retries can recover.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Time window calculation inconsistency: Using device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration) as the lower bound but device.UpdatedAt as the current time may not match the intended logic. Consider using time.Now().UTC() consistently.

false_positives.candidate:
AnonymousDeviceLimit is exposed to unauthenticated clients

`AnonymousDeviceLimit int64` is added unconditionally to `FrontendSettingsDTO`, which is returned by `GET /api/frontend/settings` to every caller, including fully anonymous users. The value is also exposed via the matching `anonymousDeviceLimit` field in the runtime config. While the limit is not strictly secret, it is server-capacity information that helps an attacker probe the configured ceiling by attempting to register many fake `X-Grafana-Device-Id` values until `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is observed in the auth response. Consider omitting the field when `AnonymousEnabled` is false, or rounding/omitting it for non-admin sessions.

New `device_limit` setting is not documented in conf/defaults.ini

`readAuthSettings` now reads `auth.anonymous.device_limit`, but `conf/defaults.ini` (the canonical user-facing reference for Grafana configuration) is not in the change set. Operators have no way to discover the option, its key name, or the meaning of `0` (no limit) from the shipped configuration. Add a commented entry under `[auth.anonymous]` describing `device_limit`, its default, and the `0 = unlimited` semantics, and update any related docs (e.g., the anonymous-auth admin guide).

New device-limit path is not covered by tests beyond the obvious case

`TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit` only exercises the 'insert device A then reject new device B with limit=1' scenario. There is no test for the stale-but-existing device case (a device whose `updated_at` is older than 30 days that comes back when the active count is at the limit), nor for the TOCTOU race, nor for the `deviceLimit == 0` path confirming that the COUNT/UPDATE branch is fully bypassed. The stale-device case in particular hides a real bug (see separate finding); adding a regression test for it would have caught it.
