false_positives.candidate:
Matcher isAccessTokenId slices wrong characters for the grant shortcut

The encoded prefix has layout [session 0-1][token 2-3][grant 4-5], so the grant shortcut is at indices 4-5. The matcher uses `items[0].substring(3, 5)`, which returns the last character of the token type and the first character of the grant type, not the grant type itself. It should be `substring(4, 6)`. Combined with the inverted logic, the matcher never actually verifies the grant type and accepts any 6-char prefix as long as the UUID part is valid.

TokenContextEncoderSpi marked internal, contradicts stated extensibility goal

`isInternal()` returns `true`, which in Keycloak restricts the SPI to a single implementation (the default). The PR description explicitly motivates the SPI by saying 'provider adds ability for someone to introduce his own provider'. To match that intent, `isInternal()` must return `false`, otherwise third parties cannot supply an alternative encoder.

Public copy constructor of OAuth2GrantType.Context removed without notice

The previous public `Context(Context context)` copy constructor is deleted by this PR. The constructor was on a public nested class of a public SPI, so any downstream code that created derived or copied Contexts will fail to compile. The PR description does not call out this removal, and there is no replacement, so this is an undocumented SPI breaking change.

Constant name GRANT_TYPE is misleading

`public static final String GRANT_TYPE = OAuth2Constants.GRANT_TYPE;` resolves to the literal string `"grant_type"`, which is a key name used as a `ClientSessionContext` attribute key, not a grant-type value. The name suggests a grant type such as `authorization_code`. Either the constant should be renamed to make clear it is a session-context attribute key (e.g. `CLIENT_SESSION_CTX_GRANT_TYPE`) or the Javadoc should explain it is the OAuth2 parameter/attribute name, not a grant type value, to avoid misuse such as `ctx.getAttribute(Constants.GRANT_TYPE, OAuth2Constants.AUTHORIZATION_CODE)` style calls.

getTokenContextFromTokenId does not handle null encodedTokenId

`getTokenContextFromTokenId(String encodedTokenId)` immediately calls `encodedTokenId.indexOf(':')` with no null check. If a caller passes null (for example from `token.getId()` returning null), this throws an NPE instead of returning the UNKNOWN/UNKNOWN/UNKNOWN/encodedTokenId context the method otherwise provides for unencoded ids. It should guard against null and treat it the same as an old (unprefixed) id.

getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext NPEs on null userSession

`clientSessionContext.getClientSession().getUserSession()` is dereferenced for both `getPersistenceState()` and `isOffline()` without a null check. In some flows (e.g. when a client session is not yet bound to a user session, or in OID4VCI issuance paths that build a token without a persisted user session) this can be null, producing an NPE in the encoder. The provider should treat a null userSession as UNKNOWN rather than failing token issuance.

Both `getShortcutByGrantType` and `getGrantTypeByShortcut` do a non-atomic check-then-put into the `ConcurrentHashMap`s. Two threads can simultaneously take the `null` branch and both write. More importantly, nothing prevents a new grant factory from registering with a shortcut that collides with an existing one after `postInit`, which silently overwrites the existing entry in `grantsByShortcuts` and corrupts lookups in both directions; the startup-only size check in `postInit` does not protect against this hot path.

Federated recovery codes not marked as used after validation

In `isValid()` for `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE`, the implementation returns true as soon as the input matches any raw key in `myUser.recoveryCodes.getCredentialData()` but never mutates the stored credential to remove or flag the consumed code. Recovery codes are one-time-use credentials; the local `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider` marks codes as used when validated. Here the same code can be reused indefinitely, so the security guarantee of recovery codes is lost whenever the user lives in federated storage.

Federated recovery-codes credential can never be removed

Because `isValid()` does not track per-code consumption, the `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel` built by `getCredentials()` from the stored raw `credentialData` will always have `allCodesUsed() == false`. Consequently the branch in `RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator.isRecoveryAuthnCodeInputValid` that calls `credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(...)` will never run for a federated user, so the recovery-codes credential sticks around forever, the user is never re-prompted via `CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES`, and the user storage is never asked to delete the credential.

Raw recovery codes persisted in federated credentialData

`updateCredential` saves the JSON produced by `CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential` (which serializes the raw codes) straight into `credentialData` without hashing. The local `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider` hashes the codes before storage (it relies on `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.hashRawCode` with `NOM_ALGORITHM_TO_HASH`). Storing raw codes in `credentialData` diverges from that posture, so any path that exposes `credentialData` (DB dumps, debug logging, serialized credential model) leaks the user's recovery codes in plaintext. The model reconstructed by `getCredentials()` will also carry these raw codes through `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues`, so callers that read `RecoveryCode.getValue()` get the cleartext code.

`testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin` only exercises a single successful entry of one recovery code. Given that `RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator.isRecoveryAuthnCodeInputValid` now also targets federated credentials (via `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential`), the test should additionally assert that (a) re-entering the same recovery code is rejected by the federated validator, and (b) once the last code is consumed, the federated credential is removed and the user is asked to configure new codes. Without these assertions the two real bugs above are not caught by CI.

The test 'test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling' sends two messages to the same subscription (so they end up in the same queue) and asserts `assert len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`. However, `OrderedQueueWorker.run()` wraps `self.result_processor(...)` in `try/except Exception/finally`, and the `finally` block always calls `self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(...)`. false_positives.candidate:
Unbounded queues with no backpressure despite docstring claim

In `FixedQueuePool.__init__`, each work queue is created with `queue.Queue()` (no maxsize). The class docstring promises 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up', but there is no fill - the queues are infinite. If a single group is slow or backed up (e.g. one subscription id hashes to the same queue and processing of one item blocks for a long time, or that group simply gets a burst of messages), items accumulate forever. Each `WorkItem` holds a reference to the original `Message` (and therefore the decoded `result` plus `KafkaPayload`), so the memory footprint is non-trivial. An unbounded queue in front of a single-worker-per-queue setup is a straightforward OOM risk and contradicts the docstring.

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.join ignores its timeout parameter

`SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.join(self, timeout: float | None = None)` accepts a timeout but does not use it - it just calls `self.close()`. The arroyo framework passes a deadline via this argument so it knows how long to wait for graceful shutdown before forcefully terminating. By ignoring the timeout the strategy can exceed the caller's deadline, causing the consumer to be killed by the orchestrator and any in-flight offsets to be left as 'outstanding' (forcing re-delivery on the next start). `join` should propagate `timeout` to `self.commit_thread.join(timeout=...)` and to `FixedQueuePool.shutdown`/worker joins, and `close()` should also respect a deadline.

commit_function failure leaves offsets un-committed in the tracker and is silently retried forever

In `_commit_loop`, `self.commit_function(committable)` is called and only on success does the loop mark the offsets via `mark_committed`. If the commit raises (Kafka unavailable, broker timeout, etc.), the whole `except Exception` just logs and the same offsets are returned by the next `get_committable_offsets()` call and retried. Two problems: (1) if the commit partially succeeded before raising, the same offsets get re-committed to Kafka (duplicate commit), and (2) there is no backoff or alerting, so a persistent failure becomes an infinite tight retry loop that floods the logs and pegs CPU. The metric `remote_subscriptions.queue_pool.offsets_committed` is also incremented before the commit call, so it counts 'attempted' rather than 'succeeded' commits, which is misleading.

get_committable_offsets does an O(max_offset) scan per partition

`get_committable_offsets` iterates `for offset in range(start, max_offset + 1)` looking for the highest contiguous committed offset. If a partition has a small offset (e.g. 100) and a very large one (e.g. 1_000_000) - whether from a bug, rebalance after restart, or just a sparse stream - this allocates and walks ~1M ints per call, every second, from the commit thread. For a multi-partition topic with any sparse offsets this can dominate CPU. The check should walk the sorted `outstanding` set instead of scanning the integer range.

Group-to-queue assignment uses Python's randomized hash()

`get_queue_for_group` is `return hash(group_key) % self.num_queues`. Python's built-in `hash()` for strings is salted by `PYTHONHASHSEED` and is therefore not stable across processes. Within a single consumer lifetime the assignment is consistent (so per-group ordering is preserved), but after a restart the same subscription id may land on a different queue and worker. This is undocumented and brittle - if anything ever relies on a stable group->queue mapping across restarts (e.g. for deterministic drain order on partial shutdown, or for replay tooling), it will silently break. Use a stable hash like `hashlib.md5(group_key.encode()).digest()` or `zlib.crc32(group_key.encode())`.

submit() silently drops messages whose value is not a BrokerValue when an error occurs

In `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit`, the `except Exception` handler only marks the offset complete when `isinstance(message.value, BrokerValue)`. If the message value is anything else (e.g. an `ImpulseValue` or any future arroyo value type) and either the decoder raises or the `assert isinstance(message.value, BrokerValue)` itself fails, the offset is never recorded. The message disappears from the strategy but arroyo will not have been told to commit it, so on restart the same message is re-delivered. If the failure is permanent (e.g. the codec can never decode that value type) this becomes an infinite redelivery of poison messages, with no observability beyond the one log entry.

Redirect-follow loop limit lowered from 10000 to 1000 silently breaks deep segment trees

The previous code used `for i = 0, 10000 do` and carried a comment explaining that exceeding this limit means segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly. The new code lowers the bound to `for i = 0, 1000 do` without any rationale, so any trace whose redirect chain exceeds 1000 hops will resolve to a `set_span_id` that is not the true root. The subsequent `zunionstore`/`zpopmin` will then operate on the wrong set, leaving the actual root segment orphaned and producing an incomplete or empty flushed segment. This is a silent data-integrity regression for deep traces.

Default SUM aggregate in ZUNIONSTORE corrupts `end_timestamp_precise` scores for duplicate payloads

`zunionstore set_key 2 set_key span_key` is invoked with the implicit default `AGGREGATE SUM`. If a member (span payload) ever exists in both `set_key` and `span_key` (which can occur on Kafka retries or any path where the same payload was inserted twice with different timestamps), its score after the union becomes the arithmetic sum of the two timestamps rather than either one. Those scores drive eviction (`zpopmin`) and any downstream ordering; a corrupted score means the wrong spans get evicted and the 'oldest-first' eviction contract is broken. The script should pass an explicit `AGGREGATE MIN` (or `MAX`) to preserve a single timestamp per payload.

Span NamedTuple adds a required field in the middle, breaking positional construction

`Span` is a public NamedTuple exported from `sentry.spans.buffer`. The new `end_timestamp_precise: float` is inserted between `payload` and `is_segment_span`, has no default, and shifts `is_segment_span` to the last position. Any caller that constructs `Span(...)` positionally (the 7th argument previously implied `is_segment_span`) will silently mis-bind: a positional `True` becomes the `end_timestamp_precise` value and `is_segment_span` defaults to `False`, causing incorrect is-segment logic downstream. It also breaks unpickling of old `Span` pickles and any external code that mirrors this shape. The field should be added at the end (with a default) or supplied only via keyword to preserve positional compatibility.

Removed `max_segment_spans` Python guard while Lua hardcodes a different (1000) limit

The old `_load_segment_data` had `if len(payloads[key]) > self.max_segment_spans: ... skip segment`. This guard is deleted, so the only cap on segment size is the new Lua eviction at line 62 (`if span_count > 1000 then redis.call('zpopmin', set_key, span_count - 1000) end`). Two issues: (1) `SpansBuffer.__init__` still accepts and stores `max_segment_bytes`/`max_segment_spans`, so the configurable Python limit is now dead and will diverge from the Lua hardcode if anyone changes the constant. (2) The Lua limit is 1000 but `max_segment_spans` defaults to 1001, so the effective cap silently drops by 1. If the Lua eviction is bypassed (e.g., a Redis upgrade changes `ZUNIONSTORE` cardinality semantics, or a future code path skips the script), there is no Python backstop and segments can grow unbounded.

OptimizedCursorPaginator duplicates BasePaginator without any actual optimization

`OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result` is a near-verbatim copy of `BasePaginator.get_result`. The only behavioral difference is the `enable_advanced_features and cursor.offset < 0` branch (which, per the other finding, crashes Django). There is no optimized query path, no streamlined boundary handling, and no measurable performance benefit. The docstring's claims of 'performance optimizations for high-traffic endpoints' and 'Optimized query path for large datasets' are unsubstantiated. A subclass that only adds one (broken) branch is significant duplication that will drift from the base implementation.

Comments and docstrings lie about safety, optimization, and Django support

Several new comments are misleading: (1) `paginator.py` line 179: 'Performance optimization: ... allow negative offsets to enable efficient bidirectional pagination' — the change actually clamps non-prev offsets to 0, it does not allow them. (2) `paginator.py` line 877: 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' — Django explicitly asserts `k.start >= 0` and raises on negative slicing. (3) `paginator.py` line 879: 'This is safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level' — permissions don't gate which rows an offset selects, only which rows the queryset can see; an admin user can still trigger a crash or expensive scan. (4) `organization_auditlogs.py` lines 68-76 repeat the same false framing about 'optimized paginator for high-performance' navigation. (5) `cursors.py` lines 26-27 add a 'Performance optimization' comment over a line that is byte-identical to the original. These comments will mislead future maintainers about the actual semantics and risks.

`max(0, offset)` silently changes BasePaginator behavior for callers passing negative non-prev offsets

In the DeleteCollection async goroutine, the elapsed time of d.Legacy.DeleteCollection is fed to d.recordStorageDuration(...). Every other write path correctly uses recordLegacyDuration for the legacy leg; this one is mislabeled, so DeleteCollection legacy latency will be merged into the unified-storage histogram and the real legacy histogram will not see those calls.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same copy-paste/mislabeled metric bug in the DeleteCollection method, where recordStorageDuration is used instead of recordLegacyDuration (or vice versa in the error/async path).

true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete success path labels metric with name instead of Kind

On successful d.Storage.Delete, d.recordStorageDuration is called with `name` as the kind label, while every other path (and the failing branch on line 103) uses options.Kind. true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: using `name` instead of `options.Kind` when recording metrics, which is inconsistent with other methods/paths.

false_positives.candidate:
Create records storage failure as legacy duration

In DualWriterMode3.Create, when d.Storage.Create fails the code calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...) instead of recording the storage duration. Because recordLegacyDuration and recordStorageDuration are distinct Prometheus metrics, a storage-side failure will be misattributed to the legacy backend. Anyone alerting or graphing on legacy failures will see storage failures, and storage failures will be invisible. Use recordStorageDuration(true, ...) here.

Update records storage failure as legacy duration

In DualWriterMode3.Update, when d.Storage.Update fails the code calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...) instead of recordStorageDuration. Same effect as in Create: a unified-storage Update failure is reported as a legacy failure, silently corrupting the two latency/error time series. Use recordStorageDuration(true, ...).

Async legacy Create inherits request context that is cancelled when the response returns

The async Create goroutine derives its timeout from the inbound request context: `ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, time.Second*10, ...)`. That ctx is the apiserver request context, which is cancelled as soon as the handler writes the response and returns. The whole purpose of mode 3 is to write to legacy "as a safe measure" after the request returns; here that guarantee is broken, and the legacy write will frequently be aborted by ctx.Done() before completing. Use a detached context (e.g., context.Background()) with the klog logger still attached.

Async legacy Delete inherits request context

Same problem as the Create goroutine on line 51: the Delete goroutine derives its context from the request context with WithTimeoutCause(... 10s). The legacy Delete will be cancelled when the apiserver request finishes, so the safety-net legacy delete is not guaranteed to run to completion.

Async legacy Update inherits request context

The async Update goroutine derives its context from the request context with WithTimeoutCause(... 10s). The legacy Update will be cancelled when the apiserver request finishes, so the safety-net legacy update is not guaranteed to run. The legacy store can therefore permanently diverge from unified storage on any request that finishes inside 10s.

Async legacy DeleteCollection inherits request context

Same as above: the DeleteCollection goroutine derives its context from the request context with WithTimeoutCause(... 10s), so the legacy bulk delete will be cancelled when the handler returns and the two stores will diverge.

Async legacy Create uses the pre-storage object, not the stored object

After d.Storage.Create succeeds, the returned `created` object contains the UID, resourceVersion, creation timestamp, etc. that unified storage assigned. The async goroutine calls d.Legacy.Create with the original `obj` parameter instead, so the legacy store never sees the metadata assigned by storage (or assigns its own), producing two records with different identities for what should be the same resource. The legacy record is effectively orphaned from the unified one.

Async legacy Update re-evaluates UpdatedObjectInfo against legacy's current state

The async Update goroutine passes the original objInfo to d.Legacy.Update. UpdatedObjectInfo.UpdatedObject is called inside the legacy store against whatever it currently holds, not against the state storage just wrote. The previous implementation wrapped objInfo around the resolved object and passed the same wrapped value to both stores so they would apply identical changes; here the legacy store can compute and persist a different version, causing legacy and storage to diverge.

Mode3 doc comment describes the wrong write order

The comment on newDualWriterMode3 says "Mode 3 represents writing to LegacyStorage and Storage and reading from Storage." The actual behavior implemented below is: write synchronously to Storage, then fire-and-forget an asynchronous write to LegacyStorage, and read only from Storage. The comment therefore misleads readers about both the ordering and the async nature of mode 3.

TestMode3_Create never asserts that the legacy async Create actually ran

TestMode3_Create registers an expectation on the legacy store mock via setupLegacyFn but the goroutine that should satisfy it is never synchronized with (no wait, no channel, no AssertExpectations). The test currently passes even if the legacy async write is removed or short-circuited, so the very behavior mode 3 introduces - the legacy safety-net write - is effectively untested.

TestMode3_Update never asserts the legacy async Update ran

TestMode3_Update registers a mock expectation for legacy Update but does not synchronize with or assert against the async goroutine. The same problem as Create: the legacy safety-net update is not actually verified.

TestMode3_DeleteCollection has no legacy setup or assertion at all

The testCase struct does not include setupLegacyFn and no mock expectation is registered for d.Legacy.DeleteCollection. The implementation runs an async legacy DeleteCollection but nothing in this test exercises it - the safety-net behavior on the bulk-delete path is entirely uncovered.

TestMode3_Get does not verify legacy Get is never called

Mode 3 reads must come from storage only, but TestMode3_Get never asserts that the legacy store is not called (the analogous TestMode1_Get uses us.AssertNotCalled on Delete). A future change that accidentally adds a legacy Get would not be caught.

TestMode3_Get uses a local prometheus registry while the rest of the file uses the package-level p

All other tests in dualwriter_mode3_test.go and dualwriter_mode1_test.go use the package-level `p`; TestMode3_Get creates its own `p := prometheus.NewRegistry()` inside the test body, masking the global and being a leftover from before the global existed. Minor, but should be aligned.

false_positives.candidate:
Tests mock the wrong ability hook for RuleActionsButtons (stale comment and mocks)

The mock table and all assertions are built around `useAlertRuleAbility` (singular), with the comment 'RuleActionsButtons uses: useAlertRuleAbility (singular)'. After this PR, `RuleActionsButtons.V2.tsx` no longer calls `useAlertRuleAbility` — it calls `useRulerRuleAbility` for the ruler-side edit ability and `useGrafanaPromRuleAbility` (with `skipToken`) for the prom-side fallback. As a result the per-test overrides of `useAlertRuleAbility` (e.g. for Update/Delete) have no effect on what is rendered, and the previous default `[false, false]` from `useRulerRuleAbility` is what actually drives `canEditRule`/`canDelete` etc. Concretely:

- The 'Should not render Delete button for users without the delete permission' test never sets `useRulerRuleAbility`/`useRulerRuleAbilities` for Grafana, so it appears to pass for the wrong reason (and only because the grafana-side plural hook is overridden); it does not exercise the OR-of-abilities logic in `AlertRuleMenu`.
- The 'Should render Delete button for users with the delete permission' test depends on the same gap.

Update the mocks and the explanatory comment so that the singular/plural ruler and grafana-prom hooks used by the V2 components are what is being stubbed, and assert against the actual hook calls. Otherwise a regression in `useRulerRuleAbility`/abilities OR'ing would go undetected.

Pause and Delete menu items are silently unavailable in the list view (rulerRule is now undefined)

`AlertRuleMenu` still gates the Pause and Delete entries on the presence of the ruler-side data:

- Pause: `{canPause && rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule) && groupIdentifier.groupOrigin === 'grafana' && (<MenuItemPauseRule rule={rulerRule} ... />)}`
- Delete: `{canDelete && rulerRule && (... onClick={() => handleDelete(rulerRule, groupIdentifier)} ...)}`

After this PR the grafana list view (`GrafanaRuleListItem`, `FilterView`) constructs the actions tree with only `promRule`, so `rulerRule` is `undefined` everywhere and both menu items disappear — not because the user lacks permissions (the abilities are still `[supported, allowed]` via the grafana-prom fallback) but because the underlying click handlers need the full ruler payload. This is a behavior regression vs. the previous list view and is not described in the PR description. Users will have to drill into each rule's detail page to pause or delete it, and any bulk operations built on the list will also break. Either plumb through enough ruler data (or use a prom-based delete path) so these actions keep working in the list, or call out this UX change explicitly and gate the entire removal behind a feature flag.

Dropping ruler fallback loses the 'Creating' / 'Deleting' rule states

Before this change `GrafanaGroupLoader` fetched ruler data, paired it with the prom response via `matchRules`, and rendered outstanding rulers with `RuleOperation.Creating` and unmatched prom rules with `RuleOperation.Deleting`. After removing the ruler fetch (and `matchRules`/`RulerRuleLoadingError`), the component only renders `promResponse.data.groups.at(0)?.rules` directly. As a consequence:

- A rule that has been accepted by the ruler but not yet propagated to Prometheus (window of eventual consistency) disappears from the list instead of being shown with the 'Creating' badge.
- A rule that has been deleted from the ruler but is still in the prom response no longer appears as 'Deleting'.

Previously these intermediates were explicitly logged with `logWarning` because they are rare/expected; now they are silently absent, hiding the operation from the user. Either keep the ruler fetch + match (same call it makes today) just for status derivation, or update the prom API so the rule DTO carries a creation/in-flight marker that the list can render without a second query. This should be flagged in the PR description and either preserved or have tests covering the in-flight state.

This means clicking 'Silence notifications' for these rules has no visible effect, even when abilities indicate silencing is allowed.

false_positives.candidate:
$__range queries no longer routed to non-splitting path because detection happens after interpolation

In `runSplitQuery`, `datasource.applyTemplateVariables` is now invoked on every kept target (line 299) BEFORE `partition(..., query => !querySupportsSplitting(query))` is evaluated (line 300). `querySupportsSplitting` relies on `isQueryWithRangeVariable(query.expr)` which uses `expr.includes('$__range')`. Because `templateSrv.replace` substitutes `$__range`/`$__range_s`/`$__range_ms` with numeric values, those strings are gone from `expr` by the time the check runs. As a result, queries such as `rate({app="frontend"}[$__range])` are now placed in `normalQueries` and get split across chunks instead of being routed to `nonSplittingQueries`. This is exactly the case the in-source comment on lines 285-287 warns against: when the chunk reaches the backend, `$__range` would be (re-)interpolated against the split timeRange and the result would be incorrect. Before this PR, `runSplitQuery` did not interpolate, so the `isQueryWithRangeVariable` check worked. The interpolation must be deferred until after the `$__range` / `querySupportsSplitting` classification, or the non-splitting partition must be computed from the original `request.targets`.

Mock `replace` does not handle built-in variables, masking the $__range regression

The new test `'Interpolates queries before execution'` (and the corresponding one in `shardQuerySplitting.test.ts`) override `replace` to substitute only `$__auto` and `$step`. They leave `$__range`/`$__range_s`/`$__range_ms` untouched. The real Grafana `templateSrv.replace` substitutes these built-ins. Because the mock preserves them, any future test using `$__range` will pass (the substring check finds the literal) while production silently drops them, so the regression described for `querySplitting.ts` cannot be caught by the current mock setup. The mocks should also replace built-in variables (e.g. `$__range` → `300s`) to reflect production, and a test asserting that a `$__range` query is not split should be added.

Queries are interpolated twice on the shard-splitting path

`runShardSplitQuery` (lines 49-52) maps every kept target through `datasource.applyTemplateVariables` and hands the resulting array to `splitQueriesByStreamShard`, which then constructs a `subRequest` whose `targets` are derived from those already-interpolated queries and passes that subRequest to `runSplitQuery` (line 163). `runSplitQuery` now also calls `applyTemplateVariables` on every kept target. So in the shard path each target is interpolated twice. Beyond wasted work, this is fragile: if `templateSrv.replace` (or a downstream format handler) is ever non-idempotent for any variable, the second pass would produce different output. The interpolation in `runShardSplitQuery` is redundant once `runSplitQuery` performs it itself; one of the two should be removed.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The applyTemplateVariables method is called with request.filters as the third parameter, but this parameter is not used in the corresponding test setup.

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TOCTOU race lets concurrent inserts bypass the device limit

`CreateOrUpdateDevice` does a `SELECT COUNT(*)` followed by an INSERT/UPSERT, with no transaction or row-level lock. Two simultaneous requests for distinct new device IDs can both observe `count < deviceLimit`, both fall through to the INSERT branch, and both succeed, pushing the active-device count above the configured `device_limit`. The same race exists between the count check and the subsequent UPDATE inside `updateDevice`. Wrap the count and the mutation in a single transaction (or otherwise serialize) so the limit is actually enforced under load.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same race condition where concurrent requests can bypass the device limit check (TOCTOU) and create more devices than allowed, and both suggest using a database transaction or lock to resolve it.

true_positives.golden_comment: Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device tagging is now synchronous on every anonymous authentication

The previous implementation dispatched `TagDevice` in a goroutine with a `context.Background()` and a 2-minute timeout, so DB latency and DB errors did not block the auth path. The new code calls `a.anonDeviceService.TagDevice(ctx, httpReqCopy, ...)` inline using the request context. Every anonymous authentication now incurs an extra COUNT/INSERT/UPDATE round-trip plus, on Postgres/MySQL, the per-statement latency, and any transient DB error (or client disconnect that cancels `ctx`) will surface as a failed authentication even when no limit is configured. Consider keeping the fire-and-forget pattern (or a small bounded background context) for the no-limit case and only doing the synchronous, error-returning path when `AnonymousDeviceLimit > 0`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same code change: moving `anonDeviceService.TagDevice` from an asynchronous goroutine to a synchronous, blocking call during anonymous authentication, which causes authentication to fail when `TagDevice` returns an error (such as the device limit being reached).

true_positives.golden_comment: The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Stale devices cannot be re-activated when limit is reached

In `CreateOrUpdateDevice`, when `count >= s.deviceLimit` the code delegates to `updateDevice`, which only matches rows whose `updated_at` is within the last 30 days (`BETWEEN device.UpdatedAt - anonymousDeviceExpiration AND device.UpdatedAt + time.Minute`). Because the active-count query already excludes rows older than 30 days, a device that has not been seen for >30 days does not count toward the limit; but `updateDevice` still treats it as 'not found' and returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached`, so a legitimate returning device is rejected. The same code path returns the same error for a truly new device, conflating the two cases and breaking device re-activation for users who have been away longer than the expiration window. Either the limit-saturated path should DELETE/INSERT stale rows (since they don't count toward the active count) or it should fall back to the regular upsert when no existing row matches the device ID, regardless of age.
true_positives.reasoning: The golden comment points out the semantic mismatch inside `updateDevice` where `rowsAffected == 0` returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached` even though it actually means the device doesn't exist or is outside the time window. The candidate comment explains the exact same mechanism (`updateDevice` returning `ErrDeviceLimitReached` when no rows match due to not existing or being outside the 30-day window), though it frames the bug around the caller's context (`CreateOrUpdateDevice` when the limit is reached) and the impact on stale devices. However, in the context of the caller, returning `ErrDeviceLimitReached` for a non-existent device when the limit is already reached is likely intentional, whereas the golden comment critiques the error type returned by `updateDevice` in isolation. Despite the slightly different framing on how to fix it, both directly identify the core issue that `updateDevice` conflates 'not found / outside time window' with `ErrDeviceLimitReached`.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Local cache is populated before the DB write, hiding failures

In `tagDeviceUI` the local cache is `SetDefault`ed *before* `a.anonStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice` is called. If the DB write fails for any reason (DB blip, transient error, or the new ErrDeviceLimitReached that is returned for stale devices), the cache will continue to short-circuit writes for that device for the full 29-minute TTL, so the device will silently be absent from the DB even after the underlying problem clears. Set the cache entry only after a successful DB write, or pair it with a delete-on-error so retries can recover.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same bug in `tagDeviceUI`: the local cache is populated before calling `CreateOrUpdateDevice`, so if `ErrDeviceLimitReached` (or another error) occurs, the cache entry persists for the 29-minute TTL and causes subsequent calls to bypass the check/write.

false_positives.candidate:
Request context cancellation can lose device tags

`TagDevice` now uses the inbound request `ctx`. If the client disconnects mid-auth (a common case for an anonymous browser session that redirects away), the context is cancelled and the DB write is aborted, but the request handler then continues and returns success. The device is therefore neither in the DB nor counted for future requests until it is seen again. The previous implementation used `context.Background()` with its own timeout precisely to avoid this. The new design should derive a detached context (e.g., `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` or a fresh background context) for the device-tag DB write so client cancellation doesn't drop the write.

New device-limit path is not covered by tests beyond the obvious case

`TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit` only exercises the 'insert device A then reject new device B with limit=1' scenario. There is no test for the stale-but-existing device case (a device whose `updated_at` is older than 30 days that comes back when the active count is at the limit), nor for the TOCTOU race, nor for the `deviceLimit == 0` path confirming that the COUNT/UPDATE branch is fully bypassed. The stale-device case in particular hides a real bug (see separate finding); adding a regression test for it would have caught it.

New `device_limit` setting is not documented in conf/defaults.ini

`readAuthSettings` now reads `auth.anonymous.device_limit`, but `conf/defaults.ini` (the canonical user-facing reference for Grafana configuration) is not in the change set. Operators have no way to discover the option, its key name, or the meaning of `0` (no limit) from the shipped configuration. Add a commented entry under `[auth.anonymous]` describing `device_limit`, its default, and the `0 = unlimited` semantics, and update any related docs (e.g., the anonymous-auth admin guide).

AnonymousDeviceLimit is exposed to unauthenticated clients

`AnonymousDeviceLimit int64` is added unconditionally to `FrontendSettingsDTO`, which is returned by `GET /api/frontend/settings` to every caller, including fully anonymous users. The value is also exposed via the matching `anonymousDeviceLimit` field in the runtime config. While the limit is not strictly secret, it is server-capacity information that helps an attacker probe the configured ceiling by attempting to register many fake `X-Grafana-Device-Id` values until `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is observed in the auth response. Consider omitting the field when `AnonymousEnabled` is false, or rounding/omitting it for non-admin sessions.

Test name and assertions don't verify that the first device was actually counted

`TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit` only asserts that the second `CreateOrUpdateDevice` returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached`. It does not assert on `CountDevices` before the second call to confirm the count actually reached the configured limit, so a regression that makes the limit check silently no-op (e.g., if `s.deviceLimit` were not threaded through) would still pass the test. Add an explicit `CountDevices` assertion between the two `CreateOrUpdateDevice` calls.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Time window calculation inconsistency: Using device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration) as the lower bound but device.UpdatedAt as the current time may not match the intended logic. Consider using time.Now().UTC() consistently.

false_positives.candidate:
SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym raises NoMethodError when default_locale is nil

`FallbackLocaleList#[]` evaluates `SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym` on every call, and `FallbackLocaleList#ensure_loaded!` (called from `ApplicationController#set_locale` on every request) also reaches this expression. If `SiteSetting.default_locale` is nil (e.g. before the site settings row exists, during a fresh install/seed, or in a misconfigured environment), `to_sym` raises NoMethodError and crashes the request. The trailing `.compact` does not guard this case, because the exception is raised before `compact` runs. Use a safe form such as `[locale, SiteSetting.default_locale&.to_sym, :en].compact.uniq` and ensure there is at least one non-nil element.

FallbackLocaleList inherits from Hash but does not implement the I18n::Locale::Fallbacks contract

The class replaces the standard `I18n::Locale::Fallbacks` (which itself extends Hash) but only overrides `[]` and adds `ensure_loaded!`. The real class also defines `[]=`, `defaults`, and `defaults=`. With this replacement, any caller that does `I18n.fallbacks[locale] = [...]` or reads/writes `I18n.fallbacks.defaults` will silently use Hash defaults — our `[]` always recomputes from `SiteSetting.default_locale`, so any explicitly configured fallbacks are ignored without warning. Iterating `I18n.fallbacks.each` will likewise yield nothing because the underlying hash is empty. Either implement the missing methods (store explicit overrides and consult them before computing) or stop inheriting from Hash so the misleading API surface is removed and behaviour is explicit.

`compact` silently swallows a nil I18n.locale instead of surfacing the bug

`[locale, SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym, :en].uniq.compact` relies on `compact` to drop a nil `locale`. A nil `I18n.locale` is an upstream problem (e.g. `current_user.effective_locale` returning nil in `ApplicationController#set_locale`) and translations will still resolve via `[default_locale, :en]`, hiding the misconfiguration. Either remove `compact` so the nil propagates as a real error, or replace it with an explicit guard that logs/warns when `locale` is nil and falls back intentionally.

No specs cover the new server-side localization fallback behaviour

The diff adds a non-trivial behaviour change (custom `FallbackLocaleList` with a `[locale, SiteSetting.default_locale, :en]` chain, eager loading via `I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!` from a `before_filter`, and a new `I18n.ensure_loaded!` patch in `translate_accelerator.rb`) but ships without any test files. At minimum there should be specs covering: the fallback order when user_locale, default_locale and `:en` are distinct; that a missing key in the user locale falls back to the default locale and then English; that `set_locale` preloads all three locales so the first `I18n.t` call after a switch does not return a missing translation; and the `uniq`/`compact` behaviour when `default_locale == :en` or `user_locale == default_locale`. Without these, regressions in fallback ordering or loading will not be caught.

Fallback array is rebuilt on every request and every translation lookup

`FallbackLocaleList#[]` allocates a fresh `[locale, SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym, :en].uniq.compact` array on every call. After this PR, it is invoked once per request by `I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!` and again on every `I18n.t` lookup through the `Fallbacks` backend. The standard `I18n::Locale::Fallbacks` memoises the result per locale. Caching the array (e.g. with a `@cache = {}` keyed by `locale.to_sym`) avoids the per-call allocation and the repeated `SiteSetting.default_locale`/`to_sym` work in the hot path.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The @loaded_locales instance variable in translate_accelerator.rb is lazily initialized and accessed by multiple concurrent threads without synchronization.

Consider normalizing the input locale (e.g., to a symbol) when checking/loading here to avoid double-loading if the same locale is passed as a String vs Symbol (also applies to other locations in the PR).

The targetOrigin must be a fixed, server-controlled value such as the configured `SiteSetting.embeddable_host` origin, not the per-request referer.

`perform_retrieve` calls `Jobs::PollFeed.new.execute({})` inline (line 41) before falling through to the HTTP fetch. This is also a concurrency hazard: concurrent retrieves can each trigger an independent synchronous poll, the job runs without Sidekiq retry/visibility, and any failure in the feed poll propagates into the per-URL retrieve. false_positives.candidate:
Webhook endpoint allows writing credentials for arbitrary user IDs with a single shared secret

The endpoint authenticates the caller only with a single shared header secret (lines 24-29). Once that secret is known (it is shared by every Cal.com deployment enabling this feature and there is no per-tenant signing), any caller can POST `{userId: <int>, appSlug, keys}` and overwrite that user's credentials. `userId` is a sequential integer from the users table, so attackers can iterate. There is no per-user HMAC, no per-deployment signing key bound to the user, and no proof that the caller is authorized to manage that specific user's third-party account. Concretely this lets one compromised self-host instance push attacker-controlled OAuth tokens (which can include an `access_token` issued to the attacker's account on Google/Microsoft/Zoom/etc.) into any user's Cal.com account, which the app will then use to read/insert calendar events and create meetings on behalf of the victim. Also note the header comparison `req.headers[name] !== secret` is non-constant-time and will throw/always-fail if the header is sent twice (Next.js parses duplicate headers as an array).

SalesforceCalendarService.refreshes access token on every getClient() call

Lines 75-100 unconditionally POST to Salesforce's token endpoint inside `getClient`, then overwrite `credential.key` in the database, even when the existing access token is still valid. `getClient` is called once per service instance (line 57), so a service that is held across many operations will refresh exactly once per construction - but more importantly, every API operation that constructs a new `SalesforceCalendarService` (which is the typical usage pattern in this repo, see e.g. how other CalendarService implementations are instantiated per-call) hits Salesforce for a token refresh whether or not refresh is required. This both wastes a refresh_token use (Salesforce will eventually return `invalid_grant` once the refresh token rotates out) and can trip rate limits. Refresh should be gated on token expiry, mirroring the other integrations (`isExpired` checks before calling refresh).

fetch() to sync endpoint has no Content-Type header and no auth

The body is `new URLSearchParams({...})` but no `Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded` header is set, so the receiving server is not guaranteed to parse the body as a form (it will see an empty body in many frameworks, and `calcomUserId`/`appSlug` will be undefined server-side, making every refresh call effectively a no-op). Additionally, there is no authentication on this outbound call: the sync endpoint cannot distinguish a request coming from this Cal.com instance from any other HTTP client that knows the URL. The endpoint should at minimum require a shared secret / signature header that the self-hoster validates.

Sync endpoint HTTP errors are not detected; raw Response is returned

The function returns the `Response` object unconditionally (line 15) without checking `response.ok`. If the self-hoster's sync endpoint returns 401/403/429/500, the raw error response body is handed to downstream code as if it were a successful token response, then parsed with the (already broken) `minimumTokenResponseSchema` and discarded, leaving the credential unchanged on disk with no error logged. The caller has no way to know refresh failed. A `if (!response.ok) throw new Error(...)` is required, and the function should surface token refresh failures.

findFirst + create/update on credentials is not atomic (race condition / duplicate rows)

Lines 62-90 do a `findFirst` followed by either `update` or `create` on `prisma.credential` based on whether a row was found. There is no transaction or unique constraint check; if two webhook calls for the same (userId, appId) race (e.g. the self-hoster retries, or a user reinstalls while a webhook is in flight), both can observe no existing row and both `create`, producing two credential rows for the same user/app. Subsequent refresh/lookup code in this repo commonly uses `findFirst` for these (e.g. office365video callback line 79 does `findMany` and deletes duplicates by hand, but the webhook path does not), which means the duplicate row will be silently picked up by whichever path queries first and the other becomes dead weight (or causes the wrong row to be updated). The (userId, appId) pair needs a unique constraint or the write needs to use an upsert/transaction.

Decryption failure and bad payload not handled

`symmetricDecrypt` will throw if the encrypted blob is malformed or the key is wrong, and `JSON.parse` will throw if the decrypted plaintext is not valid JSON. Neither is caught, so the handler returns a 500 with the stack trace leaking to the caller instead of a 4xx with a clear message. Also, after a successful decrypt+parse, `keys` is `unknown` (since it is `JSON.parse(...)`); it is written to `credential.key` without any schema check (no zod, no type guard), so any JSON object - including something that isn't a valid OAuth token shape - will be persisted. At minimum the handler should validate `keys` is an object with the fields the downstream app actually expects, and wrap the decrypt+parse in try/catch returning 400.

The `refreshOAuthTokens` function is passed `credentialId` instead of `userId`, which breaks the credential sync functionality by causing incorrect user lookups. This issue can lead to failures in syncing user credentials, impacting user experience.

The Salesforce integration checks `response.statusText` instead of `response.ok` when handling OAuth token refresh responses. This can lead to unreliable behavior, as a successful response may not be correctly identified, resulting in the use of stale credentials and potential authentication failures.

The `jsforce.Connection` is created using stale `credentialKey.access_token` and `credentialKey.instance_url` after a token refresh, which can lead to authentication failures and incorrect data access. Ensure that the connection is established using the refreshed token values instead.

The `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse` function can throw on invalid payloads, resulting in 500 Internal Server Errors instead of the expected 400 Bad Request responses. This can lead to confusion for clients and hinder proper error handling.

When SendGrid returns an error (e.g., 100 pending cancellations reached, or batch already dispatched) the only record is a console line and the email still goes out.

`if (referenceId) { await twilio.cancelSMS(referenceId); }` followed by `prisma.workflowReminder.delete(...)` inside a single try means that if `twilio.cancelSMS` rejects, the catch block runs and the DB row is never deleted. Combined with the cascade delete on the booking, this is bounded, but the row will live forever in the (rarer) case of an SMS scheduling retry or a bug elsewhere that cancels a non-existent SID.

The `for (const reminder of remindersToCancel)` loop (lines 56–73) calls `await client.request(...)` and pushes the DB delete into `workflowRemindersToDelete`. The whole block is inside a single `try { ... } catch (error) { console.log(...) }`. When any SendGrid call rejects (very likely once you approach the 100‑pending‑cancel cap, which is the very issue this PR exists to mitigate), the for-of terminates, none of the remaining reminders in `remindersToCancel` are processed in this run, and the partial `workflowRemindersToDelete` is never `Promise.all`'d. The next run will only re-pick those whose `scheduledDate` is still within the next hour; everything else is silently lost and the email goes out. Consider processing each reminder in its own try/catch (or `Promise.allSettled`) so a single failure does not abort the rest.

`remindersToCancel` is processed one SendGrid call at a time inside a `for ... of` with no `Promise.all`/`allSettled` and no explicit batch size. If a spike of cancellations lands within the one-hour window (the case the PR is built for), the CRON's 15-minute budget can easily be exceeded; at scale it will also amplify the chance of hitting SendGrid's 100‑pending‑cancellation limit per request. Batching the SendGrid calls (or at least running them in parallel with a concurrency limit) would reduce wall time and make the CRON more predictable.

The condition for rendering the phone-number block was changed from `(isPhoneNumberNeeded || isSenderIdNeeded)` to `isPhoneNumberNeeded`. The regex `replaceAll("_[a-zA-Z-_]*\\.properties", "_en.properties")` contains the character class `[a-zA-Z-_]`. In Java regex, the dash '-' that is not at the start or end of the class and not escaped is interpreted as a range operator. With the previous 'A-Z' range ending at 'Z' (0x5A), the '-_' is parsed as a range from 'Z' (0x5A) to '_' (0x5F), which silently adds '[', '\', ']', '^', and '_' to the matched character set. The author clearly intended `[a-zA-Z_]` (or `[a-zA-Z_-]` with '-' placed last so it is a literal). For typical locale codes (letters + underscore) this happens to work, but the regex is incorrect and could match unintended characters in path components containing '[', '\', etc. Fix by writing `[a-zA-Z_-]` (dash at the end of the class, making it literal) or `[a-zA-Z_]`.

Stale Matcher iterates over the original string while value is mutated In `santizeAnchors`, `Matcher matcher = ANCHOR_PATTERN.matcher(value)` is created once against the original `value`, but `value` is reassigned inside the loop via `value = value.replaceFirst(...)`. Java's Matcher retains a reference to the original CharSequence and continues iterating from where it left off in that original buffer even after `value` now points to a newly-allocated string. Consequence: the matcher can 'find' anchors that have already been removed from the current `value`, and conversely can miss anchors that only exist in the modified string. With repeated anchors (e.g. translation `a b` vs English `x`), iteration will process the second `` against an exhausted EnglishMatcher and report "Didn't find anchor tag ... in original string", producing a false-positive. The fix is to either (a) re-create `matcher = ANCHOR_PATTERN.matcher(value)` after each `replaceFirst`, or (b) iterate via `Matcher.results()` and build a new string, or (c) tokenize the string with the matcher and rebuild.

replaceFirst only removes the first occurrence of a repeated anchor

`value.replaceFirst(Pattern.quote(englishMatcher.group()), "")` only replaces the FIRST match in `value`, not all matches. If a translation legitimately reuses the same anchor tag more than once and the English source only has one occurrence, only the first occurrence is stripped; the remaining occurrences are then passed to the OWASP sanitizer, which (with `POLICY_SOME_HTML` not allowing `<a>`) will escape them and produce a spurious "Illegal HTML" error. Combined with the stale-Matcher issue above, the second `<a href="X">` is also reported as "Didn't find anchor tag ... in original string". Use `replaceAll`, or iterate via the matcher and reconstruct the string, to handle repeated anchors correctly.

Comment mischaracterises '<1>' as a "numeric tag"

The comment states the sanitizer escapes 'numeric tags like `<1>`'. There is no concept of a numeric tag in HTML or in the OWASP sanitizer; the sanitizer simply treats the literal text `<1>` as an invalid HTML tag (because tag names must start with a letter per the policy) and escapes the '<' and '>' characters. `<1>` here is an i18next / React-Intl style indexed placeholder, not a numeric tag. The wording will mislead future maintainers about what the sanitizer is doing and why `<1>` survives the round-trip via `unescapeHtml4`.

Breaking change to i18next escape syntax in JS-side resource bundle

The value of `error-invalid-multivalued-size` was changed from `Attribute {{0}} must have at least {{1}} and at most {{2}} value(s).` to `Attribute {0} must have at least {1} and at most {2} {2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}.`. The double-brace form `{{0}}` / `{{1}}` / `{{2}}` is i18next's escape syntax for producing literal `{0}`/`{1}`/`{2}` text, which is what account-ui uses. After this change, i18next will interpret `{0}`, `{1}`, `{2}` and the `{2,choice,...}` clause as placeholders / interpolation tokens. i18next does not implement Java MessageFormat choice format, and `{2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}` is not valid i18next interpolation syntax, so the message will either fail to interpolate or be displayed verbatim with broken `{...}` text instead of the localized error. The previous value (`value(s)`) was a deliberate, working i18next-compatible rendering of the message; this PR regresses that. The new format belongs only on the Java side (e.g. `themes/src/main/resources/theme/base/login/messages/messages_en.properties`), where it does belong.

Same i18next breaking change in admin-ui resource bundle

Same regression as in the account-ui bundle: `error-invalid-multivalued-size` changed from `Attribute {{0}} must have at least {{1}} and at most {{2}} value(s).` to Java MessageFormat syntax (`{0}`, `{1}`, `{2,choice,...}`). The admin-ui is also a React/i18next app, so the change replaces working placeholder-escaping with placeholders that i18next will try to interpolate, and embeds a Java MessageFormat choice clause (`{2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}`) that i18next does not understand. Result at runtime: malformed interpolation and/or broken/untranslated text shown to the admin user.

No positive test that valid HTML in a translation is accepted The four new tests only assert that illegal HTML is detected (`verifyIllegalHtmlTagDetected`, `verifyNoHtmlAllowed`, `verifyNoChangedAnchors`) and that duplicates are detected. There is no positive test that exercises the happy path of `verifySafeHtml`: e.g. an English value containing `bar` and a translation containing `bar` (or `bar`) that should NOT be reported. Without it, a regression in the sanitizer flow (e.g. always escaping ``) would not be caught by the test suite. Add a test resource pair (`allowedHtml_en.properties` + `allowedHtml_de.properties`) with matching allowed tags and assert that the message list does not contain "Illegal HTML".

No test for the `{2,choice,...}` normalization of `error-invalid-multivalued-size`

`normalizeValue` strips `{N,choice,...}` clauses for `linkExpirationFormatter.timePeriodUnit.*` and `error-invalid-multivalued-size` specifically. This special case is central to the PR because that key was just rewritten across every bundle to use this Java MessageFormat choice syntax. There is no test fixture nor assertion that (a) a translation whose choice clause differs from the English (e.g. different `1#value|1<values` text) is still accepted, and (b) a translation with literal `<` outside a choice clause is rejected. The whole point of this PR is to make `error-invalid-multivalued-size` valid, but the only protection against regressing it is the production code itself, with no regression test in `VerifyMessagePropertiesTest`.

File is read and parsed twice per verification

`verify()` reads the file with `Files.readString(file.toPath())` for duplicate-key detection, and then `verifySafeHtml()` opens another `FileInputStream` and parses the same file as `PropertyResourceBundle`. The two reads produce no consistency guarantee (a file could change between reads) and double the I/O. Either parse once into a `PropertyResourceBundle` and reuse it for both checks, or read the bytes once and wrap them in two parsers. Not a correctness bug, but the verifier runs over hundreds of message bundles during a theme build, so the duplication is non-trivial.

Trailing newline stripped from `error-invalid-multivalued-size`

The unified diff shows the file ends with `\ No newline at end of file` after this change (the `-` line also had `\ No newline at end of file`). Many editors, linters, and POSIX text tools require files to end with a newline, and several Keycloak bundles historically did so. The fact that the previous version ended without a newline was already a minor smell, but the change also touches a line at the end of the file without restoring the newline. This will show up as a noisy diff in future PRs and may violate any project policy on POSIX file endings.

false_positives.candidate:
Matcher isAccessTokenId slices wrong characters for the grant shortcut

The encoded prefix has layout [session 0-1][token 2-3][grant 4-5], so the grant shortcut is at indices 4-5. The matcher uses `items[0].substring(3, 5)`, which returns the last character of the token type and the first character of the grant type, not the grant type itself. It should be `substring(4, 6)`. Combined with the inverted logic, the matcher never actually verifies the grant type and accepts any 6-char prefix as long as the UUID part is valid.

TokenContextEncoderSpi marked internal, contradicts stated extensibility goal

`isInternal()` returns `true`, which in Keycloak restricts the SPI to a single implementation (the default). The PR description explicitly motivates the SPI by saying 'provider adds ability for someone to introduce his own provider'. To match that intent, `isInternal()` must return `false`, otherwise third parties cannot supply an alternative encoder.

Public copy constructor of OAuth2GrantType.Context removed without notice

The previous public `Context(Context context)` copy constructor is deleted by this PR. The constructor was on a public nested class of a public SPI, so any downstream code that created derived or copied Contexts will fail to compile. The PR description does not call out this removal, and there is no replacement, so this is an undocumented SPI breaking change.

Constant name GRANT_TYPE is misleading

`public static final String GRANT_TYPE = OAuth2Constants.GRANT_TYPE;` resolves to the literal string `"grant_type"`, which is a key name used as a `ClientSessionContext` attribute key, not a grant-type value. The name suggests a grant type such as `authorization_code`. Either the constant should be renamed to make clear it is a session-context attribute key (e.g. `CLIENT_SESSION_CTX_GRANT_TYPE`) or the Javadoc should explain it is the OAuth2 parameter/attribute name, not a grant type value, to avoid misuse such as `ctx.getAttribute(Constants.GRANT_TYPE, OAuth2Constants.AUTHORIZATION_CODE)` style calls.

getTokenContextFromTokenId does not handle null encodedTokenId

`getTokenContextFromTokenId(String encodedTokenId)` immediately calls `encodedTokenId.indexOf(':')` with no null check. If a caller passes null (for example from `token.getId()` returning null), this throws an NPE instead of returning the UNKNOWN/UNKNOWN/UNKNOWN/encodedTokenId context the method otherwise provides for unencoded ids. It should guard against null and treat it the same as an old (unprefixed) id.

getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext NPEs on null userSession

`clientSessionContext.getClientSession().getUserSession()` is dereferenced for both `getPersistenceState()` and `isOffline()` without a null check. In some flows (e.g. when a client session is not yet bound to a user session, or in OID4VCI issuance paths that build a token without a persisted user session) this can be null, producing an NPE in the encoder. The provider should treat a null userSession as UNKNOWN rather than failing token issuance.

Dynamic grant-type insertion is racy and can corrupt the shortcut maps

Both `getShortcutByGrantType` and `getGrantTypeByShortcut` do a non-atomic check-then-put into the `ConcurrentHashMap`s. Two threads can simultaneously take the `null` branch and both write. More importantly, nothing prevents a new grant factory from registering with a shortcut that collides with an existing one after `postInit`, which silently overwrites the existing entry in `grantsByShortcuts` and corrupts lookups in both directions; the startup-only size check in `postInit` does not protect against this hot path.

Federated recovery codes not marked as used after validation

In `isValid()` for `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE`, the implementation returns true as soon as the input matches any raw key in `myUser.recoveryCodes.getCredentialData()` but never mutates the stored credential to remove or flag the consumed code. Recovery codes are one-time-use credentials; the local `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider` marks codes as used when validated. Here the same code can be reused indefinitely, so the security guarantee of recovery codes is lost whenever the user lives in federated storage.

Federated recovery-codes credential can never be removed

Because `isValid()` does not track per-code consumption, the `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel` built by `getCredentials()` from the stored raw `credentialData` will always have `allCodesUsed() == false`. Consequently the branch in `RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator.isRecoveryAuthnCodeInputValid` that calls `credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(...)` will never run for a federated user, so the recovery-codes credential sticks around forever, the user is never re-prompted via `CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES`, and the user storage is never asked to delete the credential.

Raw recovery codes persisted in federated credentialData

`updateCredential` saves the JSON produced by `CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential` (which serializes the raw codes) straight into `credentialData` without hashing. The local `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider` hashes the codes before storage (it relies on `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.hashRawCode` with `NOM_ALGORITHM_TO_HASH`). Storing raw codes in `credentialData` diverges from that posture, so any path that exposes `credentialData` (DB dumps, debug logging, serialized credential model) leaks the user's recovery codes in plaintext. The model reconstructed by `getCredentials()` will also carry these raw codes through `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues`, so callers that read `RecoveryCode.getValue()` get the cleartext code.

Test does not verify single-use semantics or credential cleanup

`testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin` only exercises a single successful entry of one recovery code. Given that `RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator.isRecoveryAuthnCodeInputValid` now also targets federated credentials (via `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential`), the test should additionally assert that (a) re-entering the same recovery code is rejected by the federated validator, and (b) once the last code is consumed, the federated credential is removed and the user is asked to configure new codes. Without these assertions the two real bugs above are not caught by CI.

The method `SpanFlusher._create_process_for_shard(shard)` (lines 127-132) is defined but has no callers. With `flusher_processes=2` and 4 shards, the docstring is misleading and the round-robin assignment also has performance implications (e.g., adjacent shards can end up in different processes and cross shard/processes). The docstring should describe the actual grouping behavior.

CLI help for `--flusher-processes` is misleading

`help="Maximum number of processes for the span flusher. Defaults to 1."` implies that passing e.g. `--flusher-processes 8` always gives 8 processes. In reality `SpanFlusher.__init__` clamps via `self.num_processes = min(self.max_processes, len(buffer.assigned_shards))`, and the help also describes the CLI default of 1 rather than the SpanFlusher default of `len(assigned_shards)`. If a user passes a value greater than the number of assigned partitions, they will silently get fewer processes than expected. The help should note the cap.

`flusher_processes=0` is silently coerced to `len(assigned_shards)`

In `SpanFlusher.__init__`, `self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` treats 0 as falsy and falls back to one process per shard. An operator passing `--flusher-processes 0` likely expects 'no flusher' or an error, not a default-override that spawns more processes than they asked for. Use an explicit `None` check instead of `or`, or document/validate that 0 is not accepted.

`test_flusher_processes_limit` never submits a message

The new test only asserts `len(flusher.processes) == 2`, `flusher.max_processes == 2`, `flusher.num_processes == 2` and that 4 shards are present in `process_to_shards_map`. It does not submit a payload, does not advance drift, and does not assert that any segment reaches the `produce_to_pipe`. The whole point of the multiprocess refactor is that shards split across processes are still flushed end-to-end; this test will silently pass even if the new `_create_process_for_shards` does not correctly wire shards to buffers or if the threading path is broken. Add at least one submit + flush assertion that exercises the cross-process flusher wiring.

`if not process:` guard in `_ensure_processes_alive` is dead

`self.processes` is populated in `_create_process_for_shards` and never has `None` values, so `if not process: continue` (line 222) is unreachable. Either remove the check or, if the intent was to skip dead slots, document why None entries would ever appear (e.g., a future graceful-shutdown slot).

Per-submit Redis memory probe now scales with process count

Original code did one `self.buffer.get_memory_info()` call per submit. New code iterates `for buffer in self.buffers.values(): memory_infos.extend(buffer.get_memory_info())`, so the consumer issues N Redis probes per submit where N equals the number of flusher processes (up to one per shard). Even though `submit` is described as not hot, on every call we now do N network round-trips to gather data that conceptually represents the same underlying Redis memory. Consider caching or aggregating memory info once per flush cycle instead of once per submit.

`process.kill()` followed by immediate respawn can produce duplicate flushes

In `_ensure_processes_alive`, the unhealthy process is `kill()`-ed (non-blocking) and `_create_process_for_shards` is invoked immediately. The old subprocess may still be alive for some time (kill delivery, Redis I/O in flight), during which both the old and new flusher processes can independently call `buffer.flush_segments` and `producer.produce` on the same shard. That can produce duplicate `BUFFERED_SEGMENTS` messages on Kafka. The original code had a similar race but only one flusher existed; now that shards are shared across processes, the blast radius is wider. Consider `process.join(timeout)` before respawn, or use `terminate()` plus a join so the previous process truly exits first.

`process_restarts` threshold allows one more restart than the constant suggests

The check is `if self.process_restarts[process_index] > MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS`, followed by increment + respawn. Tracing the counter: it starts at 0, is checked then incremented. With `MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS = 10` the counter reaches 11 before `11 > 10` triggers, so the consumer actually restarts the process 11 times before raising, not 10. This is an off-by-one that pre-dates this PR, but it is worth aligning either the constant (to `MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS - 1`) or the comparison (`>= MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS`) so the cap matches the name.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
Negative-offset path is misleadingly documented and unsafe

The `enable_advanced_features and cursor.offset < 0` branch claims in its comments that 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically', that it 'enables access to data beyond normal pagination bounds', and that 'This is safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level'. None of these are true: Django translates `queryset[-N:M]` into `LIMIT (M-N) OFFSET -N`, which PostgreSQL rejects as a non-positive OFFSET, so the request 500s. The framing of 'efficient bidirectional pagination' misrepresents what negative slicing does — it returns the last N rows of the queryset, not an arbitrary position. The 'safe because permissions' justification conflates row-level authorization (which the queryset already enforces) with pagination-boundary integrity; allowing a client to choose a negative offset bypasses the `offset >= 0` invariant that BasePaginator and the rest of the pagination pipeline assume. The whole branch should be removed; it adds no legitimate functionality and exists only behind a parameter that is already gated to superusers, which makes the misleading comments more concerning.

true_positives.golden_comment: get_item_key assumes a numeric key, but the paginator is used with order_by=-datetime in the audit logs endpoint; calling math.floor/ceil on a datetime will raise a TypeError.

OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key does `value = getattr(item, self.key)` and then `int(math.floor(value) ... )`. When used with `order_by="-datetime"` (as the new audit-logs endpoint does), `value` is a `datetime` object, and `math.floor(datetime)` raises `TypeError: float argument required, not datetime.datetime`. The existing DateTimePaginator has special handling (`float(value.strftime("%s.%f")) * self.multiplier`) for exactly this reason; OptimizedCursorPaginator is essentially a copy of `Paginator` (numeric-only) and is not a drop-in replacement for DateTimePaginator. The new `?optimized_pagination=true` path on the audit logs endpoint will 500 for any superuser/global-admin caller.

The caller (BasePaginator.build_queryset) substitutes it into `WHERE <col> <= %s`, producing a comparison between a `datetime` column and an integer like `... WHERE datetime <= 1699999999000`, which PostgreSQL rejects with `operator does not exist: timestamp without time zone >= integer`. DateTimePaginator converts the integer back to a datetime; OptimizedCursorPaginator does not. Together with the get_item_key issue, the optimized audit-logs path is broken end-to-end.

The PR title and description only mention audit logs and contain no mention of this base-class change, so reviewers of the other endpoints will not see it. The accompanying comment ('allow negative offsets to enable efficient bidirectional pagination') is the opposite of what the code does for non-prev cursors — it clamps negative offsets to 0, restricting rather than allowing them. Previously, two concurrent calls to `BuildIndex` for the same `key` were serialized, so `bleve.New(dir, mapper)` (lines ~96-102) was only ever invoked once per directory. With the new finer-grained locking, two callers that race through `getOrCreateIndex` for the same key when `size > b.opts.FileThreshold` will both call `bleve.New(dir, mapper)` on the same directory. bleve's New on an already-existing directory either errors or reopens stale state; one call returns an error to a caller even though the index they wanted was successfully created and is sitting in the cache. `searchSupport.getOrCreateIndex` already has a TODO admitting it has no per-key mutex, so this relaxation of the backend's serialization makes a known race easier to trigger. `NewResourceServer` now passes its locally constructed `ctx` (a `context.WithCancel(context.Background(), ...)` wrapping a static service-account identity) into `s.Init(ctx)`.
