In `FixedQueuePool.__init__`, each work queue is created with `queue.Queue()` (no maxsize). The class docstring promises 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up', but there is no fill - the queues are infinite. If a single group is slow or backed up (e.g. one subscription id hashes to the same queue and processing of one item blocks for a long time, or that group simply gets a burst of messages), items accumulate forever. Each `WorkItem` holds a reference to the original `Message` (and therefore the decoded `result` plus `KafkaPayload`), so the memory footprint is non-trivial. An unbounded queue in front of a single-worker-per-queue setup is a straightforward OOM risk and contradicts the docstring.

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.join ignores its timeout parameter

`SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.join(self, timeout: float | None = None)` accepts a timeout but does not use it - it just calls `self.close()`. The arroyo framework passes a deadline via this argument so it knows how long to wait for graceful shutdown before forcefully terminating. By ignoring the timeout the strategy can exceed the caller's deadline, causing the consumer to be killed by the orchestrator and any in-flight offsets to be left as 'outstanding' (forcing re-delivery on the next start). `join` should propagate `timeout` to `self.commit_thread.join(timeout=...)` and to `FixedQueuePool.shutdown`/worker joins, and `close()` should also respect a deadline.

commit_function failure leaves offsets un-committed in the tracker and is silently retried forever

In `_commit_loop`, `self.commit_function(committable)` is called and only on success does the loop mark the offsets via `mark_committed`. If the commit raises (Kafka unavailable, broker timeout, etc.), the whole `except Exception` just logs and the same offsets are returned by the next `get_committable_offsets()` call and retried. Two problems: (1) if the commit partially succeeded before raising, the same offsets get re-committed to Kafka (duplicate commit), and (2) there is no backoff or alerting, so a persistent failure becomes an infinite tight retry loop that floods the logs and pegs CPU. The metric `remote_subscriptions.queue_pool.offsets_committed` is also incremented before the commit call, so it counts 'attempted' rather than 'succeeded' commits, which is misleading.

get_committable_offsets does an O(max_offset) scan per partition

`get_committable_offsets` iterates `for offset in range(start, max_offset + 1)` looking for the highest contiguous committed offset. If a partition has a small offset (e.g. 100) and a very large one (e.g. 1_000_000) - whether from a bug, rebalance after restart, or just a sparse stream - this allocates and walks ~1M ints per call, every second, from the commit thread. For a multi-partition topic with any sparse offsets this can dominate CPU. The check should walk the sorted `outstanding` set instead of scanning the integer range.

Group-to-queue assignment uses Python's randomized hash()

`get_queue_for_group` is `return hash(group_key) % self.num_queues`. Python's built-in `hash()` for strings is salted by `PYTHONHASHSEED` and is therefore not stable across processes. Within a single consumer lifetime the assignment is consistent (so per-group ordering is preserved), but after a restart the same subscription id may land on a different queue and worker. This is undocumented and brittle - if anything ever relies on a stable group->queue mapping across restarts (e.g. for deterministic drain order on partial shutdown, or for replay tooling), it will silently break. Use a stable hash like `hashlib.md5(group_key.encode()).digest()` or `zlib.crc32(group_key.encode())`.

submit() silently drops messages whose value is not a BrokerValue when an error occurs

In `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit`, the `except Exception` handler only marks the offset complete when `isinstance(message.value, BrokerValue)`. If the message value is anything else (e.g. an `ImpulseValue` or any future arroyo value type) and either the decoder raises or the `assert isinstance(message.value, BrokerValue)` itself fails, the offset is never recorded. The message disappears from the strategy but arroyo will not have been told to commit it, so on restart the same message is re-delivered. If the failure is permanent (e.g. the codec can never decode that value type) this becomes an infinite redelivery of poison messages, with no observability beyond the one log entry.

The new `OptimizedCursorPaginator` branch uses `results = list(queryset[start_offset:stop])` with `start_offset = cursor.offset` when `cursor.offset < 0`. Django's `QuerySet.__getitem__` asserts `k.start >= 0` and raises `AssertionError('Negative indexing is not supported.')` on any slice whose `start` is negative. Therefore the only thing the 'advanced feature' does is make the request raise 500. The accompanying comment 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is false. The audit logs endpoint unconditionally passes `enable_advanced_features=True`, so any client that supplies a cursor with a negative offset (or any code path that constructs one) will crash.

false_positives.candidate:
Redirect-follow loop limit lowered from 10000 to 1000 silently breaks deep segment trees

The previous code used `for i = 0, 10000 do` and carried a comment explaining that exceeding this limit means segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly. The new code lowers the bound to `for i = 0, 1000 do` without any rationale, so any trace whose redirect chain exceeds 1000 hops will resolve to a `set_span_id` that is not the true root. The subsequent `zunionstore`/`zpopmin` will then operate on the wrong set, leaving the actual root segment orphaned and producing an incomplete or empty flushed segment. This is a silent data-integrity regression for deep traces.

Default SUM aggregate in ZUNIONSTORE corrupts `end_timestamp_precise` scores for duplicate payloads

`zunionstore set_key 2 set_key span_key` is invoked with the implicit default `AGGREGATE SUM`. If a member (span payload) ever exists in both `set_key` and `span_key` (which can occur on Kafka retries or any path where the same payload was inserted twice with different timestamps), its score after the union becomes the arithmetic sum of the two timestamps rather than either one. Those scores drive eviction (`zpopmin`) and any downstream ordering; a corrupted score means the wrong spans get evicted and the 'oldest-first' eviction contract is broken. The script should pass an explicit `AGGREGATE MIN` (or `MAX`) to preserve a single timestamp per payload.

Span NamedTuple adds a required field in the middle, breaking positional construction

`Span` is a public NamedTuple exported from `sentry.spans.buffer`. The new `end_timestamp_precise: float` is inserted between `payload` and `is_segment_span`, has no default, and shifts `is_segment_span` to the last position. Any caller that constructs `Span(...)` positionally (the 7th argument previously implied `is_segment_span`) will silently mis-bind: a positional `True` becomes the `end_timestamp_precise` value and `is_segment_span` defaults to `False`, causing incorrect is-segment logic downstream. It also breaks unpickling of old `Span` pickles and any external code that mirrors this shape. The field should be added at the end (with a default) or supplied only via keyword to preserve positional compatibility.

Removed `max_segment_spans` Python guard while Lua hardcodes a different (1000) limit

The old `_load_segment_data` had `if len(payloads[key]) > self.max_segment_spans: ... skip segment`. This guard is deleted, so the only cap on segment size is the new Lua eviction at line 62 (`if span_count > 1000 then redis.call('zpopmin', set_key, span_count - 1000) end`). Two issues: (1) `SpansBuffer.__init__` still accepts and stores `max_segment_bytes`/`max_segment_spans`, so the configurable Python limit is now dead and will diverge from the Lua hardcode if anyone changes the constant. (2) The Lua limit is 1000 but `max_segment_spans` defaults to 1001, so the effective cap silently drops by 1. If the Lua eviction is bypassed (e.g., a Redis upgrade changes `ZUNIONSTORE` cardinality semantics, or a future code path skips the script), there is no Python backstop and segments can grow unbounded.

OptimizedCursorPaginator duplicates BasePaginator without any actual optimization

`OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result` is a near-verbatim copy of `BasePaginator.get_result`. The only behavioral difference is the `enable_advanced_features and cursor.offset < 0` branch (which, per the other finding, crashes Django). There is no optimized query path, no streamlined boundary handling, and no measurable performance benefit. The docstring's claims of 'performance optimizations for high-traffic endpoints' and 'Optimized query path for large datasets' are unsubstantiated. A subclass that only adds one (broken) branch is significant duplication that will drift from the base implementation.

Comments and docstrings lie about safety, optimization, and Django support

Several new comments are misleading: (1) `paginator.py` line 179: 'Performance optimization: ... allow negative offsets to enable efficient bidirectional pagination' — the change actually clamps non-prev offsets to 0, it does not allow them. (2) `paginator.py` line 877: 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' — Django explicitly asserts `k.start >= 0` and raises on negative slicing. (3) `paginator.py` line 879: 'This is safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level' — permissions don't gate which rows an offset selects, only which rows the queryset can see; an admin user can still trigger a crash or expensive scan. (4) `organization_auditlogs.py` lines 68-76 repeat the same false framing about 'optimized paginator for high-performance' navigation. (5) `cursors.py` lines 26-27 add a 'Performance optimization' comment over a line that is byte-identical to the original. These comments will mislead future maintainers about the actual semantics and risks.

`max(0, offset)` silently changes BasePaginator behavior for callers passing negative non-prev offsets

The diff replaces `results = list(queryset[offset:stop])` with `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset`. For non-prev cursors, any negative `cursor.offset` previously propagated to Django (which would raise on negative slicing); now the offset is silently clamped to 0 and the first page is returned as if no cursor were supplied. Any caller that intentionally relied on the old raise-on-bad-cursor semantics (e.g., for validation) will instead get a wrong page returned with no error. The change is presented as a 'performance optimization' rather than a behavior change; if the intent really is to silently coerce, that contract should be explicit and documented.

Rolling deploy will see WRONGTYPE errors until old SET data expires

The new code treats every `span-buf:s:*` and `span-buf:sr:*` key as a sorted set (`zcard`, `zunionstore`, `zpopmin`). The previous version stored these as plain Redis sets (`sunionstore`, `scard`). Any keys written by the old version that are still within their TTL will cause `WRONGTYPE Operation against a key holding the wrong kind of value` errors on the next `EVALSHA` of this script, crashing the consumer's `process_spans` pipeline. There is no migration step in the diff, no versioned key prefix, and no defensive `TYPE` check in the Lua script. This will produce a noisy, multi-TTL-window outage during cutover in any environment with non-empty Redis state.

No tests for new eviction logic, score semantics, or OptimizedCursorPaginator

The Lua eviction block lines 58-64 (`if span_count > 1000 then zpopmin ...`) and the SUM-aggregate implication of `zunionstore` are entirely untested: no test inserts >1000 spans into a single segment to verify the eviction, no test verifies that `end_timestamp_precise` is preserved through unions, and no test exercises the off-by-one between the Lua cap (1000) and `max_segment_spans` (1001). Likewise `OptimizedCursorPaginator` (paginator.py lines 821-911) has no tests at all - not for the normal path, not for the negative-offset branch, and not for the `enable_advanced_features` flag. Without tests, the silent regressions above (redirect loop reduction, score corruption, Django crash) cannot be caught.

Denial cache can return stale results when permissions change

The permDenialCache is only ever written (at line 154) and never invalidated when a user's permissions change. Because the denial-cache lookup at line 117 runs before the permission cache (line 123) and the DB requery, a stale denial entry will short-circuit the request and return Allowed=false even after the user has been granted access. With shortCacheTTL = 30s, any grant that lands within 30s of an earlier deny will be ignored. Concrete scenario: user is denied → denial entry written; admin grants access via role/team within 30s; next Check returns false even though both the DB and the (refreshed) permission cache would now allow it. If the parent folder is later moved under an ancestor that the user does have access to, a previously-cached denial for (user, action, name, parent) will keep returning false for up to 30s even though the inherited permission check would now succeed. Example: dashboard X in folder A (user lacks access) → denial entry written; folder A is moved under folder B (user has access); user checks X → denial hit → denied. userPermDenialCacheKey is keyed by namespace + userUID + action + name + parent, where action is derived from (group, resource, verb). SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym raises NoMethodError when default_locale is nil

`FallbackLocaleList#[]` evaluates `SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym` on every call, and `FallbackLocaleList#ensure_loaded!` (called from `ApplicationController#set_locale` on every request) also reaches this expression. If `SiteSetting.default_locale` is nil (e.g. before the site settings row exists, during a fresh install/seed, or in a misconfigured environment), `to_sym` raises NoMethodError and crashes the request. The trailing `.compact` does not guard this case, because the exception is raised before `compact` runs. Use a safe form such as `[locale, SiteSetting.default_locale&.to_sym, :en].compact.uniq` and ensure there is at least one non-nil element.

FallbackLocaleList inherits from Hash but does not implement the I18n::Locale::Fallbacks contract

The class replaces the standard `I18n::Locale::Fallbacks` (which itself extends Hash) but only overrides `[]` and adds `ensure_loaded!`. The real class also defines `[]=`, `defaults`, and `defaults=`. With this replacement, any caller that does `I18n.fallbacks[locale] = [...]` or reads/writes `I18n.fallbacks.defaults` will silently use Hash defaults — our `[]` always recomputes from `SiteSetting.default_locale`, so any explicitly configured fallbacks are ignored without warning. Iterating `I18n.fallbacks.each` will likewise yield nothing because the underlying hash is empty. Either implement the missing methods (store explicit overrides and consult them before computing) or stop inheriting from Hash so the misleading API surface is removed and behaviour is explicit.

`compact` silently swallows a nil I18n.locale instead of surfacing the bug

`[locale, SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym, :en].uniq.compact` relies on `compact` to drop a nil `locale`. A nil `I18n.locale` is an upstream problem (e.g. `current_user.effective_locale` returning nil in `ApplicationController#set_locale`) and translations will still resolve via `[default_locale, :en]`, hiding the misconfiguration. Either remove `compact` so the nil propagates as a real error, or replace it with an explicit guard that logs/warns when `locale` is nil and falls back intentionally.

No specs cover the new server-side localization fallback behaviour

The diff adds a non-trivial behaviour change (custom `FallbackLocaleList` with a `[locale, SiteSetting.default_locale, :en]` chain, eager loading via `I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!` from a `before_filter`, and a new `I18n.ensure_loaded!` patch in `translate_accelerator.rb`) but ships without any test files. At minimum there should be specs covering: the fallback order when user_locale, default_locale and `:en` are distinct; that a missing key in the user locale falls back to the default locale and then English; that `set_locale` preloads all three locales so the first `I18n.t` call after a switch does not return a missing translation; and the `uniq`/`compact` behaviour when `default_locale == :en` or `user_locale == default_locale`. Without these, regressions in fallback ordering or loading will not be caught.

Fallback array is rebuilt on every request and every translation lookup

`FallbackLocaleList#[]` allocates a fresh `[locale, SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym, :en].uniq.compact` array on every call. After this PR, it is invoked once per request by `I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!` and again on every `I18n.t` lookup through the `Fallbacks` backend. The standard `I18n::Locale::Fallbacks` memoises the result per locale. Caching the array (e.g. with a `@cache = {}` keyed by `locale.to_sym`) avoids the per-call allocation and the repeated `SiteSetting.default_locale`/`to_sym` work in the hot path.

true_positives.golden_comment: The include_website_name method is missing the required ? suffix. Rails serializers expect include_ methods to end with ? for conditional attribute inclusion, a convention followed by other methods in this serializer. Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. include_website_name missing trailing question mark

The new inclusion guard is defined as `def include_website_name` (without `?`), but ActiveModel::Serializer looks for a predicate method named `include_#{attr}?` (with the `?`) to decide whether to include an attribute. Every other inclusion guard in this file uses the `?` suffix (e.g. `include_email?`, `include_card_image_badge?`, `include_stats?`, `include_suspend_reason?`, `include_suspended_till?`, `include_user_fields?`, `include_topic_post_count?`). Without the `?` the framework will not recognize this as an inclusion check, so `website_name` will be serialized whenever it is non-nil even when `website` is blank, and the `website.present?` check becomes dead code. URI(website.to_s) parsed repeatedly in website_name

`website_name` calls `URI(website.to_s)` up to three times (once for `.host`, and up to twice more for `.path` in the branches that append the path). `website` is also re-invoked via the `def website` method each time, which makes another user_profile lookup. `URI(website.to_s).path` returns only the path component; the query string and fragment are discarded. For a URL like `http://example.com/users?section=profile#bio` the displayed name will be `example.com/users`, losing information the user entered. If only the host/path is desired, that is fine, but it should be a deliberate choice; if the full URL minus scheme/userinfo is the goal then `request_uri` minus the scheme/host (or the original string with scheme stripped) would preserve the query/fragment. There is also no handling for non-ASCII/percent-encoded paths or trailing slashes (e.g. `http://example.com/` displays as `example.com/`).

Line 17 validates incoming postMessage events with `if (discourseUrl.indexOf(e.origin) === -1) { return; }`. This requires `e.origin` to be a substring of `discourseUrl`, which is the wrong shape for an origin check. It silently rejects legitimate origins whenever the configured `discourseUrl` and the browser's `e.origin` differ by a port (e.g. `http://example.com` vs `http://example.com:8080`), and conversely accepts attackers whose origin happens to be a prefix of the configured URL. true_positives.golden_comment: The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.

X-Frame-Options ALLOWALL is not a recognized value

Line 28 sets `response.headers['X-Frame-Options'] = "ALLOWALL"`. ALLOWALL is not one of the standardized values (DENY, SAMEORIGIN, or the deprecated ALLOW-FROM). Browsers that don't recognize it fall back to treating the header as absent, which means the embed page can be framed by any origin on the web, not just `SiteSetting.embeddable_host`. The intent of the referer check is undermined because the response is now freely embeddable anywhere. The recommended replacement is a `Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors <embeddable_host>` header.

#{I18n.t('embed.imported_from', link: "#{url}")} "`. The `url` originates from RSS item `link`/`id` (poll_feed.rb) or the Disqus XML import (disqus.thor), and is then persisted as `post.raw` with `cook_method = :raw_html`. Because the cooking pipeline is bypassed for `:raw_html`, the raw HTML is stored verbatim and rendered with `<%= raw post.cooked %>` in app/views/embed/best.html. A URL containing a single quote (e.g. `http://x.com/'>` attribute and injects arbitrary HTML/JS that executes inside the Discourse iframe origin. The XSS is persistent in a post authored by the configured `embed_by_username` (typically a privileged system user), giving the attacker the ability to act as that user against the Discourse API.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same unescaped URL interpolation and resulting XSS vulnerability in TopicEmbed.import. It does not mention the additional nil-contents NoMethodError, but directly matches the golden comment's XSS concern.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
NoMethodError if RSS items lack a content element

Line 35 calls `CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)` without a nil check. RSS and Atom feeds vary: some items expose the body as `description`, `summary`, or `content:encoded`, and `i.content` is nil for items that only have one of the others. When that happens `.scrub` raises NoMethodError, which aborts the entire scheduled poll and prevents any items in the feed (including valid ones already in the loop) from being imported. Guard with `content = i.content && CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)` (and similarly for `i.title`).
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: calling .scrub on a potentially nil i.content when a feed lacks a content field. The candidate proposes a nil guard rather than the golden comment's description fallback, but the underlying issue matches.

false_positives.candidate:
postMessage targetOrigin is set to request.referer, which can be empty

Line 11 passes `<%= request.referer %>` as the `targetOrigin` to `parent.postMessage(...)`. The HTTP Referer header is browser-controlled and frequently null (direct navigation, referrer policies, missing header). When it is nil the rendered output becomes `parent.postMessage(..., '')`, and an empty-string targetOrigin is treated as `*` (any origin) per the HTML5 spec, leaking the iframe height to any parent window. The targetOrigin must be a fixed, server-controlled value such as the configured `SiteSetting.embeddable_host` origin, not the per-request referer.

Scheduled PollFeed job is executed synchronously inside a per-request job

`perform_retrieve` calls `Jobs::PollFeed.new.execute({})` inline (line 41) before falling through to the HTTP fetch. PollFeed downloads the entire RSS feed and processes every item, so every embed retrieval blocks on a full feed poll. This is also a concurrency hazard: concurrent retrieves can each trigger an independent synchronous poll, the job runs without Sidekiq retry/visibility, and any failure in the feed poll propagates into the per-URL retrieve. The synchronous call should be removed (let the scheduled job do its work independently) or replaced with `Jobs.enqueue(:poll_feed)`.

Race condition between TopicEmbed existence check and create

Lines 15-30 do `TopicEmbed.where(embed_url: url).first` and then, if blank, `TopicEmbed.create!` inside `Topic.transaction`. The check and the create are not atomic: two concurrent `import` calls for the same URL both observe `embed.blank?` and both proceed to `create!`, at which point the second one raises `ActiveRecord::RecordNotUnique` (the migration adds a unique index on `embed_url`). The exception is not rescued, so the post is rolled back but the caller (a job or a controller) sees an error and the user-visible 'Loading...' view loops forever. Use `find_or_create_by` with a rescue, or `TopicEmbed.lock` / an upsert to serialize the create.

embed_url column length is too small for many real URLs

Line 6 declares `t.string :embed_url, null: false`, which Rails maps to `varchar(255)` in PostgreSQL. embed_url is the lookup key used both to find the existing embed (TopicEmbed.topic_id_for_embed) and as the unique index target. Real-world embed URLs with tracking query parameters or deep paths routinely exceed 255 characters, so inserts will raise `value too long for type character varying(255)` and the import will be lost. Use `t.text` (and a btree index on a hash, or a length-bounded variant) so longer URLs are not truncated or rejected.

TopicEmbed.import mutates the caller's contents argument in place

`import` appends the `imported_from` footer to `contents` via `contents << ...` (line 13). This mutates the caller's string in place. In `poll_feed.rb` the argument is `i.content` from SimpleRSS, and in `import_remote` it is `doc.content` from Readability; both are inputs the caller may still be holding. Beyond being surprising, the mutation also changes the SHA-1 of `contents` (computed on line 16 from the now-augmented string), so the content_sha1 stored in the embed reflects the appended footer rather than the imported article body. Use `contents +` or assign to a local variable.

Stray require_dependency for unused email/sender

Line 1 has `require_dependency 'email/sender'`, but `email/sender` is not referenced anywhere in `Jobs::RetrieveTopic#execute`. It looks like a copy/paste leftover from another job. It forces Rails to load the mailer framework on every RetrieveTopic invocation for no reason; remove it.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.
The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.

An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.

The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.

Dead duplicate `downsize` method shadows real definition

Lines 145-147 define `self.downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})`, and lines 149-151 then redefine `self.downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={})`. In Ruby the second definition wins and the first is unreachable. true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).

Client-side upload validation hardcoded to 10MB, ignores site setting

The previous code read the per-type cap from `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']`; it has been replaced with a hardcoded `10 * 1024` (10MB). This is a regression: site administrators who configure `max_image_size_kb` (or `max_attachment_size_kb`) to any value other than 10240 will see inconsistent behavior. Files between the configured limit and 10MB pass the client-side check but are rejected by the server (HTTP 413); files over 10MB are rejected by the client even though the server would accept them when the configured limit is higher. The validation must continue to honor `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: hardcoding the upload limit to 10 * 1024 KB instead of honoring per-type Discourse.SiteSettings causes client-side validation to diverge from server-configured limits. The candidate matches the core issue despite not explicitly addressing the 413 handler's hardcoded limit.

true_positives.golden_comment: Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Animated GIFs cannot be downsized: gifsicle rejects percentage strings

The controller calls `OptimizedImage.downsize(tempfile.path, tempfile.path, "80%", allow_animation: SiteSetting.allow_animated_thumbnails)`. For `.gif` inputs with `allow_animation: true`, `optimize` dispatches to `downsize_instructions_animated` (lines 137-139), which forwards to `resize_instructions_animated` (lines 115-124). That helper shells out to `gifsicle --resize-fit #{dimensions}`. gifsicle's `--resize-fit` requires pixel dimensions (`WxH`) and does not accept percentage strings like `"80%"`, so the command fails. `convert_with` swallows the failure (it only logs), the return value is ignored by the controller, the file size never decreases, and after 5 iterations the oversized file is uploaded anyway. The downsize path must either pass pixel dimensions, compute an actual size target from `max_image_size_kb`, or use an ImageMagick-only path for the size-reduction loop (the thumbnail for the post can still be done with gifsicle separately).
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: passing "80%" for animated GIF downsizing reaches gifsicle --resize-fit, which requires WxH geometry, causing downsizing to fail silently when animated thumbnails are enabled.

413 error message hardcodes 10MB instead of site limit

The 413 handler previously displayed `Discourse.SiteSettings.max_image_size_kb` in the `file_too_large` i18n message; it now displays a hardcoded `10 * 1024`. When an upload is rejected by the server because it exceeds the configured `max_image_size_kb`, the user sees the wrong limit (e.g. "10240 KB") rather than the actual configured limit, which is confusing and undermines the purpose of the setting.

Loop continues without checking whether downsize succeeded or met the target

After the downsize attempt, the controller neither checks the boolean returned by `OptimizedImage.downsize` nor verifies that `tempfile.size` actually shrank. A failure (e.g. animated GIF, broken image, ImageMagick error) leaves the file at its original size, so the `attempt > 0 && tempfile.size > SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes` guard is satisfied until `attempt` runs out, at which point `Upload.create_for` is called with an oversized file. The user receives no indication that automatic downsizing failed and the resulting upload will be rejected (or worse, stored over the limit) downstream. After the loop, the code must verify `tempfile.size <= SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes` and return an error payload (with an i18n message) when it is not.

Synchronous ImageMagick downsize runs on the upload request thread

The downsize loop runs up to five ImageMagick invocations inline in `create_upload`, which is called from `UploadsController#create` either directly (API synchronous path) or via `Scheduler::Defer` (asynchronous path). For images up to 10MB and concurrent uploads, blocking the worker on CPU-bound image processing for many seconds per upload will back up the queue and lengthen upload latency. The resize work should be moved into a dedicated background job (`Jobs.enqueue(:downsize_upload, ...)` or similar) and the controller should merely mark the upload as `pending_optimization`.

URL-downloaded tempfiles are now trusted up to 10MB before validation

`FileHelper.download` is called with `10.megabytes` instead of the previous `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes`. Combined with the new in-process downsize, any user (when `is_api?`) can submit a URL pointing to a 10MB payload, force a full download, and only then attempt downsizing. There is no rate limit, content-type check before download, or guard against repeated large fetches, so this widens the resource-exhaustion surface for the API. The download cap should remain bounded by `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb` (with a configurable, smaller multiple) rather than a hardcoded 10MB, and/or the URL path should require admin privileges.

New automatic-downsize feature has no tests

The PR adds non-trivial logic (size reduction loop, animated handling, integration with `OptimizedImage.downsize`, the new dimension-string API, and the change to URL download limits) but the changed-files list contains only production source. There are no controller specs verifying that oversized images are actually reduced, that GIFs in `allow_animation` mode are handled, that failures surface as errors, that the loop terminates, or that URL-downloaded files are bounded correctly. At minimum: a spec that an oversized PNG is downsized and accepted; a spec for an oversized animated GIF; a spec for the case where the image cannot be reduced below the limit within 5 attempts; and a spec for the JS-side validation against the site setting.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.

false_positives.candidate:
deleteCache mutation does not invalidate connectedCalendars query

Add an `expiresAt: { gte: new Date(Date.now()) }` filter (or document explicitly that the status is intentionally historical).

Existing rows get DEFAULT NOW() which misrepresents staleness

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Working hours check uses identical start/end, ignoring eventLength

In checkIfIsAvailable the local variables `start` and `end` are both set to `slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute()`. The intent is clearly to compare the slot's start and end (start + eventLength) against workingHour.startTime/endTime, but because `end` is identical to `start`, the slot's duration is never checked. A slot that begins inside the working window but extends past workingHour.endTime (e.g. a 60-min event at 16:30 with working hours 9:00-17:00, ending at 17:30) will be accepted as within working hours. This directly breaks the fixed-host round-robin fix: fixed hosts can be booked for slots that run past the end of their working hours.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: the end time is calculated from slotStartTime rather than slotEndTime, making start and end identical and failing to check whether the slot extends beyond working hours.

false_positives.candidate:
checkIfIsAvailable compares UTC slot times against organizer's timezone values

slotStartTime is computed as `time.utc()`, putting it in UTC mode, while workingHour.days/startTime/endTime and the override's start/end are in the organizer's timezone. The day-of-week test `workingHour.days.includes(slotStartTime.day())` therefore compares a UTC day against the organizer's days array, and `slotStartTime.hour()/minute()` return UTC values that are compared against minutes-since-midnight in the organizer's tz. For a host in IST (+5:30), a slot at 14:00 IST (08:30 UTC) is in workingHour.days for Monday in IST but slotStartTime.day() reports the UTC day, and slotStartTime.hour() returns 8 which is less than workingHour.startTime=540 (9:00 IST) - the slot is wrongly marked outside working hours. Same mismatch affects the override range check, so the date-override fix is broken for any non-UTC host.

Date comparison uses system local timezone, giving inconsistent results across servers

Both sides of the comparison `dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes").format("YYYY MM DD") === slotStartTime.format("YYYY MM DD")` rely on the dayjs default (system local) timezone. When the server's timezone differs from organizerTimeZone, a slot that falls on the next day in the organizer's tz can still format to the same date string as the override on a UTC server, causing an incorrect match. The PR adds `timeZone?: string` to the TimeRange type, and the router populates it from availability.timeZone (and now respects each override's own timeZone if set). For overrides whose stored timeZone differs from the host's current timeZone (e.g. user created an override while travelling), `dayjs.tz(date.start, organizerTimeZone)` will compute the wrong utcOffset and the override will be matched against the wrong time range. The type should be widened to include `timeZone?: string` and the body should prefer `date.timeZone ?? organizerTimeZone`.

The PR description and the linked issues (#8207, #8329) state that the bug being fixed is that date overrides on fixed hosts were not honoured for round-robin events. The only test added in this PR extends the existing single-user test with a second timezone check; it does not create a round-robin event type with a fixed host and a non-fixed host, set a date override on the fixed host, and assert that slots are restricted to times when the fixed host is available. Without such a test the primary fix is unverified and regressions in checkIfIsAvailable (such as the UTC/organizer-tz mismatch above) will not be caught.

The new code calls `dayjs(override.start.toString()).tz(override.timeZone).utcOffset()`. The TimeRange type declares `timeZone?: string`, and the only place in the codebase that supplies it is the trpc router (`timeZone: availability.timeZone`). If any other caller of `getSlots` (or legacy date-override rows that don't carry timeZone through whatever fetcher is used) supplies an override without timeZone, `.tz(undefined)` will fall back to the system timezone (or throw depending on dayjs-tz behaviour) and the conversion `offset = inviteeUtcOffset - organizerUtcOffset` will be wrong for every override on that event type, silently producing bogus slots. A safe fallback like `override.timeZone ?? timeZone` or requiring callers to always provide it would prevent this. true_positives.golden_comment: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Lost-update race condition on retryCount increment

Both the else branch (line 184) and the catch block (line 195) update retryCount via a read-modify-write: `retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1`. The `reminder.retryCount` value was read by the initial `findMany` at the start of the handler. If a second instance of this cron handler (or an overlapping invocation) has already updated the same row between the read and this update, the second writer will overwrite the first writer's increment using the stale value. The net retryCount will be off by at least one, causing premature (or never-triggered) deletion. The fix is to use Prisma's atomic increment: `data: { retryCount: { increment: 1 } }`, which does not require reading the current value. This is especially relevant because the cleanup at the top of the handler (line 29) will delete the row once `retryCount > 1`, so a lost update can directly cause data loss.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same stale read-modify-write race on retryCount in both the else and catch blocks and recommends the same Prisma atomic increment fix. Its additional claims about deletion consequences do not change the underlying match.

true_positives.golden_comment: The deletion logic in scheduleSMSReminders.ts incorrectly deletes non-SMS workflow reminders (e.g., Email, WhatsApp) that have retryCount > 1. This occurs because the retryCount condition within the OR clause for deletion lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing it to apply to all reminder types instead of only SMS reminders, which is the intended scope of this function.

deleteMany cleanup deletes non-SMS reminders with retryCount > 1

The new OR branch in the cleanup deleteMany (lines 38-42) deletes any WorkflowReminder with `retryCount > 1` regardless of `method`. true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same missing SMS method filter in the retryCount > 1 deletion OR branch, which can incorrectly delete non-SMS workflow reminders. The candidate also proposes the exact scoping fix described by the golden comment.

The catch block (lines 189-199) wraps the entire try body, which includes non-Twilio work: `prisma.profile.findFirst`, `getBookerBaseUrl`, `customTemplate`, `smsReminderTemplate`, and `bookingMetadataSchema.parse`. A transient failure in any of these (DB blip, malformed booking metadata, template variable missing) will increment retryCount exactly the same as a permanent Twilio failure like an invalid phone number. After 2 such transient errors the reminder is permanently deleted even though `twilio.scheduleSMS` was never reached or would have succeeded. The retry-counting should be scoped to the `twilio.scheduleSMS` call (and its returned falsy case), not the whole try block, or transient errors should not count toward the retry budget.

The else branch that increments retryCount (lines 178-187) is nested inside `if (message?.length && message?.length > 0 && sendTo)`. If `message` is empty/null or `sendTo` is missing, neither the success path nor the retryCount increment runs, but `scheduled` remains false. Such reminders will never have retryCount incremented, so they will never be cleaned up by the new `retryCount > 1` branch and will sit indefinitely (only deleted when `scheduledDate <= now`). This was a pre-existing latent issue but is now more relevant because the new cleanup logic was specifically introduced to prevent indefinite retention of unprocessable reminders. The PR introduces a non-trivial state machine: a new column, a new cleanup branch (`retryCount > 1`), and two new retryCount increments (else + catch). None of these behaviors are covered by tests. The PR description says "after scheduling failed twice we delete the workflow reminder", but the implementation starts retryCount at 0 and deletes when `retryCount > 1`, meaning the row is deleted after the second failure only on the *third* cron invocation (the third invocation's cleanup deletes it because retryCount is now 2). The initial state counts as the first attempt, so the reminder is actually scheduled twice before being given up on. If the intent is "after 2 failed attempts", the description is accurate but ambiguous; if the intent is "try once, then retry once, then give up", that's what the code does. Either way, a comment near the cleanup query documenting the semantics (`retryCount > 1` means "has already been retried once") would prevent future confusion. This is also a documentation defect because the comment on line 28 ("delete all scheduled sms reminders where scheduled date is past current date") was not updated to reflect the new OR branch.

true_positives.golden_comment: The parseRefreshTokenResponse function incorrectly sets refresh_token to the hardcoded string 'refresh_token' when it's missing from the OAuth refresh token response. This invalidates the token, breaking subsequent token refreshes and causing authentication failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Placeholder string 'refresh_token' written into credential.key.refresh_token

When the parsed response has no `refresh_token`, the code sets `refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token = "refresh_token"` (a literal placeholder). That string is then persisted into `credential.key.refresh_token` via the callers (e.g. googlecalendar `CalendarService.ts` writes `key` into the DB, office365calendar writes the merged `o365AuthCredentials`, etc.). On the next refresh cycle the placeholder will be used as the actual `refresh_token` against Google/Microsoft/etc. and will be rejected as invalid_grant, permanently breaking the credential. If the sync endpoint does not return a `refresh_token`, refresh tokens must be left undefined and the credential marked invalid instead of being silently corrupted.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: a missing refresh_token in the response is replaced with the literal string 'refresh_token', corrupting the credential and causing subsequent refresh attempts to fail.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Zod schema in parseRefreshTokenResponse uses computed property keys [z.string().toString()] and [z.string().optional().toString()] in minimumTokenResponseSchema, which is invalid Zod syntax and will throw a runtime error.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
minimumTokenResponseSchema Zod schema does not validate what the comments claim

Computed property keys in object literals evaluate to fixed strings at runtime: `[z.string().toString()]` yields the literal string `"ZodString"` (the ZodType's toString), not 'any string key'. The resulting schema is therefore `z.object({ access_token: z.string(), ZodString: z.number(), ZodOptional: z.unknown().optional() })`. Real token responses from the self-hoster's sync endpoint don't include a `ZodString` number field, so `safeParse` will fail (the required `ZodString` number is missing), throwing "Invalid refreshed tokens were returned". The comments claim it allows any number property as expiry and any other properties, but neither is true. The correct way to express that is `.catchall(z.unknown())` on the object, or leaving the schema as-is and not adding the placeholder keys.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the computed Zod property keys in minimumTokenResponseSchema as the underlying bug causing valid refresh-token responses to fail at runtime. The candidate explains the resulting fixed-key validation failure rather than describing it as invalid Zod syntax, but targets the same code issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Webhook endpoint allows writing credentials for arbitrary user IDs with a single shared secret

The endpoint authenticates the caller only with a single shared header secret (lines 24-29). Once that secret is known (it is shared by every Cal.com deployment enabling this feature and there is no per-tenant signing), any caller can POST `{userId: <int>, appSlug, keys}` and overwrite that user's credentials. `userId` is a sequential integer from the users table, so attackers can iterate. There is no per-user HMAC, no per-deployment signing key bound to the user, and no proof that the caller is authorized to manage that specific user's third-party account. Concretely this lets one compromised self-host instance push attacker-controlled OAuth tokens (which can include an `access_token` issued to the attacker's account on Google/Microsoft/Zoom/etc.) into any user's Cal.com account, which the app will then use to read/insert calendar events and create meetings on behalf of the victim. Also note the header comparison `req.headers[name] !== secret` is non-constant-time and will throw/always-fail if the header is sent twice (Next.js parses duplicate headers as an array).

SalesforceCalendarService.refreshes access token on every getClient() call

Lines 75-100 unconditionally POST to Salesforce's token endpoint inside `getClient`, then overwrite `credential.key` in the database, even when the existing access token is still valid. `getClient` is called once per service instance (line 57), so a service that is held across many operations will refresh exactly once per construction - but more importantly, every API operation that constructs a new `SalesforceCalendarService` (which is the typical usage pattern in this repo, see e.g. how other CalendarService implementations are instantiated per-call) hits Salesforce for a token refresh whether or not refresh is required. This both wastes a refresh_token use (Salesforce will eventually return `invalid_grant` once the refresh token rotates out) and can trip rate limits. Refresh should be gated on token expiry, mirroring the other integrations (`isExpired` checks before calling refresh).

fetch() to sync endpoint has no Content-Type header and no auth

The body is `new URLSearchParams({...})` but no `Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded` header is set, so the receiving server is not guaranteed to parse the body as a form (it will see an empty body in many frameworks, and `calcomUserId`/`appSlug` will be undefined server-side, making every refresh call effectively a no-op). Additionally, there is no authentication on this outbound call: the sync endpoint cannot distinguish a request coming from this Cal.com instance from any other HTTP client that knows the URL. The endpoint should at minimum require a shared secret / signature header that the self-hoster validates.

Sync endpoint HTTP errors are not detected; raw Response is returned

The function returns the `Response` object unconditionally (line 15) without checking `response.ok`. If the self-hoster's sync endpoint returns 401/403/429/500, the raw error response body is handed to downstream code as if it were a successful token response, then parsed with the (already broken) `minimumTokenResponseSchema` and discarded, leaving the credential unchanged on disk with no error logged. The caller has no way to know refresh failed. A `if (!response.ok) throw new Error(...)` is required, and the function should surface token refresh failures.

findFirst + create/update on credentials is not atomic (race condition / duplicate rows)

Lines 62-90 do a `findFirst` followed by either `update` or `create` on `prisma.credential` based on whether a row was found. There is no transaction or unique constraint check; if two webhook calls for the same (userId, appId) race (e.g. the self-hoster retries, or a user reinstalls while a webhook is in flight), both can observe no existing row and both `create`, producing two credential rows for the same user/app. Subsequent refresh/lookup code in this repo commonly uses `findFirst` for these (e.g. office365video callback line 79 does `findMany` and deletes duplicates by hand, but the webhook path does not), which means the duplicate row will be silently picked up by whichever path queries first and the other becomes dead weight (or causes the wrong row to be updated). The (userId, appId) pair needs a unique constraint or the write needs to use an upsert/transaction.

Decryption failure and bad payload not handled

`symmetricDecrypt` will throw if the encrypted blob is malformed or the key is wrong, and `JSON.parse` will throw if the decrypted plaintext is not valid JSON. Neither is caught, so the handler returns a 500 with the stack trace leaking to the caller instead of a 4xx with a clear message. Also, after a successful decrypt+parse, `keys` is `unknown` (since it is `JSON.parse(...)`); it is written to `credential.key` without any schema check (no zod, no type guard), so any JSON object - including something that isn't a valid OAuth token shape - will be persisted. At minimum the handler should validate `keys` is an object with the fields the downstream app actually expects, and wrap the decrypt+parse in try/catch returning 400.

The Salesforce integration checks `response.statusText` instead of `response.ok` when handling OAuth token refresh responses. This can lead to unreliable behavior, as a successful response may not be correctly identified, resulting in the use of stale credentials and potential authentication failures.

The `jsforce.Connection` is created using stale `credentialKey.access_token` and `credentialKey.instance_url` after a token refresh, which can lead to authentication failures and incorrect data access. Ensure that the connection is established using the refreshed token values instead.

The `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse` function can throw on invalid payloads, resulting in 500 Internal Server Errors instead of the expected 400 Bad Request responses. This can lead to confusion for clients and hinder proper error handling.

The non-paid branch correctly uses `await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes));` at line 652. This should be `await Promise.all(apiDeletes);`. When called with multiple credentials (e.g. from `getBusyVideoTimes`), the dynamic imports run sequentially rather than concurrently. Since dynamic imports are independent I/O operations (Webpack fetches chunks in parallel), this serializes what could be parallel work. The previous synchronous reduce was effectively zero-cost per iteration, but the new version pays the full latency of each import sequentially. Using `Promise.all(withCredentials.map(...))` would allow the chunks to load concurrently, reducing total latency.

replaceFirst only removes the first occurrence of a repeated anchor

`value.replaceFirst(Pattern.quote(englishMatcher.group()), "")` only replaces the FIRST match in `value`, not all matches. If a translation legitimately reuses the same anchor tag more than once and the English source only has one occurrence, only the first occurrence is stripped; the remaining occurrences are then passed to the OWASP sanitizer, which (with `POLICY_SOME_HTML` not allowing `<a>`) will escape them and produce a spurious "Illegal HTML" error. The candidate describes a translation with repeated anchors beyond what the English source has, which leads to wrong validation (spurious errors). It also mentions the 'Didn't find anchor tag' error and the stale matcher. That is closely related: mismatched anchor counts between translation and English causing incorrect results. The candidate focuses on replaceFirst rather than unvalidated matcher consumption, but the scenario and outcome are essentially the same.

false_positives.candidate:
Regex character class too broad due to '-' being treated as range operator

The regex `replaceAll("_[a-zA-Z-_]*\\.properties", "_en.properties")` contains the character class `[a-zA-Z-_]`. In Java regex, the dash '-' that is not at the start or end of the class and not escaped is interpreted as a range operator. With the previous 'A-Z' range ending at 'Z' (0x5A), the '-_' is parsed as a range from 'Z' (0x5A) to '_' (0x5F), which silently adds '[', '\', ']', '^', and '_' to the matched character set. The author clearly intended `[a-zA-Z_]` (or `[a-zA-Z_-]` with '-' placed last so it is a literal). For typical locale codes (letters + underscore) this happens to work, but the regex is incorrect and could match unintended characters in path components containing '[', '\', etc. Fix by writing `[a-zA-Z_-]` (dash at the end of the class, making it literal) or `[a-zA-Z_]`.

Comment mischaracterises '<1>' as a "numeric tag"

The comment states the sanitizer escapes 'numeric tags like `<1>`'. There is no concept of a numeric tag in HTML or in the OWASP sanitizer; the sanitizer simply treats the literal text `<1>` as an invalid HTML tag (because tag names must start with a letter per the policy) and escapes the '<' and '>' characters. `<1>` here is an i18next / React-Intl style indexed placeholder, not a numeric tag. The wording will mislead future maintainers about what the sanitizer is doing and why `<1>` survives the round-trip via `unescapeHtml4`.

Breaking change to i18next escape syntax in JS-side resource bundle

The value of `error-invalid-multivalued-size` was changed from `Attribute {{0}} must have at least {{1}} and at most {{2}} value(s).` to `Attribute {0} must have at least {1} and at most {2} {2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}.`. The double-brace form `{{0}}` / `{{1}}` / `{{2}}` is i18next's escape syntax for producing literal `{0}`/`{1}`/`{2}` text, which is what account-ui uses. After this change, i18next will interpret `{0}`, `{1}`, `{2}` and the `{2,choice,...}` clause as placeholders / interpolation tokens. i18next does not implement Java MessageFormat choice format, and `{2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}` is not valid i18next interpolation syntax, so the message will either fail to interpolate or be displayed verbatim with broken `{...}` text instead of the localized error. The previous value (`value(s)`) was a deliberate, working i18next-compatible rendering of the message; this PR regresses that. The new format belongs only on the Java side (e.g. `themes/src/main/resources/theme/base/login/messages/messages_en.properties`), where it does belong.

Same i18next breaking change in admin-ui resource bundle

Same regression as in the account-ui bundle: `error-invalid-multivalued-size` changed from `Attribute {{0}} must have at least {{1}} and at most {{2}} value(s).` to Java MessageFormat syntax (`{0}`, `{1}`, `{2,choice,...}`). The admin-ui is also a React/i18next app, so the change replaces working placeholder-escaping with placeholders that i18next will try to interpolate, and embeds a Java MessageFormat choice clause (`{2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}`) that i18next does not understand. Result at runtime: malformed interpolation and/or broken/untranslated text shown to the admin user.

No positive test that valid HTML in a translation is accepted The four new tests only assert that illegal HTML is detected (`verifyIllegalHtmlTagDetected`, `verifyNoHtmlAllowed`, `verifyNoChangedAnchors`) and that duplicates are detected. There is no positive test that exercises the happy path of `verifySafeHtml`: e.g. an English value containing `bar` and a translation containing `bar` (or `bar`) that should NOT be reported. Without it, a regression in the sanitizer flow (e.g. always escaping ``) would not be caught by the test suite. Add a test resource pair (`allowedHtml_en.properties` + `allowedHtml_de.properties`) with matching allowed tags and assert that the message list does not contain "Illegal HTML".

No test for the `{2,choice,...}` normalization of `error-invalid-multivalued-size`

`normalizeValue` strips `{N,choice,...}` clauses for `linkExpirationFormatter.timePeriodUnit.*` and `error-invalid-multivalued-size` specifically. This special case is central to the PR because that key was just rewritten across every bundle to use this Java MessageFormat choice syntax. There is no test fixture nor assertion that (a) a translation whose choice clause differs from the English (e.g. different `1#value|1<values` text) is still accepted, and (b) a translation with literal `<` outside a choice clause is rejected. The whole point of this PR is to make `error-invalid-multivalued-size` valid, but the only protection against regressing it is the production code itself, with no regression test in `VerifyMessagePropertiesTest`.

File is read and parsed twice per verification

`verify()` reads the file with `Files.readString(file.toPath())` for duplicate-key detection, and then `verifySafeHtml()` opens another `FileInputStream` and parses the same file as `PropertyResourceBundle`. The two reads produce no consistency guarantee (a file could change between reads) and double the I/O. Either parse once into a `PropertyResourceBundle` and reuse it for both checks, or read the bytes once and wrap them in two parsers. Not a correctness bug, but the verifier runs over hundreds of message bundles during a theme build, so the duplication is non-trivial.

Trailing newline stripped from `error-invalid-multivalued-size`

The unified diff shows the file ends with `\ No newline at end of file` after this change (the `-` line also had `\ No newline at end of file`). Many editors, linters, and POSIX text tools require files to end with a newline, and several Keycloak bundles historically did so. The fact that the previous version ended without a newline was already a minor smell, but the change also touches a line at the end of the file without restoring the newline. This will show up as a noisy diff in future PRs and may violate any project policy on POSIX file endings.

`public static final String GRANT_TYPE = OAuth2Constants.GRANT_TYPE;` resolves to the literal string `"grant_type"`, which is a key name used as a `ClientSessionContext` attribute key, not a grant-type value. The name suggests a grant type such as `authorization_code`. `getTokenContextFromTokenId(String encodedTokenId)` immediately calls `encodedTokenId.indexOf(':')` with no null check. It should guard against null and treat it the same as an old (unprefixed) id.

`clientSessionContext.getClientSession().getUserSession()` is dereferenced for both `getPersistenceState()` and `isOffline()` without a null check. Both `getShortcutByGrantType` and `getGrantTypeByShortcut` do a non-atomic check-then-put into the `ConcurrentHashMap`s. Two threads can simultaneously take the `null` branch and both write. Here the same code can be reused indefinitely, so the security guarantee of recovery codes is lost whenever the user lives in federated storage.

Because `isValid()` does not track per-code consumption, the `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel` built by `getCredentials()` from the stored raw `credentialData` will always have `allCodesUsed() == false`. The local `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider` hashes the codes before storage (it relies on `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.hashRawCode` with `NOM_ALGORITHM_TO_HASH`). Storing raw codes in `credentialData` diverges from that posture, so any path that exposes `credentialData` (DB dumps, debug logging, serialized credential model) leaks the user's recovery codes in plaintext. The model reconstructed by `getCredentials()` will also carry these raw codes through `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues`, so callers that read `RecoveryCode.getValue()` get the cleartext code.

`testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin` only exercises a single successful entry of one recovery code. The new test only asserts `len(flusher.processes) == 2`, `flusher.max_processes == 2`, `flusher.num_processes == 2` and that 4 shards are present in `process_to_shards_map`. It does not submit a payload, does not advance drift, and does not assert that any segment reaches the `produce_to_pipe`. The whole point of the multiprocess refactor is that shards split across processes are still flushed end-to-end; this test will silently pass even if the new `_create_process_for_shards` does not correctly wire shards to buffers or if the threading path is broken. Add at least one submit + flush assertion that exercises the cross-process flusher wiring.

`if not process:` guard in `_ensure_processes_alive` is dead

`self.processes` is populated in `_create_process_for_shards` and never has `None` values, so `if not process: continue` (line 222) is unreachable. Either remove the check or, if the intent was to skip dead slots, document why None entries would ever appear (e.g., a future graceful-shutdown slot).

Per-submit Redis memory probe now scales with process count

Original code did one `self.buffer.get_memory_info()` call per submit. New code iterates `for buffer in self.buffers.values(): memory_infos.extend(buffer.get_memory_info())`, so the consumer issues N Redis probes per submit where N equals the number of flusher processes (up to one per shard). Even though `submit` is described as not hot, on every call we now do N network round-trips to gather data that conceptually represents the same underlying Redis memory. Consider caching or aggregating memory info once per flush cycle instead of once per submit.

`process.kill()` followed by immediate respawn can produce duplicate flushes

In `_ensure_processes_alive`, the unhealthy process is `kill()`-ed (non-blocking) and `_create_process_for_shards` is invoked immediately. The old subprocess may still be alive for some time (kill delivery, Redis I/O in flight), during which both the old and new flusher processes can independently call `buffer.flush_segments` and `producer.produce` on the same shard. That can produce duplicate `BUFFERED_SEGMENTS` messages on Kafka. The original code had a similar race but only one flusher existed; now that shards are shared across processes, the blast radius is wider. Consider `process.join(timeout)` before respawn, or use `terminate()` plus a join so the previous process truly exits first.

`process_restarts` threshold allows one more restart than the constant suggests

The check is `if self.process_restarts[process_index] > MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS`, followed by increment + respawn. Tracing the counter: it starts at 0, is checked then incremented. With `MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS = 10` the counter reaches 11 before `11 > 10` triggers, so the consumer actually restarts the process 11 times before raising, not 10. This is an off-by-one that pre-dates this PR, but it is worth aligning either the constant (to `MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS - 1`) or the comparison (`>= MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS`) so the cap matches the name.

true_positives.golden_comment: The OptimizedCursorPaginator in organization_auditlogs.py attempts to use negative slice offsets on Django querysets, but Django querysets do not support negative slicing and will raise an AssertionError.

None of these are true: Django translates `queryset[-N:M]` into `LIMIT (M-N) OFFSET -N`, which PostgreSQL rejects as a non-positive OFFSET, so the request 500s. The framing of 'efficient bidirectional pagination' misrepresents what negative slicing does — it returns the last N rows of the queryset, not an arbitrary position. The 'safe because permissions' justification conflates row-level authorization (which the queryset already enforces) with pagination-boundary integrity; allowing a client to choose a negative offset bypasses the `offset >= 0` invariant that BasePaginator and the rest of the pagination pipeline assume. The whole branch should be removed; it adds no legitimate functionality and exists only behind a parameter that is already gated to superusers, which makes the misleading comments more concerning.

true_positives.golden_comment: get_item_key assumes a numeric key, but the paginator is used with order_by=-datetime in the audit logs endpoint; calling math.floor/ceil on a datetime will raise a TypeError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator crashes with datetime ordering

OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key does `value = getattr(item, self.key)` and then `int(math.floor(value) ... )`. When used with `order_by="-datetime"` (as the new audit-logs endpoint does), `value` is a `datetime` object, and `math.floor(datetime)` raises `TypeError: float argument required, not datetime.datetime`. The existing DateTimePaginator has special handling (`float(value.strftime("%s.%f")) * self.multiplier`) for exactly this reason; OptimizedCursorPaginator is essentially a copy of `Paginator` (numeric-only) and is not a drop-in replacement for DateTimePaginator. The new `?optimized_pagination=true` path on the audit logs endpoint will 500 for any superuser/global-admin caller.

OptimizedCursorPaginator.value_from_cursor returns raw timestamp instead of datetime

The caller (BasePaginator.build_queryset) substitutes it into `WHERE <col> <= %s`, producing a comparison between a `datetime` column and an integer like `... WHERE datetime <= 1699999999000`, which PostgreSQL rejects with `operator does not exist: timestamp without time zone >= integer`. DateTimePaginator converts the integer back to a datetime; OptimizedCursorPaginator does not. Together with the get_item_key issue, the optimized audit-logs path is broken end-to-end.

The diff replaces `results = list(queryset[offset:stop])` with `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` and `results = list(queryset[start_offset:stop])`. This is a behavior change on a shared base class that affects every paginator inheriting from BasePaginator (DateTimePaginator, Paginator, MergingOffsetPaginator callers, etc.), not just the new OptimizedCursorPaginator. The PR title and description only mention audit logs and contain no mention of this base-class change, so reviewers of the other endpoints will not see it. The accompanying comment ('allow negative offsets to enable efficient bidirectional pagination') is the opposite of what the code does for non-prev cursors — it clamps negative offsets to 0, restricting rather than allowing them. Gating behind `is_superuser or has_global_access` does not mitigate these issues; it just limits who sees the 500s. A security-relevant control surface (pagination of the audit log) is being routed through a new, untested code path with multiple bugs and a misleadingly-commented 'advanced' feature.

The PR introduces a new paginator class with non-trivial behavior (enable_advanced_features flag, negative-offset branch, datetime-incompatible get_item_key/value_from_cursor) and modifies BasePaginator.get_result, but adds no tests. There are no tests covering: (1) the optimized audit-logs endpoint path, (2) pagination of datetime-ordered querysets through OptimizedCursorPaginator, (3) the negative-offset branch under enable_advanced_features, (4) the new max(0, offset) clamping in BasePaginator for non-prev cursors. With the new finer-grained locking, two callers that race through `getOrCreateIndex` for the same key when `size > b.opts.FileThreshold` will both call `bleve.New(dir, mapper)` on the same directory. bleve's New on an already-existing directory either errors or reopens stale state; one call returns an error to a caller even though the index they wanted was successfully created and is sitting in the cache. `searchSupport.getOrCreateIndex` already has a TODO admitting it has no per-key mutex, so this relaxation of the backend's serialization makes a known race easier to trigger. It still identifies the same underlying unsynchronized map iteration in TotalDocs and the same panic risk, and proposes the fix of taking the lock.

After this change, both `searchSupport.init` (lines ~202-213 in search.go) and `server.initWatcher` (line 752) each call `s.backend.WatchWriteEvents(...)`, which for the SQL backend (`pkg/storage/unified/sql/backend.go:558`) starts its own 100 ms poller goroutine. The `errgroup` already sets the search index up; now the broadcaster independently starts a second poller querying the same resource history tables. Two pollers every 100 ms doubles DB load, doubles history scans, and produces two independent `mostRecentRV` writers and two event streams. The order swap (initWatcher first vs. search.init first) does not change this — both sequences still leave the search support's watcher running alongside `initWatcher`. The author's stated goal was just to parallelize index build across distinct keys; the duplicate watcher is unrelated and should be removed (let the search support's handler pipe into the broadcaster, or use the broadcaster as the single event source).

The diff adds `if dbType == "postgres" { t.Skip(...) }` to the only integration test that exercises the storage server target with a real DB. A `t.Skip` is the wrong fix here: the test should be made to pass for both `Init()` orderings, or split so that the storage-server integration is verified separately for postgres. `NewResourceServer` now passes its locally constructed `ctx` (a `context.WithCancel(context.Background(), ...)` wrapping a static service-account identity) into `s.Init(ctx)`. Those calls now use a context that lives for the lifetime of the server and is only cancelled when `s.Stop` runs — they never see a deadline or the caller's cancellation. The previous per-handler `s.Init(ctx)` propagated the per-request deadline/cancellation, so a hung DB could be aborted by closing the test context. With the eager call, an unresponsive backend during index build will block `NewResourceServer` indefinitely, which in turn blocks module startup with no way to cancel it from outside.

false_positives.candidate:
Unbounded queues with no backpressure despite docstring claim

In `FixedQueuePool.__init__`, each work queue is created with `queue.Queue()` (no maxsize). The class docstring promises 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up', but there is no fill - the queues are infinite. If a single group is slow or backed up (e.g. one subscription id hashes to the same queue and processing of one item blocks for a long time, or that group simply gets a burst of messages), items accumulate forever. Each `WorkItem` holds a reference to the original `Message` (and therefore the decoded `result` plus `KafkaPayload`), so the memory footprint is non-trivial. An unbounded queue in front of a single-worker-per-queue setup is a straightforward OOM risk and contradicts the docstring.

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.join ignores its timeout parameter

`SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.join(self, timeout: float | None = None)` accepts a timeout but does not use it - it just calls `self.close()`. The arroyo framework passes a deadline via this argument so it knows how long to wait for graceful shutdown before forcefully terminating. By ignoring the timeout the strategy can exceed the caller's deadline, causing the consumer to be killed by the orchestrator and any in-flight offsets to be left as 'outstanding' (forcing re-delivery on the next start). `join` should propagate `timeout` to `self.commit_thread.join(timeout=...)` and to `FixedQueuePool.shutdown`/worker joins, and `close()` should also respect a deadline.

commit_function failure leaves offsets un-committed in the tracker and is silently retried forever

In `_commit_loop`, `self.commit_function(committable)` is called and only on success does the loop mark the offsets via `mark_committed`. If the commit raises (Kafka unavailable, broker timeout, etc.), the whole `except Exception` just logs and the same offsets are returned by the next `get_committable_offsets()` call and retried. Two problems: (1) if the commit partially succeeded before raising, the same offsets get re-committed to Kafka (duplicate commit), and (2) there is no backoff or alerting, so a persistent failure becomes an infinite tight retry loop that floods the logs and pegs CPU. The metric `remote_subscriptions.queue_pool.offsets_committed` is also incremented before the commit call, so it counts 'attempted' rather than 'succeeded' commits, which is misleading.

get_committable_offsets does an O(max_offset) scan per partition

`get_committable_offsets` iterates `for offset in range(start, max_offset + 1)` looking for the highest contiguous committed offset. If a partition has a small offset (e.g. 100) and a very large one (e.g. 1_000_000) - whether from a bug, rebalance after restart, or just a sparse stream - this allocates and walks ~1M ints per call, every second, from the commit thread. For a multi-partition topic with any sparse offsets this can dominate CPU. The check should walk the sorted `outstanding` set instead of scanning the integer range.

Group-to-queue assignment uses Python's randomized hash()

`get_queue_for_group` is `return hash(group_key) % self.num_queues`. Python's built-in `hash()` for strings is salted by `PYTHONHASHSEED` and is therefore not stable across processes. Within a single consumer lifetime the assignment is consistent (so per-group ordering is preserved), but after a restart the same subscription id may land on a different queue and worker. This is undocumented and brittle - if anything ever relies on a stable group->queue mapping across restarts (e.g. for deterministic drain order on partial shutdown, or for replay tooling), it will silently break. Use a stable hash like `hashlib.md5(group_key.encode()).digest()` or `zlib.crc32(group_key.encode())`.

submit() silently drops messages whose value is not a BrokerValue when an error occurs

In `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit`, the `except Exception` handler only marks the offset complete when `isinstance(message.value, BrokerValue)`. If the message value is anything else (e.g. an `ImpulseValue` or any future arroyo value type) and either the decoder raises or the `assert isinstance(message.value, BrokerValue)` itself fails, the offset is never recorded. The message disappears from the strategy but arroyo will not have been told to commit it, so on restart the same message is re-delivered. If the failure is permanent (e.g. the codec can never decode that value type) this becomes an infinite redelivery of poison messages, with no observability beyond the one log entry.

Redirect-follow loop limit lowered from 10000 to 1000 silently breaks deep segment trees

The previous code used `for i = 0, 10000 do` and carried a comment explaining that exceeding this limit means segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly. The new code lowers the bound to `for i = 0, 1000 do` without any rationale, so any trace whose redirect chain exceeds 1000 hops will resolve to a `set_span_id` that is not the true root. The subsequent `zunionstore`/`zpopmin` will then operate on the wrong set, leaving the actual root segment orphaned and producing an incomplete or empty flushed segment. This is a silent data-integrity regression for deep traces.

Default SUM aggregate in ZUNIONSTORE corrupts `end_timestamp_precise` scores for duplicate payloads

`zunionstore set_key 2 set_key span_key` is invoked with the implicit default `AGGREGATE SUM`. If a member (span payload) ever exists in both `set_key` and `span_key` (which can occur on Kafka retries or any path where the same payload was inserted twice with different timestamps), its score after the union becomes the arithmetic sum of the two timestamps rather than either one. Those scores drive eviction (`zpopmin`) and any downstream ordering; a corrupted score means the wrong spans get evicted and the 'oldest-first' eviction contract is broken. The script should pass an explicit `AGGREGATE MIN` (or `MAX`) to preserve a single timestamp per payload.

`Span` is a public NamedTuple exported from `sentry.spans.buffer`. The new `end_timestamp_precise: float` is inserted between `payload` and `is_segment_span`, has no default, and shifts `is_segment_span` to the last position. Any caller that constructs `Span(...)` positionally (the 7th argument previously implied `is_segment_span`) will silently mis-bind: a positional `True` becomes the `end_timestamp_precise` value and `is_segment_span` defaults to `False`, causing incorrect is-segment logic downstream. It also breaks unpickling of old `Span` pickles and any external code that mirrors this shape. The field should be added at the end (with a default) or supplied only via keyword to preserve positional compatibility.

Removed `max_segment_spans` Python guard while Lua hardcodes a different (1000) limit

The old `_load_segment_data` had `if len(payloads[key]) > self.max_segment_spans: ... skip segment`. This guard is deleted, so the only cap on segment size is the new Lua eviction at line 62 (`if span_count > 1000 then redis.call('zpopmin', set_key, span_count - 1000) end`).
